study_design: Longitudinal cohort with unsupervised clustering (k-means) across baseline to 3-year follow-up (ABCD Study)
population: 5,501 youth assessed from approximately ages 9-10 to 12-13
exposure_intervention: Data-driven executive function profiles from Stop Signal and Emotional N-Back tasks
comparator: Higher executive function cluster versus lower executive function cluster
outcome: CBCL attention problems, aggressive and rule-breaking behaviour, ADHD diagnosis
main_result: Lower executive function cluster membership was associated with greater attention problems concurrently and longitudinally and with more ADHD diagnoses, with no association to aggressive or rule-breaking behaviour, but effects were small and cluster membership was only moderately stable over time.

major_limitations: Very small effect sizes; only moderate temporal stability of EF profiles; parent-reported behavioural outcomes; community sample limiting clinical extrapolation.
individual_applicability: Supports a specific but weak developmental link between objective executive performance and attention problems; the small effects argue against strong inference from lab tasks to individual life outcomes.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised longitudinal cohort with objective tasks, downgraded for small effects, modest profile stability and single-informant outcomes.

study_design: Retrospective observational cohort with 24-month follow-up and exploratory association-rule analysis
population: 583 patients aged 4-18 years attending a first psychiatric emergency visit in Spain (2017-2023); median age 14.9 years
exposure_intervention: Baseline emergency psychiatric diagnosis
comparator: Same patients at 24-month follow-up (within-person diagnostic transition)
outcome: Diagnostic stability and transition patterns
main_result: Diagnostic stability was heterogeneous, high for schizophrenia/psychosis (71%) and low for ADHD and eating disorders, with a notable transition pattern from autism plus ADHD to conduct disorders.

major_limitations: Emergency-service sample with atypical case mix; diagnostic label stability is not the same as symptom or impairment persistence; retrospective electronic record extraction; no standardised reassessment protocol.
individual_applicability: Cautions that clinical diagnostic labels applied in crisis settings shift substantially over two years, relevant to interpreting any single diagnostic formulation.
quality_reason: Retrospective single-centre record review with a selected emergency population and outcome that only indirectly indexes trait persistence.

citation: Yuan You, Tom McAdams, Yasmin I Ahmadzadeh, Tabea Schoeler, Filip Marzecki, Helena M S Zavos. Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines. 2026;67(2):183-201. doi:10.1111/jcpp.70028. PMID:40801243.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel random-effects models; 26 studies
population: Children with ADHD followed to later developmental stages
exposure_intervention: Childhood comorbid internalizing, externalizing and neurodevelopmental conditions
comparator: ADHD without the specified comorbidity
outcome: Persistence of ADHD symptoms into later developmental stages
main_result: Childhood externalizing and, more weakly, internalizing comorbidity predicted ADHD persistence, but adjustment attenuated externalizing and eliminated the internalizing association; neurodevelopmental comorbidity did not predict persistence, and the externalizing effect appeared only with parent-reported data.
effect_estimate: Internalizing d=0.19 (adjusted d=0.06, non-significant); externalizing d=0.31 (adjusted d=0.24); neurodevelopmental comorbidity non-significant
major_limitations: Informant-dependent findings suggest common-method bias; residual confounding acknowledged; heterogeneous definitions of persistence and follow-up intervals.
individual_applicability: Shows persistence estimates are sensitive to comorbidity and informant, relevant given this individual's reported anxiety, mood and substance history.
quality_reason: Appropriate multilevel synthesis with adjusted analyses, limited by observational primary data and informant confounding.

study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022320887); 36 studies, 119 predictors, 10 meta-analysed
population: Adults diagnosed with ADHD in childhood
exposure_intervention: Childhood predictors including IQ, stimulant treatment history, symptom subtype, comorbidity, socioeconomic status
comparator: Adults with remitted versus persistent childhood ADHD; predictor contrasts within cohorts
outcome: ADHD persistence into adulthood; substance use disorder; major depressive disorder
main_result: Higher childhood IQ was associated with slightly lower odds of adult ADHD persistence, while stimulant treatment history was associated with higher persistence; persistence itself predicted substance use disorder and major depressive disorder.

individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether high intelligence signals masked persistence or genuine remission, but the IQ association is tiny and group-level.
quality_reason: Preregistered meta-analysis with quality appraisal, downgraded for observational primary studies, confounding, and small numbers of studies per predictor.

study_design: Preregistered systematic review of neuroimaging studies; 13 studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal
population: Adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD
exposure_intervention: ADHD diagnosis, symptom load or polygenic risk
comparator: Non-ADHD control participants
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations; cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD-associated fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic alterations persisted into middle and older adulthood, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation interpreted as compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR; 11 of 13 studies rated low risk of bias

individual_applicability: Consistent with a neurodevelopmental substrate persisting in adulthood, but neuroimaging group differences cannot diagnose or characterise one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with formal risk-of-bias appraisal and mostly low-risk studies, downgraded for few studies and indirect outcomes.

study_design: Retrospective chart review with 2-year follow-up of records
population: 174 adults diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood at a Korean tertiary university hospital (mean age 25.1; 73.6% male)
exposure_intervention: First ADHD diagnosis made in adulthood
comparator: None (single-cohort descriptive)
outcome: Presenting complaint, psychiatric comorbidity, medication adherence and persistence
main_result: Only 56.3% presented because of ADHD symptoms, with others presenting with interpersonal problems or depressed mood; 76.4% had at least one psychiatric comorbidity; adherence above 80% occurred in fewer than half, and persistence beyond one year was uncommon.
effect_estimate: 56.3% ADHD-related chief complaint; 76.4% comorbidity; 42.6% (methylphenidate) and 40.0% (atomoxetine) adherence >80%; 13.8% and 18.2% persistence >365 days
major_limitations: Single-site retrospective chart review without comparison group; referral and documentation bias; adult-onset recognition may reflect service access rather than masking.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that adult-first recognition of ADHD is common and frequently occurs via other presenting complaints, a pattern that resembles this narrative but does not explain its cause.
quality_reason: Uncontrolled retrospective case series at one centre; descriptive only and vulnerable to selection bias.

citation: Natividad Pardo-Palenzuela, Iban Onandia-Hinchado, Unai Diaz-Orueta. Cognitive Profile of ADHD in Older Adults: A Systematic Review. Journal of attention disorders. 2026;30(1):152-162. doi:10.1177/10870547251385758. PMID:41146423.

population: Adults aged 50 and older with a confirmed ADHD diagnosis
exposure_intervention: ADHD diagnosis in older adulthood
comparator: Older healthy controls and younger adults with ADHD
outcome: Attention, episodic memory, executive functions including working memory

quality_reason: Narrative synthesis of few, mostly cross-sectional studies with heterogeneous instruments and no pooled estimates.

Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2026;28(1):259-276. doi:10.1080/19585969.2026.2700984. PMID:42472451.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review of neuroimaging studies; 13 studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal
population: Adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD
exposure_intervention: ADHD diagnosis, symptom load or polygenic risk
comparator: Non-ADHD control participants
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations; cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD-associated fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic alterations persisted into middle and older adulthood, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation interpreted as compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR; 11 of 13 studies rated low risk of bias
major_limitations: Small number of heterogeneous studies; compensation is an interpretation of activation patterns, not a measured behavioural compensation outcome; cross-sectional designs predominate.
individual_applicability: Consistent with a neurodevelopmental substrate persisting in adulthood, but neuroimaging group differences cannot diagnose or characterise one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with formal risk-of-bias appraisal and mostly low-risk studies, downgraded for few studies and indirect outcomes.

citation: Seong Ae Lee, Ah Rah Lee, Nan-He Yoon, Chae-Bin Kim, Geon Ho Bahn, Miae Oh. Effectiveness of Group Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and the Role of Cognitive Ability in Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Psychiatry investigation. 2025;22(11):1267-1276. doi:10.30773/pi.2025.0184. PMID:41089022.
study_design: Retrospective pre-post analysis of a 10-session group CBT programme, no control group
population: 24 adults with ADHD who completed group CBT in South Korea
exposure_intervention: Structured group CBT; subgroup stratification by full-scale IQ, attendance and comorbid depression
comparator: Pre-treatment baseline; IQ subgroups (below-average, average 90-109, high)
outcome: ADHD symptoms (ASRS, K-AARS) and functional impairment (K-AARS impairment subscale)
main_result: Clinically significant ADHD symptoms and functional impairment were present and improved across all IQ strata, including above-average IQ, with the most consistent improvement in the average-IQ subgroup and greater improvement with higher attendance.
effect_estimate: NR; significance reported without effect sizes or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Very small uncontrolled retrospective sample; multiple subgroup comparisons; regression to the mean and expectancy effects; no measure of effort or compensation.
individual_applicability: Weakly consistent with impairment coexisting with higher measured ability, but the sample is too small to support inference about high-achieving adults.
quality_reason: Uncontrolled retrospective design, n=24, no effect estimates, and post hoc IQ subgrouping.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Jaap Oosterlaan, Marjolein Luman. Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Predictors of Adult Psychiatric Outcomes of Childhood Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2026;65(2):231-249. doi:10.1016/j.jaac.2025.04.012. PMID:40287009.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022320887); 36 studies, 119 predictors, 10 meta-analysed
population: Adults diagnosed with ADHD in childhood
exposure_intervention: Childhood predictors including IQ, stimulant treatment history, symptom subtype, comorbidity, socioeconomic status
comparator: Adults with remitted versus persistent childhood ADHD; predictor contrasts within cohorts
outcome: ADHD persistence into adulthood; substance use disorder; major depressive disorder
main_result: Higher childhood IQ was associated with slightly lower odds of adult ADHD persistence, while stimulant treatment history was associated with higher persistence; persistence itself predicted substance use disorder and major depressive disorder.
effect_estimate: Childhood IQ OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.00, p=.039); stimulant history OR 1.88 (1.28-2.75); persistence to SUD OR 2.12 (1.53-3.17); to MDD OR 3.19 (1.71-5.95)
major_limitations: Authors note methodological shortcomings across the literature; confounding by indication for stimulant history; IQ effect per-unit and near-null; heterogeneity and NOS quality mixed.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether high intelligence signals masked persistence or genuine remission, but the IQ association is tiny and group-level.
quality_reason: Preregistered meta-analysis with quality appraisal, downgraded for observational primary studies, confounding, and small numbers of studies per predictor.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

citation: Ana Muiño Tato. Systematic Review of Autism in Women: Invisibilised Profiles and Gender Bias. Revista de neurologia. 2026;81(4):49367. doi:10.31083/RN49367. PMID:42052784.
study_design: Systematic review of 26 studies (2015-2025) spanning observational, psychometric, technological, quasi-experimental and qualitative designs
population: Females assessed for or diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder
exposure_intervention: Female sex, social camouflaging, and standard diagnostic instruments
comparator: Males assessed for autism; standard versus gender-sensitive assessment approaches
outcome: Age at diagnosis, diagnostic identification rates, instrument sensitivity
main_result: Diagnosis was consistently delayed in girls, standard instruments showed reduced sensitivity to less externalizing presentations, and social camouflaging plus comorbidity moderated identification, indicating that compensation-related processes can delay recognition.
effect_estimate: NR; reported male-to-female diagnostic ratios up to 4.6:1 in the Spanish educational context; mean CRF-QS quality 15.7
major_limitations: Autism rather than ADHD; camouflaging largely inferred from self-report and clinical observation; heterogeneous designs preclude pooling; no direct measure of intelligence as the compensating factor.
individual_applicability: Supports delayed recognition through compensation as a real phenomenon, but the demonstrated driver is gendered presentation and instrument sensitivity, not high intelligence.
quality_reason: PRISMA-based review with quality appraisal and predominantly low risk of bias, downgraded for construct heterogeneity and indirectness to intelligence-specific masking.

citation: Pu Peng, Zhangming Chen, Silan Ren, Ying He, Jinguang Li, Aijun Liao, et al. Peer bullying victimisation and depressive symptoms as serial mediators between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms and internet gaming disorder among Chinese adolescents: A three-wave longitudinal study. General psychiatry. 2026;39(1):e70012. doi:10.1002/gps3.70012. PMID:41890162.
study_design: Three-wave prospective longitudinal cohort with serial mediation path analysis, cross-lagged and latent growth sensitivity models
population: 20,137 Chinese adolescents assessed at baseline (Nov 2020) and at 1- and 2-year follow-up
exposure_intervention: Baseline ADHD symptoms (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire)
comparator: Within-cohort variation in ADHD symptoms, adjusted for baseline covariates and prior symptom levels
outcome: Peer bullying victimisation (Multidimensional Peer Victimisation Scale), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), internet gaming disorder severity
main_result: Baseline ADHD symptoms predicted later internet gaming disorder severity both directly and indirectly through peer bullying victimisation and then depressive symptoms; the bullying pathway was present only in boys and early adolescents while depressive symptoms mediated across sex and age groups.
effect_estimate: Mediators accounted for approximately one third of the total effect; individual path coefficients NR
major_limitations: ADHD ascertained by screening scale rather than clinical diagnosis; all self-report measures (common-method bias); single-country school sample; primary distal outcome is gaming disorder rather than social functioning per se.
individual_applicability: Supports temporal ordering from ADHD symptoms to peer victimisation and mood symptoms in adolescence, but the sample is neither adult nor diagnostically confirmed.
quality_reason: Very large three-wave design with prior-symptom adjustment and multiple sensitivity analyses, weakened by scale-based ADHD definition and reliance on self-report.

citation: Yi Gao, Guojuan Chen, Jiangping Wang, Cuiwei Yang, Rongwang Yang, Kewen Jiang. The role of executive function for differentiating symptoms of ADHD in preschoolers. BMC pediatrics. 2026;26(1):112. doi:10.1186/s12887-025-06465-z. PMID:41507887.
study_design: Cross-sectional clinical study with correlation, multiple linear regression and ROC analyses
population: 141 preschoolers aged 4-5 years with ADHD
exposure_intervention: Executive function (BRIEF-P) and motor coordination (Developmental Coordination Disorder Questionnaire, Chinese version)
comparator: Within-sample associations across symptom severity; no non-ADHD control group
outcome: ADHD symptoms (SNAP-IV), social skills (PEOPSS), communication interest
main_result: ADHD symptoms were significantly associated with executive function, motor coordination, social skills and communication interest; working memory discriminated inattention, the Inhibitory Self-Control Index discriminated oppositional symptoms, and Plan/Organize discriminated hyperactivity-impulsivity more weakly.
effect_estimate: AUC 0.854 (working memory for inattention); AUC 0.852 (ISCI for oppositional symptoms); AUC 0.719 (Plan/Organize for hyperactivity-impulsivity)
major_limitations: No comparison group; all predictors and outcomes parent-rated (common-method bias); cross-sectional; preschool sample precludes inference about adult functioning; motor coordination by questionnaire rather than performance test.
individual_applicability: Documents co-variation of ADHD symptoms with parent-rated motor coordination and social skills, but in preschoolers and without separating motor difficulty from attention.
quality_reason: Single-site cross-sectional design without controls and with entirely informant-report measurement.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies, with multiple regression on pooled correlation matrices to control symptom overlap
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples; total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Symptom dimensions of ADHD-inattention (ADHD-I), ADHD-hyperactivity/impulsivity (ADHD-HI) and cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS)
comparator: Each symptom dimension after controlling shared variance with the other dimensions
outcome: Cognitive correlates including social cognition, motor coordination, perceptual-motor functioning, attention, inhibition, working memory, processing speed
main_result: Profiles looked similar in bivariate correlations but diverged in regression: ADHD-HI was associated with weaker social cognition and focused/sustained attention yet better motor coordination; ADHD-I with weaker intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, perceptual-motor functioning and memory; CDS with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: ADHD-HI: social cognition and attention betas -.24 to -.11 (p<.001); motor coordination beta = .14 (p<.001). ADHD-I: betas -.21 to -.10 (p<.01). CDS: betas -.29 to -.13 (p<.001).
major_limitations: All constituent studies cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; dimensions defined by rating scales rather than diagnoses; pooling across child and adult samples; laboratory/rating cognitive proxies rather than real-world social or motor functioning.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult reporting both inattentive and hyperactive features, but findings are group-level, symptom-scale based, and cannot attribute this person's social or motor difficulties to a specific dimension.
quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

citation: Siyi Li, Huanqing Wang, Guoqiu Chen, Xi Cheng, Yuxi Wang, Wanyan Hu, et al. Social functioning in autism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nature human behaviour. 2026;10(7):1260-1273. doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02457-w. PMID:42120904.
study_design: Systematic review with two complementary quantitative meta-analyses of behavioural studies published 1990-2025
population: 94,114 clinically diagnosed autistic and 172,847 neurotypical individuals across 32 countries and 2,622 studies
exposure_intervention: Clinically diagnosed autism
comparator: Neurotypical controls
outcome: 22 social components clustered into five domains, plus developmental timing and cross-domain organisation
main_result: Substantial overall group differences in social functioning; earliest divergence in motivation-based processes (around six months), followed by motor, emotion and inference domains, with stronger cross-domain interdependency in autism and an organisation most consistent with serial relations among domains.
major_limitations: No ADHD or DCD comparator, so incremental variance beyond ADHD is not tested; methodological heterogeneity; many underpowered constituent samples; uneven cultural representation; pooling across a very wide age range and construct set.
individual_applicability: Establishes that autistic social differences are large and replicable at group level, but cannot indicate whether autistic features add explanatory value beyond ADHD in this person.
quality_reason: Exceptionally large, diagnosis-based synthesis with quantified effects, but heterogeneous constructs and absence of neurodevelopmental comparator groups limit inference for the claim as worded.

citation: Lulu Cheng, Jianxin Zhang, Haoran Mao, Xize Jia, Linlin Zhan, Cuicui Liu. Brain activation patterns of figurative language comprehension in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: an activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis. Frontiers in neuroscience. 2026;20:1717020. doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1717020. PMID:41695975.
study_design: Activation likelihood estimation coordinate-based meta-analysis of six task fMRI studies
population: 95 individuals with ASD and 98 neurotypical controls; ages not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Figurative (non-literal) language comprehension tasks during fMRI
comparator: Neurotypical controls
outcome: Consistent activation patterns and between-group activation differences
main_result: Both groups recruited a core network (bilateral superior temporal gyrus, transverse temporal gyrus, right insula); the ASD group showed consistent hypoactivation in left superior and middle temporal gyrus, with no region of ASD hyperactivation.
effect_estimate: NR (coordinate-based ALE clusters; no behavioural accuracy effect size reported)
major_limitations: Only six studies with small samples; neural activation rather than behavioural comprehension outcomes; no ADHD, anxiety or DCD comparator; task and analysis heterogeneity; ages and IQ not reported in abstract.
individual_applicability: Consistent with a neural substrate for non-literal language difficulty in autism but provides no behavioural benchmark against which this person's reported literal interpretation could be judged.
quality_reason: Very few small studies, neuroimaging surrogate outcome, and no clinical or behavioural effect estimates.

citation: Ellie Kiger Hodge, Katherine Kuhl Meltzoff. The relationship between autistic camouflaging and mental health: a scoping review. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1701615. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1701615. PMID:42311563.
study_design: Scoping review of 48 qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method studies with charting against an adapted Cochrane checklist
population: Autistic participants across studies; several studies also included non-autistic comparison samples; ages and total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Autistic camouflaging/masking, subdivided into assimilation, compensation and masking
comparator: Lower camouflaging and, in some studies, non-autistic samples
outcome: Depression, anxiety, stress, mental wellbeing, burnout
main_result: Camouflaging was positively associated with poorer mental health, most strongly for assimilation; qualitative findings suggested a bidirectional relationship; crucially, non-autistic participants showed similar camouflaging-mental health relationships.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as ranging from small to large; specific values NR
major_limitations: Scoping design without formal risk-of-bias grading; self-report camouflaging measures; predominance of cross-sectional data; construct heterogeneity; outcome is mental health rather than social-communication performance.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the case interpretation that masking hid impairment, but the presence of the same association in non-autistic samples means masking-related distress is not diagnostically specific.
quality_reason: Scoping methodology, heterogeneous self-report measures and largely cross-sectional evidence preclude causal or specificity claims.

citation: Marta Pozo-Rodríguez, Sara Cruz, Sabela Conde-Pumpido-Zubizarreta, Angel Carracedo, María Tubío-Fungueiriño, Montse Fernández-Prieto. A systematic review on the association between executive function and emotional regulation in autism, ADHD, and autism/ADHD. Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews. 2026;183:106570. doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.106570. PMID:41579913.
study_design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis of 22 empirical articles published January 2013 to October 2024
population: Children and adults with autism (4 studies), ADHD (16 studies), or co-occurring autism/ADHD (2 studies)
exposure_intervention: Executive function, measured by task-based and report-based instruments
comparator: Comparison across autism, ADHD and co-occurring autism/ADHD groups
outcome: Emotion regulation and emotional dysregulation
main_result: Evidence overall indicated an association between executive function difficulties and emotional dysregulation across all three conditions; age and measurement approach contributed to variability, and too few studies of the co-occurring group existed to draw conclusions about differential diagnosis.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis without pooling; only two studies of the co-occurring group; heterogeneous EF and ER measures; mixed ages; publication window restricted to 2013 onward.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an executive-function-to-emotional-dysregulation pathway is shared rather than diagnosis-specific, so this pattern in the case cannot discriminate ADHD from autism.
quality_reason: Small, heterogeneous evidence base with no quantitative synthesis and near-absent data on the co-occurring phenotype of interest.

citation: Maria Giuseppina Petruzzelli, Emilia Matera, Lucia Margari, Lucia Marzulli, Alessandra Gabellone, Chiara Cotugno, et al. An update on the comorbidity of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and its clinical management. Expert review of neurotherapeutics. 2026;26(1):75-89. doi:10.1080/14737175.2025.2599856. PMID:41388592.
study_design: Targeted narrative expert review prioritising meta-analyses and umbrella reviews (PubMed search to 24 March 2025)
population: Individuals with ADHD, ASD, or both, across the lifespan
exposure_intervention: Co-occurring ADHD and ASD
comparator: Single-diagnosis presentations
outcome: Shared and distinct phenotypic, neuropsychological, genetic and neuroimaging correlates; assessment and management approaches
main_result: Reports both shared and distinct correlates of ADHD and ASD, states that the comorbidity should not be overlooked, and advises that comorbid diagnosis be made only after thorough differential assessment establishing that ADHD symptoms are not better explained by ASD; calls for research on personalised treatment and real-world outcomes.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Non-systematic targeted search with expert-opinion synthesis; no quantitative pooling, no risk-of-bias appraisal, no explicit eligibility criteria; recommendations are consensus rather than evidence-graded.
individual_applicability: Provides an explicit clinical sequencing principle for the case (differential before comorbid diagnosis) but is expert opinion, the lowest tier of the protocol's hierarchy.
quality_reason: Expert narrative review without systematic search, appraisal or effect estimates.

citation: Gabriela Garcia de Carvalho Laguna, Baltazar Fernandes Andrade, Vanessa Souto Paulo, Marina Garcia Lorenzo Aguiar, Isadora Bagues Rodrigues, Jade Ponte da Cruz, et al. Differentiation between Autism Spectrum Disorder and Personality Disorders: a systematic review. Psychology, health & medicine. 2026;1-20. doi:10.1080/13548506.2026.2691413. PMID:42319023.
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA and registered on PROSPERO, covering original articles published 2020-2024
population: 684 individuals total: 550 clinical adult participants and 134 healthcare professionals
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic assessment of adult autism spectrum disorder
comparator: Personality disorders, particularly borderline personality disorder
outcome: Differential-diagnostic criteria and their impact on diagnostic accuracy
main_result: Feature overlap, especially between ASD and borderline personality disorder, compromises diagnostic accuracy; ASD was characterised by cognitive rigidity and difficulty interpreting social norms whereas personality disorders featured emotional instability, impulsivity and fear of abandonment, and self-harm had different antecedents in each; absent standardised criteria and reliance on subjective assessment increase diagnostic error and delay.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Small pooled sample; narrow 2020-2024 publication window; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias grading reported in abstract; heterogeneous designs including professional-survey data; distinguishing framework derived within the review rather than validated prospectively.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant: adult social difficulty with emotional dysregulation can be produced by personality-disorder processes as well as autism, and the two are frequently confused in adult assessment.
quality_reason: Systematic in method but based on few, heterogeneous studies with a small aggregate sample and no quantitative accuracy estimates.

quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

study_design: Cross-sectional analysis within a birth-cohort follow-up (Jerusalem Perinatal Study) using PROCESS mediation model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples
population: 89 community-dwelling midlife adults, mean age 45.6 years (range 44.3-46.9), 47% women

main_result: Low-aligned children (7.1%) had significantly less MVPA and poorer fitness than all other profiles; over-perceivers (53.0%) had low actual competence but MVPA comparable to average- and high-competence peers, whereas fitness remained lower in all children with reduced actual competence regardless of perceived competence.

quality_reason: Cohort sample with objective motor, accelerometer and fitness measurement, but cross-sectional with no reported between-profile effect estimates.

citation: Ali Jami, Sajjad Abbaszade, Abdol-Hossein Vahabie. A review on exploration-exploitation trade-off in psychiatric disorders. BMC psychiatry. 2025;25(1):420. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-06837-w. PMID:40287643.
study_design: Systematic review of 46 studies using tasks probing exploration-exploitation balance across psychiatric disorders; PubMed search; narrative synthesis
population: Individuals with psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders including ADHD, schizophrenia, OCD, anxiety, mood disorders and addictive disorders; total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic status assessed on decision-making tasks manipulating exploration versus exploitation, novelty and reward
comparator: Healthy controls and cross-disorder comparisons
outcome: Exploration-exploitation balance, decision stability, reward sensitivity, learning and adaptability
main_result: Disorders clustered into addictive patterns, emotional/cognitive disturbances and neurological conditions. Anxiety and mood disorders often showed enhanced exploratory behaviour, and depression affected decision stability and reward sensitivity. Schizophrenia, OCD and ADHD were characterized by excessive switching and difficulty balancing exploration and exploitation, leading to impaired learning and adaptability. Addiction-like presentations showed reduced exploration and impulsive or perseverative choices.

major_limitations: Single-database (PubMed) search; narrative synthesis of highly heterogeneous computational tasks; no formal risk-of-bias appraisal; case-control designs cannot establish diagnostic specificity; ADHD findings not separated by age or medication status.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether novelty- and reward-linked performance patterns are ADHD-specific; indicates they are shared with anxiety, mood, OCD and substance-related conditions that are competing explanations in this case.
quality_reason: Systematic in intent but limited by single-database searching, absent bias appraisal, no quantitative synthesis, and marked task heterogeneity across the reviewed literature.

comparator: Non-ADHD control children and adolescents

effect_estimate: Novelty seeking SMD 1.19 (0.87-1.51); persistence SMD -1.07 (-1.33 to -0.81); effortful control SMD -1.43 (-2.14 to -0.72); conscientiousness SMD -0.95 (-1.85 to -0.04); neuroticism SMD 0.92 (0.37-1.48)

quality_reason: Formal meta-analysis with NOS appraisal and precise interval estimates, but downgraded by the authors' own acknowledgement of selective reporting, instrument heterogeneity and limited study numbers per domain.

population: Adults with ADHD employed in open-plan office environments; total N and age range NR

comparator: Alternative or enclosed office environments and the general workforce; comparator largely implicit and NR

citation: Laura Reeves, Anna Tickle. What Are the Experiences of Adults With ADHD of Engaging in ADHD Medication Treatment? A Systematic Review and Meta-Ethnography. Journal of attention disorders. 2025;29(12):1118-1133. doi:10.1177/10870547251349952. PMID:40665716.

population: 263 adults with ADHD prescribed stimulant medication; ages and settings NR
exposure_intervention: Engagement with stimulant medication treatment for ADHD in the context of academic, workplace and family demands
comparator: Within-sample contrast between adherence and non-adherence; no external comparator group
outcome: Experiences of medication treatment, adherence behaviour, and functioning in performance and social domains

quality_reason: Rigorous meta-ethnographic method with appraisal, but qualitative design, self-report basis, and the authors' acknowledged weighting limitation constrain evidentiary weight for a moderation claim.

citation: Haura Alia Herlitasari, Dini Fajariani, Reiko Miyamoto. Exploring Vocational Training Interventions for Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Scoping Review. Occupational therapy international. 2026;2026(1):e7704446. doi:10.1155/oti/7704446. PMID:41943443.
study_design: Scoping review (Arksey and O'Malley framework with PRISMA reporting); two-stage search (June 2024, updated November 2025); 26 included studies
population: Autistic adults aged 18 years and older in vocational training and employment programs; mostly United States (53.8%), Japan (15.4%), Australia (11.5%)

comparator: Not consistently defined across included studies; comparator NR
outcome: Employment-related skills, intervention components, professional roles, implementation context and sustainability
main_result: Interventions were most often delivered in workplace or community settings (57.7%) with highly variable dose (median 23.0 weeks, range 0.71-312; median 32.0 contact hours, range 2-900). individual_applicability: Describes the structure of workplace-embedded supports for autistic adults but provides no comparative outcome data, so it informs feasibility rather than individual prediction.
quality_reason: Scoping methodology by design does not appraise study quality or synthesize effects, and the authors note heterogeneous reporting that precludes conclusions about effectiveness.

study_design: Meta-analysis of 31 studies using WISC-IV, WISC-V, WAIS-III and WAIS-IV; random-effects models with Hedges' g against a normative reference (mean 100, SD 15)
population: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and co-occurring ASD plus ID; ages spanning child and adult test versions; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic group (ASD, ID, ASD+ID) assessed on Wechsler cognitive index profiles
comparator: Normative Wechsler reference values and between-group comparisons across diagnostic categories
outcome: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual/Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed, Visual Processing indices and Full-Scale IQ
main_result: ASD showed a distinct profile with greater impairment in Processing Speed and Working Memory while Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual/Fluid Reasoning and Visual Processing remained close to normative scores. ID and ASD+ID showed generalized deficits across all indices, with the lowest scores in Full-Scale IQ and broad effects above g = -2.5. individual_applicability: Supports interpreting cognitive profiles by index scatter rather than global IQ, which is relevant to the compensation and trade-off hypotheses, but provides no ADHD data and no real-world outcome link.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis across 31 studies with a consistent normative reference and version-invariance testing, downgraded for high heterogeneity, referral bias and absence of functional outcomes.

exposure_intervention: Pharmacological, genetic or stimulation-based targeting of dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems, with stress and behavioural factors examined as modifiers

quality_reason: Systematic screening approach but no clinical population, no quantitative synthesis, no bias appraisal, and the authors themselves note that systematic evidence on the core question is absent.

quality_reason: Large adult-specific meta-analysis with formal risk-of-bias and GRADE appraisal, downgraded for design heterogeneity, self-report outcomes, and short follow-up.

citation: Maria Faurholt-Jepsen, Asbjørn Risom, Caroline Fussing Bruun, Esben Budtz-Jørgensen, Maj Vinberg, Lars Vedel Kessing. Variation in sleep and instability in mood in patients with bipolar disorder and the association between these - an exploratory post hoc study on daily smartphone-based data from two separate randomised controlled trials. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122149. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122149. PMID:42320790.

comparator: Within-person periods of lower sleep variation and different sleep durations
outcome: Smartphone-based mood instability

citation: Joanne S Carpenter, Jacob J Crouse, Mathew Varidel, Emiliana Tonini, Mirim Shin, Natalia Zmicerevska, et al. population: 250 youth aged 12-30 attending early-intervention mental health services in Sydney, Australia

comparator: Within-cohort variation in sleep parameters, adjusted for age, sex, functioning, mania-like and psychotic-like experiences and medication
outcome: Transition to full-threshold mental disorders, specifically bipolar or psychotic disorders versus depressive/anxiety disorders
main_result: Longer, not shorter, baseline sleep duration predicted higher odds of and shorter time to transition to full-threshold bipolar or psychotic disorders; later sleep midpoint predicted transition to any full-threshold disorder only at uncorrected significance.

citation: Amélia Walter, Émilie Martz, Luisa Weiner, Henri Comtet, Raphaëlle Glacet, Ülker Kilic-Huck, et al. Sleep, rest-activity rhythm, cognitive and emotional symptoms in adult ADHD: unraveling the links with an actimetry-based approach. BMC psychiatry. 2026;26(1):317. doi:10.1186/s12888-026-07947-9. population: 54 adults with ADHD and 47 control adults without psychiatric or neurodevelopmental disorders

comparator: Control participants without psychiatric or neurodevelopmental disorders; age- and sex-adjusted
outcome: Self-reported inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, emotional symptoms; neuropsychological attention and executive function tests
main_result: Adults with ADHD showed a more unstable and delayed rest-activity rhythm than controls; longer sleep latency related to poorer selective attention and shorter total sleep time to weaker inhibitory control, but most correlations did not survive multiple-comparison correction and no association with emotional dysregulation was found.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Modest sample, cross-sectional correlational analyses, loss of significance after correction, subjective symptom measures; medication and comorbidity handling not described in abstract.
individual_applicability: Adult ADHD sample with objective circadian measures is highly relevant to the case's reported time-of-day variability, but the attenuated corrected findings caution against strong inference.
quality_reason: Objective exposure and cognitive outcomes with a control group, but cross-sectional design and fragile findings after multiplicity correction.

citation: Giuseppe Barbato, Barbara Tondi, Dario Morra. Sleep in Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Drug-Free Patients. Brain sciences. 2026;16(7):742. doi:10.3390/brainsci16070742. PMID:42512516.
study_design: Systematic review (107 studies) and random-effects meta-analysis of 43 case-control polysomnography studies with Egger's test and funnel-plot assessment

main_result: Total sleep time and sleep efficiency were reduced in both manic and depressive drug-free bipolar patients versus controls, delta sleep was reduced only in depression, and manic patients showed reduced stage 2 and REM time, shortened REM latency and increased REM density; drug-treated bipolar patients differed from controls only in reduced REM percentage, increased REM latency and increased REM density.
effect_estimate: Standardised mean difference was the primary outcome measure, but numeric values and confidence intervals are NR in the abstract

quality_reason: Large meta-analysis of objective drug-free polysomnography with publication-bias assessment, downgraded for cross-sectional design and unreported numeric estimates.

citation: Shivahn Garvie, Maryam Sorkhou, Tony P George. Clinical Phenomenology of Bipolar Disorder With Substance Use Disorders: A Systematic Review. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(5):e70132. doi:10.1111/bdi.70132. PMID:42286971.
study_design: Systematic review of 48 clinical studies with narrative synthesis (PubMed, PsycINFO)
population: Adults with bipolar disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, stimulants, opioids); total N and ages NR

major_limitations: Predominantly cross-sectional and observational studies synthesized narratively, no pooled effects, substantial risk of reverse causation and confounding by overall illness severity, and very sparse tobacco- and stimulant-specific evidence.

quality_reason: Large but methodologically weak observational evidence base without pooling, with authors explicitly noting the need for more rigorous designs.

citation: Ali Dadfar, Mia Ramklint, Sara von Wallenberg Pachaly. A systematic review of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)-induced activation and manic/hypomanic switch in children and adolescents. study_design: PROSPERO-registered PRISMA systematic review (CRD42023422133) of 30 articles with duplicate blinded screening; qualitative synthesis of definitions and assessments
population: 30 articles covering children and adolescents aged 6-18 years treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; total N NR
exposure_intervention: SSRI treatment, with outcomes of drug-induced activation or manic/hypomanic switch
comparator: NR (comparison was between activation and manic/hypomanic switch constructs rather than between exposure groups)
outcome: Definitions, symptom profiles, assessment instruments and inter-rater reliability for activation versus manic/hypomanic switch
main_result: Only 8 of 30 articles clearly defined activation and 4 defined mania/hypomania, one instrument existed for activation and none for mania, and only 2 reported reliability; symptoms overlapped substantially, with aggression/hostility, anxiety/panic and suicidality more often reported under activation and cognitive/thought-process and mood changes more often under mania/hypomania.
effect_estimate: NR (no incidence rates, effect sizes or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Pediatric samples only, exposure is SSRIs rather than stimulants or cannabis, no incidence or effect estimates, and vague heterogeneous definitions mean the reported symptom differences may reflect reporting conventions rather than distinct phenomena.
individual_applicability: Illustrates the general clinical problem of distinguishing medication-induced activation from a mood episode, which applies to this case, but the population and drug class differ.
quality_reason: Registered review with duplicate screening, but the underlying literature lacks validated definitions, instruments and reliability data, and no quantitative outcomes are available.

citation: Meghan Fiske, Dominique L DiDomenico, Henry W Chase, Yvette Afriyie-Agyemang, Genna Bebko, Haris A Aslam, et al. Bipolar Disorder Psychosis Risk Predicts Cue Discrimination on the AX-Continuous Performance Task Paradigm. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(4):e70129. doi:10.1111/bdi.70129. PMID:42262032.
study_design: Cross-sectional study with dimensional linear regression aims and categorical group comparisons (ANCOVA)
population: Euthymic bipolar disorder (n=27) and bipolar-at-risk individuals (n=121), total analysed sample 148; ages NR
exposure_intervention: Lifetime mania/affective-lability risk (psychomotor activation, suicidality, mixed instability) and lifetime psychosis risk indexed by the Mood Spectrum Self Report
comparator: Lower-risk individuals within the same cohort; bipolar low-risk versus high-risk groups; no healthy control group described
outcome: AX-Continuous Performance Test measures d'context (target/context discrimination) and A-cue bias
main_result: Higher lifetime psychosis and mania/affective-lability risk were associated with reduced d'context but not with altered A-cue bias, and categorical group comparisons showed no significant differences; the associations survived adjustment for current depressive symptoms but disappeared after covarying current mania severity.
effect_estimate: Dimensional associations with d'context: absolute t values >2.015, p<0.047; after covarying current mania severity absolute t values <1.26, all p>0.203; no effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional design, small bipolar subgroup (n=27), reliance on retrospective self-report for lifetime risk, single laboratory task, no reported control of medication, sleep or substance exposure, and 'euthymic' status still permitted variable current mania severity.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the state-versus-trait question in this case, showing that residual current mood elevation can account for attention deficits that look trait-like; single-timepoint group data cannot classify one person.
quality_reason: Small cross-sectional sample with self-report exposure and a single task; the key finding is a covariate-attenuation result reported without effect sizes.

citation: Jaisingh Rajput, Sandhya Narahari, Taha Arif, Rabiya Iftikhar, Turimula Arpan, Abdullah Tariq, et al. study_design: PRISMA 2020 systematic review of 8 studies appraised with AMSTAR 2, Cochrane RoB, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and SANRA; narrative synthesis
population: Studies of individuals with, or at risk for, schizophrenia; sample sizes and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis with high delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol content, contrasted with cannabidiol
comparator: Lower-THC or non-using groups; cannabidiol as comparator agent (details NR)
outcome: Risk of developing schizophrenia; positive, negative and cognitive symptom course
main_result: High-THC cannabis was associated with significantly higher risk of developing schizophrenia, particularly with familial vulnerability and regular adolescent use, and THC was reported to exacerbate positive, negative and cognitive symptoms in established schizophrenia, whereas cannabidiol evidence for benefit remained limited and based on small studies.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled effect sizes, confidence intervals or absolute risks reported in abstract)
major_limitations: Only 8 studies retained from 112 records with opaque quality-based selection, mixed designs including narrative reviews, no quantitative synthesis, and observational data vulnerable to reverse causation and confounding by other substances.
individual_applicability: Supports caution about high-potency THC in a person with psychosis-spectrum vulnerability, but the population is schizophrenia rather than ADHD or bipolar disorder and no mood-stability outcome was assessed.
quality_reason: Small, selectively assembled evidence base with no pooled estimates and reliance on heterogeneous designs including narrative reviews.

citation: Valerio Ricci, Thomas Fraccalini, Giovanni Martinotti, Giuseppe Maina. Cannabis cessation and neurocognitive recovery: Patterns, predictors, and clinical implications-a systematic review. The American journal on addictions. 2026;35(4):451-470. doi:10.1111/ajad.70156. PMID:41872072.
study_design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis of 26 studies (2000-2025) appraised with Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Cochrane risk-of-bias tools
population: 26 studies of individuals with cannabis use across abstinence periods from acute (at least 72 hours) to months or years; total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis cessation and sustained abstinence
comparator: Continued use and/or pre-cessation baseline; details NR
outcome: Neuroimaging markers (CB1 receptor availability), cognitive performance, and biomarker recovery
main_result: CB1 receptor normalization occurred within about 4 weeks and cognitive improvements within the first week of cessation, but deficits in attention and executive function persisted beyond acute cessation; adolescent-onset and heavy users showed less complete or slower recovery, and most recovery occurred within the first year.

individual_applicability: Directly informs how long verified abstinence should last before attributing residual executive or attentional difficulty to a trait, but cannot establish the recovery trajectory for one person.
quality_reason: Observational evidence base synthesized narratively with heterogeneous abstinence definitions and no quantitative pooling or GRADE rating reported.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. The risk of psychosis associated with cannabis use by people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of 3 heterogeneous studies; risk of bias rated fair (k=1) and good (k=2)
population: People with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder exposed to cannabis; sample sizes, ages and diagnostic methods NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use in individuals with ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD who use cannabis, and/or ADHD individuals without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis outcomes
main_result: Two of three studies indirectly suggested that cannabis use does not increase psychosis risk among people with ADHD, and the third indicated that cannabis had a similar impact on psychosis risk in people with and without ADHD; the authors conclude there is very little evidence for a heightened ADHD-specific risk.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates; synthesis without meta-analysis)
major_limitations: Only three studies, two of which addressed the question indirectly, almost certainly underpowered to detect an interaction, exposure and diagnostic ascertainment not described, and absence of evidence is reported rather than evidence of absence.
individual_applicability: Directly targets the proposed ADHD-by-cannabis interaction relevant to this case, but the evidence base is too thin to exclude a clinically meaningful individual effect.
quality_reason: Very small number of studies with indirect inference and no quantitative synthesis, despite generally fair-to-good individual study ratings.

citation: Lauren V Moran, Joseph P Skinner, Ann K Shinn, Kathryn Nielsen, Vinod Rao, S Trevor Taylor, et al. Risk of Incident Psychosis and Mania With Prescription Amphetamines. The American journal of psychiatry. 2024;181(10):901-909. doi:10.1176/appi.ajp.20230329. PMID:39262211.
study_design: Case-control study using electronic health records with dose stratification
population: 1374 cases hospitalized for incident psychosis or mania and 2748 control patients with an initial psychiatric hospitalization for other reasons (commonly depression/anxiety), ages 16-35, McLean Hospital, 2005-2019
exposure_intervention: Past-month prescription amphetamine use, divided into terciles of dextroamphetamine equivalents; secondary analysis of methylphenidate
comparator: No past-month prescription stimulant use, within hospitalized control subjects
outcome: Incident psychosis or mania requiring first psychiatric hospitalization
main_result: Past-month prescription amphetamine use was associated with increased odds of incident psychosis or mania compared with no use, with a dose-response gradient; high doses above 30 mg dextroamphetamine equivalents carried the largest odds, whereas past-month methylphenidate use was not associated with increased odds.
effect_estimate: Amphetamines adjusted OR 2.68 (95% CI 1.90-3.77); >30 mg dextroamphetamine equivalents 5.28-fold increased odds (CI NR); methylphenidate adjusted OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.54-1.55)
major_limitations: Authors note selection bias from hospitalized controls, exposure ascertained from records rather than verified intake, no absolute risks reported, and prodromal symptoms could drive both stimulant escalation and subsequent hospitalization (confounding by indication and reverse causation).
individual_applicability: Age range and outpatient-to-hospitalization pathway are reasonably close to this case; supports agent- and dose-specific caution rather than a class-wide effect.
quality_reason: Large adjusted case-control with dose-response and a negative control exposure, downgraded for hospitalized-control selection bias and residual confounding.

citation: Gonzalo Salazar de Pablo, Claudia Aymerich, Juan Pablo Chart-Pascual, Marco Solmi, Javier Torres-Cortes, Nessma Abdelhafez, et al. Occurrence of Psychosis and Bipolar Disorder in Individuals With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treated With Stimulants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA psychiatry. 2025;82(11):1103-1112. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2025.2311. PMID:40900605.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of observational and other designs (PRISMA, MOOSE; Newcastle-Ottawa and Cochrane RoB2)
population: 16 studies, N=391,043 individuals with DSM/ICD-defined ADHD; mean age 12.6 years (range 8.5-31.1); 288,199 (73.7%) male
exposure_intervention: Prescribed stimulant medication (amphetamines or methylphenidate)
comparator: Mostly none (proportion estimates); head-to-head amphetamines versus methylphenidate for the psychosis comparison
outcome: Occurrence of psychotic symptoms, psychotic disorder, and bipolar disorder
main_result: Pooled occurrence was 2.76% for psychotic symptoms, 2.29% for psychotic disorder, and 3.72% for bipolar disorder; psychosis occurrence was higher with amphetamines than methylphenidate, and increased occurrence was associated with higher stimulant dose, higher proportion of female participants, smaller samples, North American setting, and longer follow-up.
effect_estimate: Psychotic symptoms 2.76% (95% CI 0.73-9.88, k=10, n=237,035); psychotic disorder 2.29% (1.52-3.40, k=4, n=91,437); bipolar disorder 3.72% (0.77-16.05, k=4, n=92,945); amphetamine vs methylphenidate psychosis OR 1.57 (1.15-2.16, k=3, n=231,325); I-squared >95%
major_limitations: Most estimates are uncontrolled proportions without unexposed comparators, heterogeneity exceeded 95%, samples were predominantly children and adolescents, and the authors state that included studies cannot establish causality.
individual_applicability: Quantifies the low but non-negligible occurrence relevant to stimulant decisions in an adult with bipolar vulnerability, though the pooled sample is much younger than this case.
quality_reason: Large registered meta-analysis with design-appropriate appraisal, downgraded for extreme heterogeneity, absent unexposed comparators, and confounding by indication.

citation: Stefania Chiappini, Pietro Domenico Gramuglia, Alessio Mosca, Clara Cavallotto, Andrea Miuli, John Martin Corkery, et al. Methylphenidate abuse and misuse in patients affected with a psychiatric disorder and a substance use disorder: a systematic review. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2024;15:1508732. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1508732. PMID:39624511.
study_design: PROSPERO-registered PRISMA systematic review (CRD42024576724) of 12 studies; narrative counts
population: 12 studies covering 1551 individuals with dual diagnosis (psychiatric disorder plus substance use disorder); age range NR
exposure_intervention: Methylphenidate misuse or abuse, including doses higher than prescribed (n=84) and non-oral routes such as snorting (n=20)
comparator: NR (no unexposed comparator group described)
outcome: Prevalence and pattern of misuse, exacerbation of psychiatric symptoms, psychosis, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal events
main_result: Misuse clustered in people with conduct, mood, anxiety, personality and depressive disorders and with co-occurring alcohol (475/1551), cannabis (371/1551), nicotine (343/1551) and cocaine (68/1551) use disorders; adverse outcomes included exacerbation of psychiatric symptoms (1082/1551), psychosis (69/1551), cardiovascular (108/1551) and gastrointestinal events (201/1551).
effect_estimate: Counts only, no relative or absolute risk estimates or confidence intervals (NR)
major_limitations: Counts are summed across heterogeneous studies with unclear denominators, there is no unexposed comparator, misuse rather than prescribed therapeutic use was studied, and nicotine appears only as a co-occurring diagnosis rather than an exposure with measured activation outcomes.
individual_applicability: Relevant to risk stratification when prescribed stimulants coexist with cannabis or nicotine use, but the misuse context differs from guideline-dose prescribed treatment.
quality_reason: Registered review of only 12 heterogeneous studies with pooled raw counts, no comparator, and no risk-of-bias-weighted synthesis reported in the abstract.

citation: Andreea Chiorean, Brett D M Jones, Mijia Murong, Christina Gonzalez-Torres, Stefan Kloiber, Abigail Ortiz, et al. Prescribed psychostimulants and other pro-cognitive medications in bipolar disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis of recurrence of manic symptoms. Bipolar disorders. 2024;26(5):418-430. doi:10.1111/bdi.13440. PMID:38670627.
study_design: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized trials and prospective longitudinal studies
population: 27 included studies; 5 quantitatively synthesized (n=1653) of patients with bipolar disorder in euthymic or depressive states
exposure_intervention: Prescribed psychostimulants and non-stimulant medications recommended for ADHD by Canadian ADHD practice guidelines
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Emergence of (hypo)manic symptoms measured by Young Mania Rating Scale scores
main_result: Psychostimulant use in euthymic or depressed bipolar patients was not associated with increased Young Mania Rating Scale scores compared with placebo, and qualitative synthesis of the remaining studies indicated a limited risk of medication-induced manic symptoms.
major_limitations: Only 5 of 27 studies contributed to pooling, heterogeneity was high, trials were short and likely excluded unstable or rapid-cycling patients, and a continuous mania rating scale is insensitive to rare categorical switch events.
individual_applicability: Directly addresses the clinical question of stimulant-associated mood destabilization in bipolar disorder, but trial populations were selected and stabilized, unlike an untreated or substance-exposed state.
quality_reason: Preregistered review including trial-registry searching, downgraded for sparse pooling, high heterogeneity, and low sensitivity of the switch outcome.

citation: Cagatay Ermis, Antti Tanskanen, Olivier Corbeil, Johannes Lieslehto, Eduard Vieta, Christoph U Correll, et al. Reduced risk of cause-specific hospitalisations and all-cause hospitalisation/mortality during treatment with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder medications in the course of bipolar disorder: a Swedish registry-based within-subject cohort study. BMJ mental health. 2026;29(1):e302159. doi:10.1136/bmjment-2025-302159. PMID:41856665.
study_design: Nationwide register-based within-individual cohort study (each person serves as own control), Sweden 2006-2021
population: 17,971 individuals with bipolar disorder who used any ADHD medication; mean age 32.0 (SD 11.6) years; 37.6% male; 88.9% with ADHD; mean follow-up 8.9 (SD 4.4) years
exposure_intervention: Add-on ADHD medication (mainly methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine; also atomoxetine, modafinil) to concomitant antipsychotics and/or mood stabilizers
comparator: Within-person periods of antipsychotic and/or mood stabilizer treatment without ADHD medication
outcome: Psychiatric hospitalization (primary); substance-related, somatic, and mania-related hospitalization; all-cause hospitalization or mortality
main_result: Add-on stimulant use was associated with lower risks of psychiatric hospitalization, substance-use-related hospitalization, and all-cause hospitalization or mortality, with no increase in somatic or mania-related hospitalization; lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate drove the effects while atomoxetine was not associated with reduced psychiatric hospitalization.
effect_estimate: Psychiatric hospitalization aHR 0.89 (95% CI 0.85-0.93); substance-related 0.75 (0.70-0.81); all-cause hospitalization/mortality 0.90 (0.87-0.93); somatic 1.00 (0.90-1.12); mania-related 0.93 (0.72-1.20); lisdexamfetamine 0.81 (0.75-0.87); methylphenidate 0.92 (0.88-0.97)
major_limitations: Register outcomes are coarse and capture no speech, salience, or symptom-level change; within-individual design removes stable but not time-varying confounding (adherence, illness phase); stimulants were almost always co-prescribed with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant to an adult with co-occurring bipolar disorder and ADHD traits considering stimulant treatment under mood stabilization; does not speak to unmonitored or unstabilized use.
quality_reason: Large national within-person cohort minimizing between-person confounding, downgraded for outcome coarseness, residual time-varying confounding, and absence of symptom-level measures.

major_limitations: Imaginary friendship is not equivalent to maladaptive or immersive daydreaming; outcome is personality pathology rather than fantasy or impairment; single national cohort; low outcome base rates.

quality_reason: Strong prospective seven-wave design with structured diagnostic outcome, but construct mismatch with the focal daydreaming claim and no reported predictor effect sizes.

population: Millennium Cohort Study; 2,607 male and 2,791 female participants assessed at ages 11, 14 and 17
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms in adolescence
comparator: Lower ADHD symptom levels within the cohort
outcome: Internalising (anxiety and depressive) symptoms, with 14 candidate mediators including peer problems, conduct problems, self-esteem, injuries, parental relationships, academic performance, risky decision-making, parental mental health, educational motivation and general health
main_result: Regularisation did not de-select any of the 14 candidate mediators, but only two were statistically significant. The authors conclude there may be many mediators of small effect linking ADHD symptoms to later internalising problems, and identify self-esteem and parental mental health as priority mechanisms for future causal and interventional research.
effect_estimate: NR (individual path estimates and confidence intervals not reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Explicitly exploratory with 14 simultaneous mediators and no confirmatory replication; observational, so mediation remains associational; abstract does not identify which two paths were significant with estimates.
individual_applicability: Tempers the expectation that any single anxiety- or rejection-related mediator carries the functional burden; suggests distributed small effects rather than one dominant pathway.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised national cohort with three waves and appropriate regularisation, but exploratory framing, absent effect estimates and untested causal assumptions limit inference.

citation: Simin Kang, Zhao Fu, Qiurong Li, Li Yang, Qingjiu Cao. Adult-diagnosed and childhood-diagnosed attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: cognitive and environmental contributions to symptom severity across different age of diagnosis. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1782999. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1782999. PMID:42147013.
study_design: Cross-sectional comparative study with hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analysis
population: 72 adults with ADHD: 37 childhood-diagnosed (26.32 +/- 4.69 years) and 35 adult-diagnosed (25.63 +/- 4.89 years), diagnosed by structured interview
exposure_intervention: Executive function (BRIEF-A) and environmental factors: childhood trauma (CTQ), resilience (CD-RISC), parental bonding (PBI)
comparator: Childhood-diagnosed versus adult-diagnosed ADHD groups; relative variance contribution of executive versus environmental predictors
outcome: ADHD core symptom severity (ASRS inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity); emotional symptoms (SAS, SDS)
main_result: Executive function was the strongest and most consistent predictor of both inattention (beta 0.64, p<0.001) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (beta 0.47, p<0.001), whereas environmental factors contributed minimal additional explanatory power, with only a modest association between parental overprotection and inattention (beta 0.28, p=0.016). No diagnosis-specific moderation effects were observed. Adult-diagnosed participants showed lower childhood symptoms but similar adult severity, with more psychiatric comorbidity and emotional distress.
effect_estimate: beta 0.64 (inattention) and 0.47 (hyperactivity-impulsivity) for executive function; beta 0.28 (p=0.016) for parental overprotection; confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Small single-site sample; cross-sectional; retrospective childhood trauma and parenting recall; outcome is symptom severity rather than real-world functional impairment; no formal mediation testing.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult with late-recognised ADHD, and supports executive rather than adversity-related variables as the dominant symptom correlate, but small-sample and symptom-level outcomes limit transfer.
quality_reason: Structured diagnostic ascertainment is a strength, but low power, cross-sectional design and retrospective exposure measures constrain interpretation.

citation: Steve Lukito, Susie Chandler, Myrofora Kakoulidou, Kirsty Griffiths, Anna Wyatt, Eloise Funnell, et al. Emotional burden in school as a source of mental health problems associated with ADHD and/or autism: Development and validation of a new co-produced self-report measure. Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines. 2025;66(10):1577-1592. doi:10.1111/jcpp.70003. PMID:40707015.
study_design: Cross-sectional questionnaire development and validation study with group comparisons
population: 735 secondary school students: ADHD (n=100), autism (n=104), ADHD+autism (n=79), neurotypical (n=452), meeting symptom cut-offs on validated scales
exposure_intervention: Emotional burden in school, indexed by the My Emotions in School Inventory (25 commonly upsetting events rated for frequency and emotional intensity)
comparator: Neurotypical students and, for prediction, emotion-regulation deficits
outcome: Depression and anxiety symptoms; discrimination of neurodivergent from neurotypical students
main_result: Adolescents in the ADHD and/or autism groups reported higher frequency of commonly upsetting events and greater intensity of reaction than neurotypical peers, with higher overall emotional burden in all three neurodivergent groups (not differing from each other); the events generating burden differed between the autism and ADHD groups. Emotional burden and emotion-regulation deficits each contributed independently to predicting higher depression or anxiety.
effect_estimate: NR (group differences and regression coefficients not reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional with self-report exposure and outcome (common-method bias); groups defined by symptom cut-offs rather than clinical diagnosis; school setting only; new instrument with limited independent validation.
individual_applicability: Closely matches the case narrative of accumulated school-based upsetting experiences, but the sample is adolescents and the design cannot establish that burden preceded distress.
quality_reason: Well-powered and co-produced instrument, but cross-sectional design, symptom-based grouping and shared-method measurement limit inferential strength.

citation: Francesco Maria Boccaccio, Renata Rizzo, Concetta Pirrone, Jan K Buitelaar. Mapping the association between cognitive disengagement syndrome and internalizing disorders: A systematic scoping review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122159. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122159. PMID:42341946.
study_design: Systematic scoping review with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression (82 studies, 2002-2025)
population: Children, adolescents and adults from healthy and clinical samples
exposure_intervention: Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome (CDS), previously Sluggish Cognitive Tempo
comparator: Lower CDS levels; analyses controlling for ADHD inattention
outcome: Depression, anxiety and broader internalizing symptoms; functional consequences
main_result: Elevated CDS was consistently associated with depression and anxiety, with more than one-third of individuals reaching clinical thresholds; associations remained significant after controlling for ADHD inattention and were seen across ages. Meta-analyses showed the strongest link for depression (r=0.56), then anxiety (r=0.46) and internalizing symptoms (r=0.44); meta-regression identified depression as a significant moderator and inflated effect sizes in same-informant studies.
effect_estimate: r=0.56 (depression), r=0.46 (anxiety), r=0.44 (internalizing); confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Abstract does not state that CDS items index daydreaming; scarce longitudinal and multi-informant studies; no analytic control for symptom overlap despite acknowledged phenomenological similarity; same-informant inflation.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an inattention-adjacent construct tracks depression strongly and independently of ADHD inattention, relevant to differentiating mood-driven from compensation-driven inner experience.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis with moderator testing, but construct-overlap confounding is explicitly unaddressed and longitudinal evidence is sparse.

citation: Thilaanee Krishnamoorthy, Soumitra Das, Naveen Thomas. Stigma in adults with ADHD: a systematic review of types, experiences, and potential implications for quality of life. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1783271. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1783271. PMID:42137527.
study_design: Systematic review of 17 peer-reviewed studies from the past decade
population: Adults (aged 18 and over) with ADHD
exposure_intervention: Self/internalized stigma, perceived stigma, public stigma and structural stigma
comparator: Lower stigma levels or non-stigmatised comparison conditions within included studies
outcome: WHO quality-of-life domains: psychological, social relationships, environment and level of independence; functional impairment, self-esteem, treatment seeking
main_result: Greater ADHD symptomatology was positively correlated with more internalized stigma, which in turn was linked to functional impairment, worse self-esteem and poorer quality of life. Perceived stigma hindered treatment seeking, medication compliance and diagnostic disclosure, although its associations with quality of life were not significant. Public stigma was the most investigated type; few studies examined structural stigma and none directly assessed its quality-of-life outcomes.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates or confidence intervals reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis of predominantly cross-sectional self-report studies; no pooled effects or certainty grading; causal direction between symptoms, stigma and impairment untested; structural stigma under-examined.
individual_applicability: Directly concerns adults with ADHD and shame-related internalisation affecting functioning, matching the case, but cannot establish that stigma causes this individual's occupational difficulty.
quality_reason: Systematic search with typed stigma taxonomy, but heterogeneous cross-sectional evidence, no meta-analysis and explicit null findings for some quality-of-life associations.

citation: Meghan Fiske, Dominique L DiDomenico, Henry W Chase, Yvette Afriyie-Agyemang, Genna Bebko, Haris A Aslam, et al. Bipolar Disorder Psychosis Risk Predicts Cue Discrimination on the AX-Continuous Performance Task Paradigm. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(4):e70129. doi:10.1111/bdi.70129. PMID:42262032.
