study_design: Cross-sectional study with dimensional linear regression aims and categorical group comparisons (ANCOVA)
population: Euthymic bipolar disorder (n=27) and bipolar-at-risk individuals (n=121), total analysed sample 148; ages NR
exposure_intervention: Lifetime mania/affective-lability risk (psychomotor activation, suicidality, mixed instability) and lifetime psychosis risk indexed by the Mood Spectrum Self Report
comparator: Lower-risk individuals within the same cohort; bipolar low-risk versus high-risk groups; no healthy control group described
outcome: AX-Continuous Performance Test measures d'context (target/context discrimination) and A-cue bias
main_result: Higher lifetime psychosis and mania/affective-lability risk were associated with reduced d'context but not with altered A-cue bias, and categorical group comparisons showed no significant differences; the associations survived adjustment for current depressive symptoms but disappeared after covarying current mania severity.
effect_estimate: Dimensional associations with d'context: absolute t values >2.015, p<0.047; after covarying current mania severity absolute t values <1.26, all p>0.203; no effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional design, small bipolar subgroup (n=27), reliance on retrospective self-report for lifetime risk, single laboratory task, no reported control of medication, sleep or substance exposure, and 'euthymic' status still permitted variable current mania severity.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the state-versus-trait question in this case, showing that residual current mood elevation can account for attention deficits that look trait-like; single-timepoint group data cannot classify one person.
quality_reason: Small cross-sectional sample with self-report exposure and a single task; the key finding is a covariate-attenuation result reported without effect sizes.

citation: Giuseppe Barbato, Barbara Tondi, Dario Morra. Sleep in Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Drug-Free Patients. Brain sciences. 2026;16(7):742. doi:10.3390/brainsci16070742. PMID:42512516.
study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis of case-control polysomnography studies
population: 107 studies reviewed; 43 case-control studies meta-analysed: 670 bipolar patients, 520 healthy controls, 280 unipolar depression patients
exposure_intervention: Mood phase (mania versus bipolar depression) and medication status (drug-free versus drug-treated)
comparator: Healthy controls, drug-free unipolar depression, and drug-treated bipolar patients
outcome: Polysomnographic parameters: total sleep time, latency, efficiency, WASO, REM measures, slow-wave and stage sleep
main_result: Drug-free manic and depressive bipolar patients showed reduced total sleep time and efficiency versus controls; reduced delta sleep characterised depression while shortened REM latency and increased REM density characterised mania, and drug-treated patients differed little from controls except in REM measures.
effect_estimate: Standardised mean differences reported as primary outcome but numerical values NR in abstract
major_limitations: Case-control designs cannot establish direction; publication-bias and heterogeneity assessments not quantified in abstract; sleep measured concurrently with mood state; effect sizes unreported.
individual_applicability: Supports phase-specific objective sleep signatures useful for separating state from trait, and highlights medication as a major confounder relevant to the case.
quality_reason: Objective polysomnography, drug-free stratification and phase comparisons, but cross-sectional primary evidence with numbers unavailable at abstract level.

citation: Giuseppe Barbato, Barbara Tondi, Dario Morra. Sleep in Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Drug-Free Patients. Brain sciences. 2026;16(7):742. doi:10.3390/brainsci16070742. PMID:42512516.
study_design: Systematic review (107 studies) and random-effects meta-analysis of 43 case-control polysomnography studies with Egger's test and funnel-plot assessment
population: 670 patients with bipolar disorder, 520 healthy controls and 280 patients with unipolar depression; drug-free subgroups analysed separately from drug-treated patients; ages NR
exposure_intervention: Mood state (manic versus depressive episode) in drug-free bipolar disorder, and medication status
comparator: Healthy controls; drug-free unipolar depression; drug-treated bipolar patients
outcome: Polysomnographic parameters: total sleep time, sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, wake after sleep onset, REM time/percentage/latency/density, stage 1 and 2, slow wave (delta) sleep
main_result: Total sleep time and sleep efficiency were reduced in both manic and depressive drug-free bipolar patients versus controls, delta sleep was reduced only in depression, and manic patients showed reduced stage 2 and REM time, shortened REM latency and increased REM density; drug-treated bipolar patients differed from controls only in reduced REM percentage, increased REM latency and increased REM density.
effect_estimate: Standardised mean difference was the primary outcome measure, but numeric values and confidence intervals are NR in the abstract
major_limitations: Cross-sectional case-control comparisons rather than within-person longitudinal designs, so episodic causality is not established; no numeric effect sizes in the abstract; substance exposure not characterised; medication status is observational and confounded with illness severity.
individual_applicability: Supports the plausibility that sleep architecture and mood state co-vary and that medication alters these measures, which is directly relevant to interpreting this individual's sleep-linked state changes; group-level only.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis of objective drug-free polysomnography with publication-bias assessment, downgraded for cross-sectional design and unreported numeric estimates.

citation: Maria Faurholt-Jepsen, Asbjørn Risom, Caroline Fussing Bruun, Esben Budtz-Jørgensen, Maj Vinberg, Lars Vedel Kessing. Variation in sleep and instability in mood in patients with bipolar disorder and the association between these - an exploratory post hoc study on daily smartphone-based data from two separate randomised controlled trials. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122149. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122149. PMID:42320790.
study_design: Exploratory post hoc analysis of daily patient-reported smartphone data pooled from two randomised controlled trials
population: 370 patients with bipolar disorder, each contributing six months of daily smartphone ratings
exposure_intervention: Patient-reported variation in sleep over the prior three days and prior week, and average sleep duration
comparator: Within-person periods of lower sleep variation and different sleep durations
outcome: Smartphone-based mood instability
main_result: Greater short-term sleep variation was associated with greater mood instability; increasing sleep up to roughly eight hours was associated with less mood instability while longer sleep was associated with more instability.
major_limitations: Post hoc exploratory analyses; sleep and mood both patient-reported (common-method bias); temporal ordering not established, so mood may drive reported sleep.
individual_applicability: Directly matches the case's proposed within-person sleep-mood coupling and supports the value of prospective self-monitoring, but cannot demonstrate direction of effect.
quality_reason: Large within-person dataset but exploratory, wholly self-reported exposure and outcome with no temporal disentangling.

citation: João Paulo Lima Santos, Lara Labardini, Lauren Keller, Simey Chan, Danella Hafeman, Brant P Hasler, et al. White matter microstructure mediates the link between rest-activity rhythm instability and mania symptoms in individuals at risk for bipolar disorder. medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences. 2026;2026.01.13.26343956. doi:10.64898/2026.01.13.26343956. PMID:41646692.
study_design: Prospective observational study combining 14 days of actigraphy, diffusion MRI and 6-month clinical follow-up
population: 112 youth aged 16-24 years recruited across a spectrum of mania vulnerability (MOODS-SRL)
exposure_intervention: Actigraphy-derived sleep duration variability, sleep onset variability and Circadian Function Index (rest-activity rhythm robustness)
comparator: Higher versus lower rest-activity stability, moderated by baseline mania vulnerability
outcome: White matter orientation dispersion index (NODDI) and clinician-rated mania and depression symptoms at 6 months
main_result: In participants with higher mania vulnerability, lower circadian function (greater rest-activity instability) was associated with greater white matter disorganisation in cingulum and uncinate fasciculus, and uncinate ODI predicted 6-month mania symptoms and fully mediated the circadian-mania association.
effect_estimate: Cingulum β=-0.22, p=0.029; uncinate β=-0.22, p=0.020; mediation β=-0.10, 95% CI -0.14 to -0.02
major_limitations: Moderation and mediation analyses in a modest sample, single follow-up, observational design cannot exclude prodromal mood effects on rest-activity patterns.
individual_applicability: Supports rest-activity irregularity as a state modifier of mania risk in vulnerable young adults, conceptually aligned with the case's proposed amplifier pathway.
quality_reason: Objective exposure, multimodal imaging and prospective symptom outcome, offset by sample size and mediation-model assumptions.

citation: Rebecca E Cooper, Amanda E Baker, Allysa D Quick, Lan Yu, Raul Gonzalez, Duncan B Clark, et al. Sleep Health Dimensions From Wearables and Transdiagnostic Mental Health in Young Adolescents. JAMA pediatrics. 2026;180(5):535-545. doi:10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.0335. PMID:41870441.
study_design: Multicentre longitudinal cohort (ABCD Study) with wearable actigraphy and factor analysis
population: 3393 early adolescents (median age 12 years; 49% female) in the United States
exposure_intervention: Fitbit-derived sleep dimensions over 7-21 days: irregularity, timing, social jetlag, duration, weekend oversleep, continuity
comparator: Within-cohort variation across sleep dimensions; cross-sectional and 1-year prospective contrasts
outcome: Transdiagnostic symptoms: internalizing, externalizing, attention, psychotic-like and mania symptoms
main_result: Greater sleep irregularity was associated with transdiagnostic symptoms cross-sectionally but not prospectively; shorter sleep duration was associated with total, internalizing, externalizing and attention symptoms cross-sectionally and with total, attention and psychotic symptoms one year later. Effect sizes were small.
major_limitations: Early-adolescent sample only, small effect sizes, symptom rather than diagnostic outcomes, irregularity effects did not persist prospectively; consumer-grade device.
individual_applicability: Provides objective, prospective adolescent evidence relevant to the developmental component of the model, but age and measurement differ from an adult clinical case.
quality_reason: Large multicentre cohort with objective sleep exposure, replicated factor structure and prospective outcomes, tempered by small effects and non-adult sample.

citation: Cécile Heinze. Workplace Accommodations and Employment Outcomes Among Employees With Autism: A Systematic Review. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e99353. doi:10.7759/cureus.99353. PMID:41552173.
study_design: Systematic review of 10 empirical studies (randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, surveys, qualitative studies) published 2010-2025; CASP, JBI and RoB appraisal
population: Employed adults with autism; total N and age range NR
exposure_intervention: Workplace accommodations grouped as assistive technology; organizational, sensory and environmental adaptations; supervisory and relational support; skills and psychosocial support
comparator: No accommodation or usual workplace conditions; comparator definitions varied and were not uniformly reported
outcome: Job acquisition, employment stability, job satisfaction and productivity
main_result: Accommodations were generally linked to better job acquisition, stability, satisfaction and productivity, with effectiveness varying by relational quality, disclosure practice and organizational culture. Individually tailored support and respectful supervisory relationships were consistent correlates of benefit, while stigma, ignorance and uneven policy implementation persisted as barriers.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative synthesis without pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Small sample sizes and reliance on self-report across included studies; methodological heterogeneity; exclusion of broader autism groups limits generalizability; observational designs cannot establish that fit moderates impairment.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to occupational accommodation questions for an autistic or ADHD adult in professional work, though the autism-specific and heterogeneous evidence base restricts transfer.
quality_reason: Appropriate multi-tool appraisal and moderate-to-high rated primary studies, but small samples, self-report dependence, and absence of pooled estimates limit confidence.

citation: Leila Jamshidi, Esmaeel Saemi, Mohammadreza Doustan, Thomas Simpson. The Effectiveness of an OPTIMAL Theory-Based Training Program on Throwing Skill Learning in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Physical & occupational therapy in pediatrics. 2026;1-21. doi:10.1080/01942638.2026.2691950. PMID:42411300.
study_design: Randomized controlled experimental study with pretest, practice phase and 24-hour and 72-hour retention tests; convenience sampling with random allocation
population: 30 children with autism spectrum disorder aged 6-11 years (experimental n=15, control n=15)
exposure_intervention: OPTIMAL-theory-based protocol combining autonomy support (self-controlled practice), enhanced expectancy (positive normative feedback) and external focus of attention across 5 training blocks (60 trials)
comparator: Equal number of sessions and trials of overarm throwing practice without the OPTIMAL-theory manipulations
outcome: Overarm throwing accuracy during practice and at short-term (24 h) and long-term (72 h) retention
main_result: The OPTIMAL group outperformed the control group across the practice phase (p=0.032, ηp²=0.15, mean difference 6.67, 95% CI 0.61 to 12.73), short-term retention (p=0.019, ηp²=0.18, mean difference 7.15, 95% CI 1.27 to 13.02) and long-term retention (p=0.023, ηp²=0.17, mean difference 5.70, 95% CI 0.85 to 10.54). The authors state that motivational constructs were not directly measured, so mechanistic conclusions are not warranted.
major_limitations: Small sample (n=30); convenience sampling; pediatric autistic rather than adult ADHD population; blinding not reported; three motivational components bundled and not isolated; putative mediators unmeasured, as the authors acknowledge.
individual_applicability: Provides the only experimental manipulation of motivational context in this set, but the population (autistic children) and outcome (motor skill) differ substantially from adult cognitive and occupational functioning.
quality_reason: Randomized design with reported effect sizes and confidence intervals, but downgraded for very small sample, absent blinding information, bundled intervention components and unmeasured mechanisms.

citation: Merav Asher, Hagit Hochner, Tamar Bar-Shalita, Maayan Agmon. Difficulties in emotion regulation mediate the association between sensory over-responsiveness and motor coordination symptoms in community-dwelling midlife adults: a cross-sectional analysis. Frontiers in psychology. 2026;17:1779854. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1779854. PMID:42293966.
study_design: Cross-sectional analysis within a birth-cohort follow-up (Jerusalem Perinatal Study) using PROCESS mediation model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples
population: 89 community-dwelling midlife adults, mean age 45.6 years (range 44.3-46.9), 47% women
exposure_intervention: Sensory over-responsiveness (Sensory Responsiveness Questionnaire)
comparator: Lower sensory over-responsiveness; no clinically diagnosed DCD comparison group
outcome: Adult DCD symptomatology (Adult Developmental Coordination Disorders/Dyspraxia Checklist subscales B and C), with difficulties in emotion regulation (DERS) as mediator; physical activity covaried
main_result: Sensory over-responsiveness predicted adult DCD symptomatology, but the direct effect became non-significant once difficulties in emotion regulation were entered while the indirect effect remained significant, a pattern consistent with full mediation.
effect_estimate: Total effect B = 0.343 (SE 0.105, p = 0.002); direct effect B = 0.151 (SE 0.095, p = 0.114); indirect effect B = 0.192 (95% CI 0.084-0.323)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional so directionality cannot be established; n = 89; all measures self-report questionnaires (common-method bias) with no performance-based motor testing; no attention or ADHD measure; community sample without DCD diagnosis or childhood-onset documentation.
individual_applicability: The only extracted record measuring adult motor-coordination symptoms; shows adult motor complaints covary with sensory and emotion-regulation factors, which are competing explanations in this case.
quality_reason: Small cross-sectional self-report study; mediation inference rests on concurrent measurement of all three constructs.

citation: Dimitrios Adamis, Jake Tiernan, Natasha Langan, Blánaid Gavin, Fiona McNicholas. Effects of medications on sleep quality, insomnia, and circadian rhythm in adults with ADHD: A pragmatic longitudinal study. Sleep medicine. 2026;138:108721. doi:10.1016/j.sleep.2025.108721. PMID:41397339.
study_design: Prospective observational longitudinal study with five assessments over 18 months
population: 149 adults with diagnosed ADHD attending a specialist clinic in Ireland
exposure_intervention: Medication use (stimulants, non-stimulants, antidepressants, antipsychotics), comorbidity, demographics and autistic traits
comparator: Adults with ADHD not using the respective medication class; within-cohort comparisons over time
outcome: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (SDS-CL-17), chronotype
main_result: Stimulant use was associated with better sleep quality and lower insomnia odds and non-stimulants with lower insomnia and circadian disorder odds, whereas antidepressant use, female sex, higher BMI and greater psychiatric comorbidity were associated with worse sleep; autistic traits and chronotype showed no independent associations.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Observational, non-randomised medication exposure with confounding by indication; self-reported sleep outcomes; specialist clinic sample; no cognitive or functional outcomes.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant to disentangling medication and comorbidity contributions to sleep disturbance in an adult with ADHD, but no causal or cognitive-outcome inference is possible.
quality_reason: Prospective repeated measures in a directly relevant adult ADHD population, but observational treatment exposure and subjective outcomes without effect estimates in the abstract.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Barbara Franke, Catharina A Hartman, Pieter J Hoekstra, Nanda N J Rommelse, et al. Growing up with ADHD: findings from an 18-year longitudinal follow-up study of adults with childhood ADHD, their siblings, and controls. Psychiatry research. 2026;364:117308. doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2026.117308. PMID:42365682.
study_design: Prospective 18-year longitudinal follow-up cohort with sibling and control comparison groups
population: Adults with childhood ADHD (n=154, mean age 27.4, 68% male), siblings without childhood ADHD (n=138), controls (n=129)
exposure_intervention: Childhood ADHD diagnosis; secondary contrast of persistent versus remitted adult ADHD
comparator: Siblings without childhood ADHD and unrelated controls
outcome: Adult psychiatric status, behavioural/emotional problems, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognition, physical health, healthcare use
main_result: Childhood ADHD was associated with worse adult functioning on more than 60% of outcomes across all domains; siblings functioned comparably to controls; persistent ADHD showed worse functioning than remitted ADHD on psychiatric, behavioural/emotional, adaptive and physical health outcomes, while both ADHD groups were worse than controls.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as small to large; numeric estimates and confidence intervals NR in abstract
major_limitations: Attrition over 18 years not quantified in abstract; sex imbalance across groups (68% vs 35% vs 40% male); outcome instruments and covariate adjustment not specified; substantial within-group heterogeneity acknowledged.
individual_applicability: Closest available analogue to a lifelong developmental trajectory question, but group-level and cannot establish that this individual's adult difficulties originate in childhood ADHD.
quality_reason: Long prospective follow-up with two comparison groups is a strong design, downgraded for unreported effect sizes, unclear attrition, and abstract-only appraisal.

citation: Cagatay Ermis, Antti Tanskanen, Olivier Corbeil, Johannes Lieslehto, Eduard Vieta, Christoph U Correll, et al. Reduced risk of cause-specific hospitalisations and all-cause hospitalisation/mortality during treatment with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder medications in the course of bipolar disorder: a Swedish registry-based within-subject cohort study. BMJ mental health. 2026;29(1):e302159. doi:10.1136/bmjment-2025-302159. PMID:41856665.
study_design: Nationwide register-based within-individual cohort study (each person serves as own control), Sweden 2006-2021
population: 17,971 individuals with bipolar disorder who used any ADHD medication; mean age 32.0 (SD 11.6) years; 37.6% male; 88.9% with ADHD; mean follow-up 8.9 (SD 4.4) years
exposure_intervention: Add-on ADHD medication (mainly methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine; also atomoxetine, modafinil) to concomitant antipsychotics and/or mood stabilizers
comparator: Within-person periods of antipsychotic and/or mood stabilizer treatment without ADHD medication
outcome: Psychiatric hospitalization (primary); substance-related, somatic, and mania-related hospitalization; all-cause hospitalization or mortality
main_result: Add-on stimulant use was associated with lower risks of psychiatric hospitalization, substance-use-related hospitalization, and all-cause hospitalization or mortality, with no increase in somatic or mania-related hospitalization; lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate drove the effects while atomoxetine was not associated with reduced psychiatric hospitalization.
effect_estimate: Psychiatric hospitalization aHR 0.89 (95% CI 0.85-0.93); substance-related 0.75 (0.70-0.81); all-cause hospitalization/mortality 0.90 (0.87-0.93); somatic 1.00 (0.90-1.12); mania-related 0.93 (0.72-1.20); lisdexamfetamine 0.81 (0.75-0.87); methylphenidate 0.92 (0.88-0.97)
major_limitations: Register outcomes are coarse and capture no speech, salience, or symptom-level change; within-individual design removes stable but not time-varying confounding (adherence, illness phase); stimulants were almost always co-prescribed with mood stabilizers or antipsychotics.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant to an adult with co-occurring bipolar disorder and ADHD traits considering stimulant treatment under mood stabilization; does not speak to unmonitored or unstabilized use.
quality_reason: Large national within-person cohort minimizing between-person confounding, downgraded for outcome coarseness, residual time-varying confounding, and absence of symptom-level measures.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. The risk of psychosis associated with cannabis use by people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of 3 heterogeneous studies; risk of bias rated fair (k=1) and good (k=2)
population: People with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder exposed to cannabis; sample sizes, ages and diagnostic methods NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use in individuals with ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD who use cannabis, and/or ADHD individuals without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis outcomes
main_result: Two of three studies indirectly suggested that cannabis use does not increase psychosis risk among people with ADHD, and the third indicated that cannabis had a similar impact on psychosis risk in people with and without ADHD; the authors conclude there is very little evidence for a heightened ADHD-specific risk.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates; synthesis without meta-analysis)
major_limitations: Only three studies, two of which addressed the question indirectly, almost certainly underpowered to detect an interaction, exposure and diagnostic ascertainment not described, and absence of evidence is reported rather than evidence of absence.
individual_applicability: Directly targets the proposed ADHD-by-cannabis interaction relevant to this case, but the evidence base is too thin to exclude a clinically meaningful individual effect.
quality_reason: Very small number of studies with indirect inference and no quantitative synthesis, despite generally fair-to-good individual study ratings.

citation: Priyanka Panchal, Natalie Nelissen, Niall M McGowan, Lauren Z Atkinson, Kate E A Saunders, Paul J Harrison, et al. Identifying Mood Instability and Circadian Rest-Activity Patterns Using Digital Remote Monitoring and Actigraphy in Participants at Risk for Bipolar Disorder. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(5):e70156. doi:10.1111/bdi.70156. PMID:42464599.
study_design: Prospective 10-week digital remote monitoring study with actigraphy
population: 74 adults: 37 scoring >7 on the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (high MDQ, elevated bipolar risk) and 37 scoring <5 (low MDQ)
exposure_intervention: GENEActiv actigraphy-derived circadian rest-activity indices over 10 weeks
comparator: Low-MDQ participants and within-group variation in circadian indices
outcome: Daily mood and subjective state instability, weekly clinician ratings of depression, mania and anxiety
main_result: High MDQ score predicted greater mood and subjective-state instability, more negative affect and altered circadian activity profiles, but mood and subjective-state instability appeared unrelated to circadian indices.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Small sample, risk defined by questionnaire rather than diagnosis, 10-week window, null circadian-instability association may reflect limited power or index choice.
individual_applicability: Directly challenges the assumption that objectively measured circadian variation explains mood instability in bipolar-risk adults, tempering the case's proposed mechanism.
quality_reason: Prospective objective monitoring with a comparison group, but small screening-defined sample and a null finding of uncertain precision.

citation: Aja Louise Murray, Katie Dryburgh, Edmund J S Sonuga-Barke. Identifying Candidate Mediators Linking ADHD Symptoms and Internalising Problems in Adolescence: An Exploratory Longitudinal Mediation Analysis. Journal of attention disorders. 2026;30(8):986-998. doi:10.1177/10870547261419589. PMID:41789525.
study_design: Exploratory longitudinal mediation analysis using regularised structural equation modelling (lasso)
population: Millennium Cohort Study; 2,607 male and 2,791 female participants assessed at ages 11, 14 and 17
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms in adolescence
comparator: Lower ADHD symptom levels within the cohort
outcome: Internalising (anxiety and depressive) symptoms, with 14 candidate mediators including peer problems, conduct problems, self-esteem, injuries, parental relationships, academic performance, risky decision-making, parental mental health, educational motivation and general health
main_result: Regularisation did not de-select any of the 14 candidate mediators, but only two were statistically significant. The authors conclude there may be many mediators of small effect linking ADHD symptoms to later internalising problems, and identify self-esteem and parental mental health as priority mechanisms for future causal and interventional research.
effect_estimate: NR (individual path estimates and confidence intervals not reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Explicitly exploratory with 14 simultaneous mediators and no confirmatory replication; observational, so mediation remains associational; abstract does not identify which two paths were significant with estimates.
individual_applicability: Tempers the expectation that any single anxiety- or rejection-related mediator carries the functional burden; suggests distributed small effects rather than one dominant pathway.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised national cohort with three waves and appropriate regularisation, but exploratory framing, absent effect estimates and untested causal assumptions limit inference.

citation: Simin Kang, Zhao Fu, Qiurong Li, Li Yang, Qingjiu Cao. Adult-diagnosed and childhood-diagnosed attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: cognitive and environmental contributions to symptom severity across different age of diagnosis. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1782999. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1782999. PMID:42147013.
study_design: Cross-sectional comparative study with hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analysis
population: 72 adults with ADHD: 37 childhood-diagnosed (26.32 +/- 4.69 years) and 35 adult-diagnosed (25.63 +/- 4.89 years), diagnosed by structured interview
exposure_intervention: Executive function (BRIEF-A) and environmental factors: childhood trauma (CTQ), resilience (CD-RISC), parental bonding (PBI)
comparator: Childhood-diagnosed versus adult-diagnosed ADHD groups; relative variance contribution of executive versus environmental predictors
outcome: ADHD core symptom severity (ASRS inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity); emotional symptoms (SAS, SDS)
main_result: Executive function was the strongest and most consistent predictor of both inattention (beta 0.64, p<0.001) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (beta 0.47, p<0.001), whereas environmental factors contributed minimal additional explanatory power, with only a modest association between parental overprotection and inattention (beta 0.28, p=0.016). No diagnosis-specific moderation effects were observed. Adult-diagnosed participants showed lower childhood symptoms but similar adult severity, with more psychiatric comorbidity and emotional distress.
effect_estimate: beta 0.64 (inattention) and 0.47 (hyperactivity-impulsivity) for executive function; beta 0.28 (p=0.016) for parental overprotection; confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Small single-site sample; cross-sectional; retrospective childhood trauma and parenting recall; outcome is symptom severity rather than real-world functional impairment; no formal mediation testing.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult with late-recognised ADHD, and supports executive rather than adversity-related variables as the dominant symptom correlate, but small-sample and symptom-level outcomes limit transfer.
quality_reason: Structured diagnostic ascertainment is a strength, but low power, cross-sectional design and retrospective exposure measures constrain interpretation.

citation: Yujuan Zu, Tao Pang, Lingxue Luo, Chao Liufu, Zixuan Xu, Luxian Lv, et al. Dynamic relationship and pleiotropic loci of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with sleep traits. Translational psychiatry. 2026;10.1038/s41398-026-04166-4. doi:10.1038/s41398-026-04166-4. PMID:42297780.
study_design: Longitudinal cohort analysis (ABCD) with latent growth curve modelling, polygenic scores and pleiotropy analyses
population: 11,288 children/adolescents (52.1% male) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms, ADHD medication status, and genetic liability; sleep assessed with the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children
comparator: Within-cohort longitudinal contrasts and cross-cohort genetic comparison (UK Biobank insomnia)
outcome: Sleep disturbance traits over time and shared genetic loci
main_result: ADHD and sleep traits were positively correlated, ADHD medication weakened the association, and ADHD symptoms significantly predicted later sleep traits with a lag effect; polygenic associations were significant but explained very little variance and 14 pleiotropic loci were identified.
effect_estimate: Polygenic scores explained approximately 0.28-0.30% of variance; other estimates NR
major_limitations: Paediatric/adolescent sample, parent/self-reported sleep scale, lagged associations do not prove causation, very small genetic effect sizes; medication effects potentially confounded.
individual_applicability: Supports the counterclaim that ADHD symptom severity and treatment can drive apparent sleep problems rather than the reverse, an important alternative for the case's temporal interpretation.
quality_reason: Very large longitudinal cohort with genetic triangulation, but subjective sleep measure, non-adult sample and minimal explained variance.

citation: Yuan You, Tom McAdams, Yasmin I Ahmadzadeh, Tabea Schoeler, Filip Marzecki, Helena M S Zavos. The role of comorbid childhood mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions in the persistence of ADHD symptoms: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines. 2026;67(2):183-201. doi:10.1111/jcpp.70028. PMID:40801243.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel random-effects models; 26 studies
population: Children with ADHD followed to later developmental stages
exposure_intervention: Childhood comorbid internalizing, externalizing and neurodevelopmental conditions
comparator: ADHD without the specified comorbidity
outcome: Persistence of ADHD symptoms into later developmental stages
main_result: Childhood externalizing and, more weakly, internalizing comorbidity predicted ADHD persistence, but adjustment attenuated externalizing and eliminated the internalizing association; neurodevelopmental comorbidity did not predict persistence, and the externalizing effect appeared only with parent-reported data.
effect_estimate: Internalizing d=0.19 (adjusted d=0.06, non-significant); externalizing d=0.31 (adjusted d=0.24); neurodevelopmental comorbidity non-significant
major_limitations: Informant-dependent findings suggest common-method bias; residual confounding acknowledged; heterogeneous definitions of persistence and follow-up intervals.
individual_applicability: Shows persistence estimates are sensitive to comorbidity and informant, relevant given this individual's reported anxiety, mood and substance history.
quality_reason: Appropriate multilevel synthesis with adjusted analyses, limited by observational primary data and informant confounding.

citation: Rachael Sanders, Rachel Le Rossignol. Don't disable me: A scoping review of ADHD employees' experiences of working in open-plan offices. Work (Reading, Mass.). 2026;10519815261449927. doi:10.1177/10519815261449927. PMID:42132039.
study_design: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework; four databases plus reference-list searching; 22 items included
population: Adults with ADHD employed in open-plan office environments; total N and age range NR
exposure_intervention: Open-plan office work environment and related workplace conditions
comparator: Alternative or enclosed office environments and the general workforce; comparator largely implicit and NR
outcome: Creativity, productivity, wellbeing and workplace success for ADHD employees; nature and scope of existing research
main_result: The review identified 22 pieces of literature and a significant gap in empirical research on ADHD workers in open-plan offices. While empirical evidence was sparse, anecdotal evidence, professional opinion, the nature of ADHD and participants' lived experiences indicated that open-plan offices can impede the creativity and productivity of ADHD employees, with possible effects on the general workforce and organizational performance.
effect_estimate: NR; no pooled or comparative effect estimates reported
major_limitations: Predominantly non-empirical sources (anecdote, professional opinion, lived experience); no risk-of-bias appraisal reported; no controlled comparison of environments; publication and advocacy framing bias likely.
individual_applicability: Relevant to the hypothesis that standardized or high-stimulation work settings amplify impairment, but the near-absence of empirical data means it functions mainly to show the evidence gap.
quality_reason: Scoping design with explicitly sparse empirical evidence, no critical appraisal, and conclusions resting largely on opinion and lived-experience accounts.

citation: Carlos López-Pinar, Benjamin Selaskowski, Marcel Schulze, Martin Oscarsson, Javier Fenollar-Cortés, Margaret H Sibley, et al. Cognitive behavioral therapy effects on global functioning, domain-specific functioning, and quality of life in adult ADHD: A comprehensive meta-analysis. Behaviour research and therapy. 2026;201:105026. doi:10.1016/j.brat.2026.105026. PMID:41936228.
study_design: Comprehensive meta-analysis of 70 studies (38 RCTs, 4 non-randomized, 24 single-arm, 4 single-case) with GRADE
population: 5152 adults with ADHD
exposure_intervention: Cognitive behavioral therapy targeting executive dysfunction and emotion regulation
comparator: Control groups (between-group) and pre-treatment baseline (within-subject)
outcome: Global functioning, quality of life, domain-specific (social, occupational, educational) functioning at post-treatment and follow-up
main_result: Moderate improvement in global functioning that increased at follow-up, strongest for occupational functioning, moderate for social, limited for academic; quality-of-life effects were smaller and non-significant at follow-up, and symptom change did not predict functional gains.
effect_estimate: Global functioning SMD=0.47 post-treatment, 0.67 at follow-up; QoL smaller and non-significant at follow-up; confidence intervals NR in abstract
major_limitations: Inclusion of single-arm and single-case designs inflates within-subject estimates; risk of bias, self-report reliance, Western samples, and typically 3-month follow-ups; no confidence intervals reported in abstract.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to an adult seeking functional (especially occupational) benefit from executive-function-focused therapy, though mechanisms and long-term durability remain unclear.
quality_reason: Large adult-specific meta-analysis with formal risk-of-bias and GRADE appraisal, downgraded for design heterogeneity, self-report outcomes, and short follow-up.

citation: Aida Bikic, Brian Reichow, Spencer A McCauley, Karim Ibrahim, Denis G Sukhodolsky. Meta-analysis of organizational skills interventions for children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Clinical psychology review. 2017;52:108-123. doi:10.1016/j.cpr.2016.12.004. PMID:28088557.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
population: 1054 children and adolescents with ADHD (576 intervention, 478 control) across 12 RCTs
exposure_intervention: Organizational skills training (OST) targeting management of time and materials
comparator: Parent education, treatment-as-usual, or waitlist control
outcome: Teacher- and parent-rated organizational skills, inattention, teacher-rated academic performance, GPA
main_result: Moderate to large improvements in organizational skills and smaller gains in inattention and academic performance.
effect_estimate: Organizational skills: teacher g=0.54 (95% CI 0.17-0.91), parent g=0.83 (0.32-1.34); inattention: teacher g=0.26 (0.01-0.52), parent g=0.56 (0.38-0.74); academic performance g=0.33 (0.14-0.51); GPA g=0.29 (0.07-0.51)
major_limitations: Pediatric samples only; largely unblinded rater-reported outcomes with larger parent than teacher effects, suggesting expectancy/reporter bias; durability and harms not reported in abstract.
individual_applicability: Supports plausibility that explicit organizational scaffolding aids task management, but effects are demonstrated in children rather than a high-functioning adult professional.
quality_reason: Registered meta-analysis of RCTs with quantified effects and bias assessment, downgraded for rater non-blinding and pediatric-only samples.

citation: Lisanne Scholz, Jana Werle, Alexandra Philipsen, Marcel Schulze, Julien Collonges, Jochen Gensichen. Effects and feasibility of psychological interventions to reduce inattention symptoms in adults with ADHD: a systematic review. Journal of mental health (Abingdon, England). 2023;32(1):307-320. doi:10.1080/09638237.2020.1818189. PMID:32954909.
study_design: Systematic review of 19 randomized controlled trials with feasibility appraisal
population: Adults with ADHD (total n NR)
exposure_intervention: Psychological interventions grouped as ADHD coaching, neurofeedback, cognitive training, psychoeducation, and behavioral therapy
comparator: Inactive controls and active/other control conditions
outcome: Inattention symptoms; feasibility indicators (session number, session length, setting, provider qualification)
main_result: Behavioral therapy reduced inattention symptoms relative to inactive controls, whereas neurofeedback, cognitive training, and psychoeducation showed no effects; longer or individual formats did not outperform shorter or group formats.
effect_estimate: Behavioral therapy SMD range 0.44-1.71 versus inactive controls; other modalities non-significant (estimates NR)
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis without pooling; comparisons mainly against inactive controls, inflating apparent benefit; coaching evidence sparse; no durability or harms data.
individual_applicability: Suggests that not all executive-support modalities are equivalent, and that structured behavioral approaches have the better adult evidence base.
quality_reason: Systematic RCT review in adults with explicit null findings, downgraded for absence of meta-analysis and reliance on inactive comparators.

citation: Cécile Heinze. Workplace Accommodations and Employment Outcomes Among Employees With Autism: A Systematic Review. Cureus. 2025;17(12):e99353. doi:10.7759/cureus.99353. PMID:41552173.
study_design: Systematic review of 10 empirical studies (randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, surveys, qualitative studies) published 2010-2025; CASP, JBI and RoB appraisal
population: Employed adults with autism; total N and age range NR
exposure_intervention: Workplace accommodations grouped as assistive technology; organizational, sensory and environmental adaptations; supervisory and relational support; skills and psychosocial support
comparator: No accommodation or usual workplace conditions; comparator definitions varied and were not uniformly reported
outcome: Job acquisition, employment stability, job satisfaction and productivity
main_result: Accommodations were generally linked to better job acquisition, stability, satisfaction and productivity, with effectiveness varying by relational quality, disclosure practice and organizational culture. Individually tailored support and respectful supervisory relationships were consistent correlates of benefit, while stigma, ignorance and uneven policy implementation persisted as barriers.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative synthesis without pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Small sample sizes and reliance on self-report across included studies; methodological heterogeneity; exclusion of broader autism groups limits generalizability; observational designs cannot establish that fit moderates impairment.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to occupational accommodation questions for an autistic or ADHD adult in professional work, though the autism-specific and heterogeneous evidence base restricts transfer.
quality_reason: Appropriate multi-tool appraisal and moderate-to-high rated primary studies, but small samples, self-report dependence, and absence of pooled estimates limit confidence.

citation: Ana Muiño Tato. Systematic Review of Autism in Women: Invisibilised Profiles and Gender Bias. Revista de neurologia. 2026;81(4):49367. doi:10.31083/RN49367. PMID:42052784.
study_design: Systematic review of 26 studies (2015-2025) spanning observational, psychometric, technological, quasi-experimental and qualitative designs
population: Females assessed for or diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder
exposure_intervention: Female sex, social camouflaging, and standard diagnostic instruments
comparator: Males assessed for autism; standard versus gender-sensitive assessment approaches
outcome: Age at diagnosis, diagnostic identification rates, instrument sensitivity
main_result: Diagnosis was consistently delayed in girls, standard instruments showed reduced sensitivity to less externalizing presentations, and social camouflaging plus comorbidity moderated identification, indicating that compensation-related processes can delay recognition.
effect_estimate: NR; reported male-to-female diagnostic ratios up to 4.6:1 in the Spanish educational context; mean CRF-QS quality 15.7
major_limitations: Autism rather than ADHD; camouflaging largely inferred from self-report and clinical observation; heterogeneous designs preclude pooling; no direct measure of intelligence as the compensating factor.
individual_applicability: Supports delayed recognition through compensation as a real phenomenon, but the demonstrated driver is gendered presentation and instrument sensitivity, not high intelligence.
quality_reason: PRISMA-based review with quality appraisal and predominantly low risk of bias, downgraded for construct heterogeneity and indirectness to intelligence-specific masking.

citation: Natalia G Docteur, Hayley G P Huston, Avery A Krupa, Brandy L Callahan. A systematic review of neuroimaging studies of adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic and genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2026;28(1):259-276. doi:10.1080/19585969.2026.2700984. PMID:42472451.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review of neuroimaging studies; 13 studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal
population: Adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD
exposure_intervention: ADHD diagnosis, symptom load or polygenic risk
comparator: Non-ADHD control participants
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations; cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD-associated fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic alterations persisted into middle and older adulthood, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation interpreted as compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR; 11 of 13 studies rated low risk of bias
major_limitations: Small number of heterogeneous studies; compensation is an interpretation of activation patterns, not a measured behavioural compensation outcome; cross-sectional designs predominate.
individual_applicability: Consistent with a neurodevelopmental substrate persisting in adulthood, but neuroimaging group differences cannot diagnose or characterise one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with formal risk-of-bias appraisal and mostly low-risk studies, downgraded for few studies and indirect outcomes.

citation: Natalia G Docteur, Hayley G P Huston, Avery A Krupa, Brandy L Callahan. A systematic review of neuroimaging studies of adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic and genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2026;28(1):259-276. doi:10.1080/19585969.2026.2700984. PMID:42472451.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review of 13 neuroimaging studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale risk of bias (11 of 13 low risk)
population: Adults aged 35 years and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD, compared with controls; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Clinical ADHD diagnosis, elevated ADHD symptoms, or ADHD genetic risk in middle and later life
comparator: Controls without ADHD diagnosis or elevated ADHD risk
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations, with summarised cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD groups showed alterations in fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic systems implicated in executive control and attention; middle-aged adults with clinical ADHD showed more widespread cortical structural differences whereas older adults showed mainly frontal abnormalities, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation consistent with compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR (narrative synthesis; no pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Only 13 mostly cross-sectional studies, no control for current mood state, sleep or substance exposure, imaging-to-function inference is uncertain, and the authors state that longitudinal investigation is needed to clarify persistence.
individual_applicability: Consistent with ADHD-associated neurobiology persisting into mid-life, which is the age band of this case, but imaging group differences do not establish trait-level functional impairment in one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with mostly low-risk-of-bias studies, downgraded for small number of cross-sectional studies, absent state controls, and narrative synthesis.

citation: Leila Jamshidi, Esmaeel Saemi, Mohammadreza Doustan, Thomas Simpson. The Effectiveness of an OPTIMAL Theory-Based Training Program on Throwing Skill Learning in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Physical & occupational therapy in pediatrics. 2026;1-21. doi:10.1080/01942638.2026.2691950. PMID:42411300.
study_design: Randomized controlled experimental study with pretest, practice phase and 24-hour and 72-hour retention tests; convenience sampling with random allocation
population: 30 children with autism spectrum disorder aged 6-11 years (experimental n=15, control n=15)
exposure_intervention: OPTIMAL-theory-based protocol combining autonomy support (self-controlled practice), enhanced expectancy (positive normative feedback) and external focus of attention across 5 training blocks (60 trials)
comparator: Equal number of sessions and trials of overarm throwing practice without the OPTIMAL-theory manipulations
outcome: Overarm throwing accuracy during practice and at short-term (24 h) and long-term (72 h) retention
main_result: The OPTIMAL group outperformed the control group across the practice phase (p=0.032, ηp²=0.15, mean difference 6.67, 95% CI 0.61 to 12.73), short-term retention (p=0.019, ηp²=0.18, mean difference 7.15, 95% CI 1.27 to 13.02) and long-term retention (p=0.023, ηp²=0.17, mean difference 5.70, 95% CI 0.85 to 10.54). The authors state that motivational constructs were not directly measured, so mechanistic conclusions are not warranted.
major_limitations: Small sample (n=30); convenience sampling; pediatric autistic rather than adult ADHD population; blinding not reported; three motivational components bundled and not isolated; putative mediators unmeasured, as the authors acknowledge.
individual_applicability: Provides the only experimental manipulation of motivational context in this set, but the population (autistic children) and outcome (motor skill) differ substantially from adult cognitive and occupational functioning.
quality_reason: Randomized design with reported effect sizes and confidence intervals, but downgraded for very small sample, absent blinding information, bundled intervention components and unmeasured mechanisms.

citation: Beliz Yegencik, Beth T Bell, Emre Deniz. School-based randomized controlled trials for ADHD and accompanying impairments: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in psychology. 2025;16:1611145. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1611145. PMID:40761448.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
population: School-aged children and young people (4-18 years) with ADHD; 26 RCTs identified, 22 (n=1962) meta-analysed
exposure_intervention: School-based interventions (educational setting redesign and support programmes) from 1980-2024
comparator: Control conditions within included RCTs (NR)
outcome: Combined ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, academic performance, social skills, externalising problems
main_result: School-based trials improved combined ADHD symptoms, inattention, academic performance, social skills, and externalising problems, but had no significant effect on hyperactivity/impulsivity.
effect_estimate: Combined ADHD d=-0.28 (p<.0001); inattention d=-0.33 (p<.0001); academic d=0.37 (p<.0001); social skills d=0.28 (p<.001); externalising d=-0.32 (p=.001); hyperactivity/impulsivity d=-0.09 (p=.22); CIs NR
major_limitations: Search restricted to three journals; pediatric educational setting rather than adult occupational redesign; high heterogeneity and probable reporter bias acknowledged; confidence intervals not reported in abstract.
individual_applicability: Provides indirect support that redesigning the environment reduces some impairments, but does not test adult workplace redesign such as in hospital medicine.
quality_reason: Quantified meta-analysis but limited search scope, rater-based outcomes, heterogeneity, and pediatric-only setting.

citation: Gustavo Mortari Ferreira, Calliandra Maria de Souza Silva, Alexandre Sampaio Rodrigues Pereira, Larissa Sousa Silva Bonasser, Maria Gabriela do Nascimento Araújo, Marcelly de Oliveira Barros, et al. Cognitive Profile of Autism and Intellectual Disorder in Wechsler's Scales: Meta-Analysis. European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education. 2026;16(1):12. doi:10.3390/ejihpe16010012. PMID:41590022.
study_design: Meta-analysis of 31 studies using WISC-IV, WISC-V, WAIS-III and WAIS-IV; random-effects models with Hedges' g against a normative reference (mean 100, SD 15)
population: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and co-occurring ASD plus ID; ages spanning child and adult test versions; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic group (ASD, ID, ASD+ID) assessed on Wechsler cognitive index profiles
comparator: Normative Wechsler reference values and between-group comparisons across diagnostic categories
outcome: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual/Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed, Visual Processing indices and Full-Scale IQ
main_result: ASD showed a distinct profile with greater impairment in Processing Speed and Working Memory while Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual/Fluid Reasoning and Visual Processing remained close to normative scores. ID and ASD+ID showed generalized deficits across all indices, with the lowest scores in Full-Scale IQ and broad effects above g = -2.5. No significant differences emerged between Wechsler versions or age-based test types. Heterogeneity was high in ASD and ID but negligible in ASD+ID due to few studies.
effect_estimate: ASD: relative impairment in PSI and WMI with VCI, PRI/FRI and VPI near normative (mean 100, SD 15); ID and ASD+ID: broad effects above g = -2.5 across indices; index-specific point estimates NR in abstract
major_limitations: High heterogeneity in ASD and ID subgroups; few studies in the ASD+ID group; clinically referred samples subject to ascertainment bias; cross-sectional psychometric data with no functional or occupational outcome; ADHD not examined.
individual_applicability: Supports interpreting cognitive profiles by index scatter rather than global IQ, which is relevant to the compensation and trade-off hypotheses, but provides no ADHD data and no real-world outcome link.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis across 31 studies with a consistent normative reference and version-invariance testing, downgraded for high heterogeneity, referral bias and absence of functional outcomes.

citation: Merete B Bjerrum, Preben U Pedersen, Palle Larsen. Living with symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adulthood: a systematic review of qualitative evidence. JBI database of systematic reviews and implementation reports. 2017;15(4):1080-1153. doi:10.11124/JBISRIR-2017-003357. PMID:28398986.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-synthesis of qualitative studies (JBI methodology)
population: Adults with confirmed ADHD diagnosis across 10 included qualitative studies (103 findings)
exposure_intervention: Self-generated and externally provided strategies: reminders, task structuring, coaching by close others, supervisor-imposed structure and clear task rules
comparator: None (qualitative synthesis without comparator)
outcome: Experienced management of symptoms, social/academic/workplace functioning, perceived protective factors
main_result: Reminders, performing tasks within a given structure, coaching by others, and supervisor-provided task structure and clear rules were reported as protective factors supporting daily and occupational functioning.
effect_estimate: NR (qualitative synthesis; four synthesized findings from 16 categories)
major_limitations: Self-report and interpretive synthesis without objective performance measures; no comparator, effect size, or durability data; risk of positive-experience selection.
individual_applicability: Closely mirrors the narrator's reported benefit from checklists, reminders, and external structure, but is experiential rather than causal evidence.
quality_reason: Well-conducted qualitative synthesis of adults with ADHD, but design cannot establish effectiveness or durability of scaffolds.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies, with multiple regression on pooled correlation matrices to control symptom overlap
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples; total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Symptom dimensions of ADHD-inattention (ADHD-I), ADHD-hyperactivity/impulsivity (ADHD-HI) and cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS)
comparator: Each symptom dimension after controlling shared variance with the other dimensions
outcome: Cognitive correlates including social cognition, motor coordination, perceptual-motor functioning, attention, inhibition, working memory, processing speed
main_result: Profiles looked similar in bivariate correlations but diverged in regression: ADHD-HI was associated with weaker social cognition and focused/sustained attention yet better motor coordination; ADHD-I with weaker intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, perceptual-motor functioning and memory; CDS with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: ADHD-HI: social cognition and attention betas -.24 to -.11 (p<.001); motor coordination beta = .14 (p<.001). ADHD-I: betas -.21 to -.10 (p<.01). CDS: betas -.29 to -.13 (p<.001).
major_limitations: All constituent studies cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; dimensions defined by rating scales rather than diagnoses; pooling across child and adult samples; laboratory/rating cognitive proxies rather than real-world social or motor functioning.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult reporting both inattentive and hyperactive features, but findings are group-level, symptom-scale based, and cannot attribute this person's social or motor difficulties to a specific dimension.
quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Jaap Oosterlaan, Marjolein Luman. Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Predictors of Adult Psychiatric Outcomes of Childhood Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2026;65(2):231-249. doi:10.1016/j.jaac.2025.04.012. PMID:40287009.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42022320887); 36 studies, 119 predictors, 10 meta-analysed
population: Adults diagnosed with ADHD in childhood
exposure_intervention: Childhood predictors including IQ, stimulant treatment history, symptom subtype, comorbidity, socioeconomic status
comparator: Adults with remitted versus persistent childhood ADHD; predictor contrasts within cohorts
outcome: ADHD persistence into adulthood; substance use disorder; major depressive disorder
main_result: Higher childhood IQ was associated with slightly lower odds of adult ADHD persistence, while stimulant treatment history was associated with higher persistence; persistence itself predicted substance use disorder and major depressive disorder.
effect_estimate: Childhood IQ OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.00, p=.039); stimulant history OR 1.88 (1.28-2.75); persistence to SUD OR 2.12 (1.53-3.17); to MDD OR 3.19 (1.71-5.95)
major_limitations: Authors note methodological shortcomings across the literature; confounding by indication for stimulant history; IQ effect per-unit and near-null; heterogeneity and NOS quality mixed.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether high intelligence signals masked persistence or genuine remission, but the IQ association is tiny and group-level.
quality_reason: Preregistered meta-analysis with quality appraisal, downgraded for observational primary studies, confounding, and small numbers of studies per predictor.

citation: Yanxi Li, Lina Zhang. Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Combined with Pharmacotherapy Versus Pharmacotherapy Alone in Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of attention disorders. 2024;28(3):279-292. doi:10.1177/10870547231214969. PMID:38084075.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 randomized controlled trials
population: Adults with ADHD (total n NR)
exposure_intervention: Cognitive behavioral therapy combined with pharmacotherapy
comparator: Pharmacotherapy alone
outcome: ADHD symptom improvement at post-treatment, 3, 6, and 9 months
main_result: Combined CBT plus medication was superior to medication alone at 3 months, but no statistically significant differences remained at 6 and 9 months; subgroup effects varied by country income level.
effect_estimate: NR (pooled effect sizes and confidence intervals not reported in abstract)
major_limitations: Only six trials, no effect estimates in abstract, unexplained country/economy moderation, and unclear attrition at longer follow-ups.
individual_applicability: Important durability caveat: therapy-based scaffolding benefits may attenuate without continued input, relevant to planning ongoing supports.
quality_reason: Small number of trials, missing quantitative estimates, and post hoc subgroup interpretation limit confidence in the durability conclusion.

citation: Blandine French, Victoria Newell, Gamze Nalbant, Hannah Wright, David Daley, Sarah Cassidy. Adverse outcomes for autistic people: an umbrella review of mental health, physical health, social and lifestyle domains. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1702822. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1702822. PMID:42199907.
study_design: Umbrella review of 134 systematic, meta-analytic and narrative reviews identified from 13,841 records; five databases searched to June 2024; inductive narrative synthesis
population: Autistic people across the lifespan as represented in review-level evidence; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Autism diagnosis as exposure across mental health, physical health, and social and lifestyle domains
comparator: Non-autistic comparison populations as used within the included reviews; comparator definitions varied
outcome: Adverse outcomes including anxiety and mood disorders, suicidality, sleep problems, epilepsy, obesity, mortality risk, victimisation and bullying, quality of life, loneliness, relationship difficulties and unemployment
main_result: Across 134 reviews, elevated risk patterns were consistently reported for anxiety and mood disorders, suicidality and self-harm, eating and psychotic disorders, sleep problems, epilepsy, gastrointestinal difficulties, obesity, oral health problems, mortality, victimisation and bullying, reduced quality of life, loneliness, relationship difficulties and unemployment. Evidence strength varied across outcomes but elevated risk was reported across multiple independent reviews.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative umbrella synthesis of 134 reviews without pooled estimates or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Review-level rather than primary evidence with likely overlap between included reviews; narrative synthesis without pooled effects; heterogeneous review quality; does not test whether environmental modification alters these outcomes.
individual_applicability: Provides population-level context that substantial cross-domain burden persists in autism, cautioning against a formulation in which impairment is primarily attributable to environmental mismatch; not individually diagnostic.
quality_reason: Large, systematically conducted umbrella synthesis with dual screening, but narrative-only integration, unquantified review overlap and variable underlying evidence strength limit certainty.

citation: Ellie Kiger Hodge, Katherine Kuhl Meltzoff. The relationship between autistic camouflaging and mental health: a scoping review. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1701615. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1701615. PMID:42311563.
study_design: Scoping review of 48 qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method studies with charting against an adapted Cochrane checklist
population: Autistic participants across studies; several studies also included non-autistic comparison samples; ages and total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Autistic camouflaging/masking, subdivided into assimilation, compensation and masking
comparator: Lower camouflaging and, in some studies, non-autistic samples
outcome: Depression, anxiety, stress, mental wellbeing, burnout
main_result: Camouflaging was positively associated with poorer mental health, most strongly for assimilation; qualitative findings suggested a bidirectional relationship; crucially, non-autistic participants showed similar camouflaging-mental health relationships.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as ranging from small to large; specific values NR
major_limitations: Scoping design without formal risk-of-bias grading; self-report camouflaging measures; predominance of cross-sectional data; construct heterogeneity; outcome is mental health rather than social-communication performance.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the case interpretation that masking hid impairment, but the presence of the same association in non-autistic samples means masking-related distress is not diagnostically specific.
quality_reason: Scoping methodology, heterogeneous self-report measures and largely cross-sectional evidence preclude causal or specificity claims.

citation: Seong Ae Lee, Ah Rah Lee, Nan-He Yoon, Chae-Bin Kim, Geon Ho Bahn, Miae Oh. Effectiveness of Group Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and the Role of Cognitive Ability in Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Psychiatry investigation. 2025;22(11):1267-1276. doi:10.30773/pi.2025.0184. PMID:41089022.
study_design: Retrospective pre-post analysis of a 10-session group CBT programme, no control group
population: 24 adults with ADHD who completed group CBT in South Korea
exposure_intervention: Structured group CBT; subgroup stratification by full-scale IQ, attendance and comorbid depression
comparator: Pre-treatment baseline; IQ subgroups (below-average, average 90-109, high)
outcome: ADHD symptoms (ASRS, K-AARS) and functional impairment (K-AARS impairment subscale)
main_result: Clinically significant ADHD symptoms and functional impairment were present and improved across all IQ strata, including above-average IQ, with the most consistent improvement in the average-IQ subgroup and greater improvement with higher attendance.
effect_estimate: NR; significance reported without effect sizes or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Very small uncontrolled retrospective sample; multiple subgroup comparisons; regression to the mean and expectancy effects; no measure of effort or compensation.
individual_applicability: Weakly consistent with impairment coexisting with higher measured ability, but the sample is too small to support inference about high-achieving adults.
quality_reason: Uncontrolled retrospective design, n=24, no effect estimates, and post hoc IQ subgrouping.

citation: Rachael Sanders, Rachel Le Rossignol. Don't disable me: A scoping review of ADHD employees' experiences of working in open-plan offices. Work (Reading, Mass.). 2026;10519815261449927. doi:10.1177/10519815261449927. PMID:42132039.
study_design: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework; four databases plus reference-list searching; 22 items included
population: Adults with ADHD employed in open-plan office environments; total N and age range NR
exposure_intervention: Open-plan office work environment and related workplace conditions
comparator: Alternative or enclosed office environments and the general workforce; comparator largely implicit and NR
outcome: Creativity, productivity, wellbeing and workplace success for ADHD employees; nature and scope of existing research
main_result: The review identified 22 pieces of literature and a significant gap in empirical research on ADHD workers in open-plan offices. While empirical evidence was sparse, anecdotal evidence, professional opinion, the nature of ADHD and participants' lived experiences indicated that open-plan offices can impede the creativity and productivity of ADHD employees, with possible effects on the general workforce and organizational performance.
effect_estimate: NR; no pooled or comparative effect estimates reported
major_limitations: Predominantly non-empirical sources (anecdote, professional opinion, lived experience); no risk-of-bias appraisal reported; no controlled comparison of environments; publication and advocacy framing bias likely.
individual_applicability: Relevant to the hypothesis that standardized or high-stimulation work settings amplify impairment, but the near-absence of empirical data means it functions mainly to show the evidence gap.
quality_reason: Scoping design with explicitly sparse empirical evidence, no critical appraisal, and conclusions resting largely on opinion and lived-experience accounts.

citation: Fin J Schofield, Sarah Wilkie, Emily E Nielsen, Amberly Brigden, Matt W Jones, Hanna K Isotalus. Digital health technologies for adults with ADHD: a scoping review. Frontiers in digital health. 2026;8:1746732. doi:10.3389/fdgth.2026.1746732. PMID:41808914.
study_design: Scoping review with risk-of-bias analysis (registered on OSF)
population: 133 eligible studies of digital health technologies developed for adults with ADHD
exposure_intervention: Digital health technologies categorized as treatment (web/app cognitive therapy, psychoeducation, cognitive training, stimulation, neurofeedback), clinical management, or diagnosis, including machine-learning tools
comparator: Varies by study; many without controls (NR)
outcome: Mapped intended role, technological features, methodological trends, and quality of evidence
main_result: The adult ADHD digital technology field is dominated by preliminary efficacy and classification studies, with unclear clinical integration points, limited incorporation of lived experience for adherence, and few remote-monitoring technologies demonstrating value to clinicians or patients.
effect_estimate: NR (scoping review; no pooled effect estimates)
major_limitations: Scoping design without pooled effectiveness estimates; heterogeneous technologies including non-scaffolding modalities; implementation and durability outcomes largely absent from the literature mapped.
individual_applicability: Directly maps the adult ADHD digital-support evidence landscape relevant to the narrator's use of digital and AI-assisted tools, but cannot quantify benefit.
quality_reason: Comprehensive and adult-specific but descriptive scoping methodology precludes effectiveness or durability conclusions.

citation: Armin Toghi, Azar Mohammadzadeh, Zahra Alemi, Anahita Khorrami Banaraki. Transdiagnostic eye-tracking biomarkers of inattention across psychiatric disorders: a systematic review. BMC psychiatry. 2025;25(1):1007. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-07415-w. PMID:41121040.
study_design: Systematic review of 75 eye-tracking studies mapped onto three attention domains (selective, sustained, executive control)
population: Participants across ADHD, ASD, Tourette syndrome, OCD, borderline personality disorder, developmental coordination disorder and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders; ages and sample sizes not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Psychiatric or neurodevelopmental diagnosis, assessed with oculomotor paradigms
comparator: Comparison across diagnostic conditions and against normative performance
outcome: Oculomotor metrics including antisaccade direction errors, fixation duration on relevant/irrelevant areas, latency to first fixation, anticipatory and intrusive saccades, and their relation to inattention
main_result: Impairments in several oculomotor metrics were shared across the psychiatric and neurodevelopmental conditions studied, including DCD, and correlated moderately with self-reported and behavioural inattention; the authors propose these as transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific markers.
effect_estimate: NR (correlations with inattention described as moderate; no pooled estimates)
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis with no pooling or risk-of-bias grading reported; heterogeneous paradigms and metrics; diagnostic groups not matched and not separately quantified; ages, sample sizes and DCD-specific findings not extractable from the abstract.
individual_applicability: Reinforces that candidate motor/oculomotor markers do not discriminate among ADHD, autism, DCD and other conditions, and that they track inattention, cautioning against reading such findings as diagnosis-specific.
quality_reason: Descriptive mapping review without pooling, matched comparisons, or reported sample characteristics.

citation: Yuxuan Han, Xinying Li, Ruolei Gu, Qingwen Ding, Xiaodi Qu, Yue He, et al. Genetic and environmental origins of the co-occurrence of autistic traits, anxiety and depression: Evidence from meta-analysis and twin study. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;122317. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122317. PMID:42508582.
study_design: Meta-analysis of six twin studies plus an empirical multivariate genetic twin study (common vs independent pathway models)
population: Study 1: predominantly Western child and adolescent twin samples. Study 2: 178 Chinese community twin pairs (109 monozygotic, 69 dizygotic) aged 24-35
exposure_intervention: Autistic traits
comparator: Co-twin design partitioning genetic, shared and non-shared environmental variance
outcome: Internalising symptoms, specifically anxiety and depressive symptoms
main_result: Genetic and non-shared environmental influences were shared between autistic traits and internalising symptoms; the adult sample tentatively favoured a common latent factor over independent pathways, aligning with a transdiagnostic account rather than one condition causing the other.
effect_estimate: Genetic correlation rA = 0.42; non-shared environmental correlation rE = 0.15; substantial heterogeneity across the six meta-analysed studies
major_limitations: Trait measures rather than diagnoses; small adult twin sample (178 pairs); common versus independent pathway models only tentatively distinguished; substantial between-study heterogeneity; aetiological covariance is not a social-functioning outcome.
individual_applicability: Argues against treating co-occurring anxiety/depression as simply secondary to autistic traits, but says nothing about which mechanism operates in one person.
quality_reason: Genetically informative design that can separate shared liability from causation, offset by trait-level measurement, small adult sample and heterogeneity.

citation: Ali Jami, Sajjad Abbaszade, Abdol-Hossein Vahabie. A review on exploration-exploitation trade-off in psychiatric disorders. BMC psychiatry. 2025;25(1):420. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-06837-w. PMID:40287643.
study_design: Systematic review of 46 studies using tasks probing exploration-exploitation balance across psychiatric disorders; PubMed search; narrative synthesis
