population: Individuals with psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders including ADHD, schizophrenia, OCD, anxiety, mood disorders and addictive disorders; total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic status assessed on decision-making tasks manipulating exploration versus exploitation, novelty and reward
comparator: Healthy controls and cross-disorder comparisons
outcome: Exploration-exploitation balance, decision stability, reward sensitivity, learning and adaptability
main_result: Disorders clustered into addictive patterns, emotional/cognitive disturbances and neurological conditions. Anxiety and mood disorders often showed enhanced exploratory behaviour, and depression affected decision stability and reward sensitivity. Schizophrenia, OCD and ADHD were characterized by excessive switching and difficulty balancing exploration and exploitation, leading to impaired learning and adaptability. Addiction-like presentations showed reduced exploration and impulsive or perseverative choices.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative synthesis of 46 studies without pooled effect estimates
major_limitations: Single-database (PubMed) search; narrative synthesis of highly heterogeneous computational tasks; no formal risk-of-bias appraisal; case-control designs cannot establish diagnostic specificity; ADHD findings not separated by age or medication status.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether novelty- and reward-linked performance patterns are ADHD-specific; indicates they are shared with anxiety, mood, OCD and substance-related conditions that are competing explanations in this case.
quality_reason: Systematic in intent but limited by single-database searching, absent bias appraisal, no quantitative synthesis, and marked task heterogeneity across the reviewed literature.

citation: Gabriela Garcia de Carvalho Laguna, Baltazar Fernandes Andrade, Vanessa Souto Paulo, Marina Garcia Lorenzo Aguiar, Isadora Bagues Rodrigues, Jade Ponte da Cruz, et al. Differentiation between Autism Spectrum Disorder and Personality Disorders: a systematic review. Psychology, health & medicine. 2026;1-20. doi:10.1080/13548506.2026.2691413. PMID:42319023.
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA and registered on PROSPERO, covering original articles published 2020-2024
population: 684 individuals total: 550 clinical adult participants and 134 healthcare professionals
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic assessment of adult autism spectrum disorder
comparator: Personality disorders, particularly borderline personality disorder
outcome: Differential-diagnostic criteria and their impact on diagnostic accuracy
main_result: Feature overlap, especially between ASD and borderline personality disorder, compromises diagnostic accuracy; ASD was characterised by cognitive rigidity and difficulty interpreting social norms whereas personality disorders featured emotional instability, impulsivity and fear of abandonment, and self-harm had different antecedents in each; absent standardised criteria and reliance on subjective assessment increase diagnostic error and delay.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Small pooled sample; narrow 2020-2024 publication window; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias grading reported in abstract; heterogeneous designs including professional-survey data; distinguishing framework derived within the review rather than validated prospectively.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant: adult social difficulty with emotional dysregulation can be produced by personality-disorder processes as well as autism, and the two are frequently confused in adult assessment.
quality_reason: Systematic in method but based on few, heterogeneous studies with a small aggregate sample and no quantitative accuracy estimates.

citation: Fredrik Serenius, Thomas Abrahamsson, Ulrika Ådén, Kerstin Hellgren, Karin Sävman, Andreas Ohlin, et al. Neurodevelopmental Outcomes 12 Years After Extremely Preterm Birth in Sweden. Pediatrics. 2026;157(3):e2025073742. doi:10.1542/peds.2025-073742. PMID:41638598.
study_design: National prospective population-based cohort (EXPRESS) with term-born comparison group, assessed at age 12 using standardised instruments and national register diagnoses
population: 462 of 492 surviving children born before 27 weeks' gestation in Sweden (April 2004-March 2007) and 373 term-born controls
exposure_intervention: Extremely preterm birth
comparator: Term-born controls
outcome: Moderate/severe neurodevelopmental disability, ASD, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, behaviour problems, and multimorbidity at age 12
main_result: Extremely preterm children had markedly higher rates of every outcome than controls, and co-occurrence was the norm among those with moderate/severe disability; a substantial minority nonetheless had no ASD, ADHD or DCD diagnosis.
effect_estimate: Moderate/severe NDD 37.4% vs 4.6%; ASD 14.9% vs 2.41%; ADHD 21.2% vs 8.9%; DCD 29.4% vs 5.7%; behaviour problems 35.3% vs 8.13% (all p<.001). 59% of EPT children with moderate/severe NDD had at least two co-occurring conditions; 24.9% with no/mild disability had comorbidity. Pairwise ADHD-DCD overlap NR.
major_limitations: High-risk perinatal population limits generalisability to idiopathic presentations; ADHD and ASD partly register-ascertained; outcomes at age 12 with no adult follow-up in this report; the specific ADHD-and-DCD co-occurrence proportion is not given.
individual_applicability: Demonstrates that neurodevelopmental multimorbidity including DCD is common and that perinatal history is a major competing explanation, so birth history should be established before attributing motor difficulty to idiopathic DCD.
quality_reason: Near-complete national cohort with a concurrent term-born control group and standardised cognitive, motor and behavioural instruments.

citation: Aja Louise Murray, Katie Dryburgh, Edmund J S Sonuga-Barke. Identifying Candidate Mediators Linking ADHD Symptoms and Internalising Problems in Adolescence: An Exploratory Longitudinal Mediation Analysis. Journal of attention disorders. 2026;30(8):986-998. doi:10.1177/10870547261419589. PMID:41789525.
study_design: Exploratory longitudinal mediation analysis using regularised structural equation modelling (lasso)
population: Millennium Cohort Study; 2,607 male and 2,791 female participants assessed at ages 11, 14 and 17
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms in adolescence
comparator: Lower ADHD symptom levels within the cohort
outcome: Internalising (anxiety and depressive) symptoms, with 14 candidate mediators including peer problems, conduct problems, self-esteem, injuries, parental relationships, academic performance, risky decision-making, parental mental health, educational motivation and general health
main_result: Regularisation did not de-select any of the 14 candidate mediators, but only two were statistically significant. The authors conclude there may be many mediators of small effect linking ADHD symptoms to later internalising problems, and identify self-esteem and parental mental health as priority mechanisms for future causal and interventional research.
effect_estimate: NR (individual path estimates and confidence intervals not reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Explicitly exploratory with 14 simultaneous mediators and no confirmatory replication; observational, so mediation remains associational; abstract does not identify which two paths were significant with estimates.
individual_applicability: Tempers the expectation that any single anxiety- or rejection-related mediator carries the functional burden; suggests distributed small effects rather than one dominant pathway.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised national cohort with three waves and appropriate regularisation, but exploratory framing, absent effect estimates and untested causal assumptions limit inference.

citation: Francesco Maria Boccaccio, Renata Rizzo, Concetta Pirrone, Jan K Buitelaar. Mapping the association between cognitive disengagement syndrome and internalizing disorders: A systematic scoping review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122159. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122159. PMID:42341946.
study_design: Systematic scoping review with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression (82 studies, 2002-2025)
population: Children, adolescents and adults from healthy and clinical samples
exposure_intervention: Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome (CDS), previously Sluggish Cognitive Tempo
comparator: Lower CDS levels; analyses controlling for ADHD inattention
outcome: Depression, anxiety and broader internalizing symptoms; functional consequences
main_result: Elevated CDS was consistently associated with depression and anxiety, with more than one-third of individuals reaching clinical thresholds; associations remained significant after controlling for ADHD inattention and were seen across ages. Meta-analyses showed the strongest link for depression (r=0.56), then anxiety (r=0.46) and internalizing symptoms (r=0.44); meta-regression identified depression as a significant moderator and inflated effect sizes in same-informant studies.
effect_estimate: r=0.56 (depression), r=0.46 (anxiety), r=0.44 (internalizing); confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Abstract does not state that CDS items index daydreaming; scarce longitudinal and multi-informant studies; no analytic control for symptom overlap despite acknowledged phenomenological similarity; same-informant inflation.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an inattention-adjacent construct tracks depression strongly and independently of ADHD inattention, relevant to differentiating mood-driven from compensation-driven inner experience.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis with moderator testing, but construct-overlap confounding is explicitly unaddressed and longitudinal evidence is sparse.

citation: Ali Dadfar, Mia Ramklint, Sara von Wallenberg Pachaly. A systematic review of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)-induced activation and manic/hypomanic switch in children and adolescents. Scandinavian journal of child and adolescent psychiatry and psychology. 2025;13(1):117-134. doi:10.2478/sjcapp-2025-0011. PMID:41404486.
study_design: PROSPERO-registered PRISMA systematic review (CRD42023422133) of 30 articles with duplicate blinded screening; qualitative synthesis of definitions and assessments
population: 30 articles covering children and adolescents aged 6-18 years treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; total N NR
exposure_intervention: SSRI treatment, with outcomes of drug-induced activation or manic/hypomanic switch
comparator: NR (comparison was between activation and manic/hypomanic switch constructs rather than between exposure groups)
outcome: Definitions, symptom profiles, assessment instruments and inter-rater reliability for activation versus manic/hypomanic switch
main_result: Only 8 of 30 articles clearly defined activation and 4 defined mania/hypomania, one instrument existed for activation and none for mania, and only 2 reported reliability; symptoms overlapped substantially, with aggression/hostility, anxiety/panic and suicidality more often reported under activation and cognitive/thought-process and mood changes more often under mania/hypomania.
effect_estimate: NR (no incidence rates, effect sizes or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Pediatric samples only, exposure is SSRIs rather than stimulants or cannabis, no incidence or effect estimates, and vague heterogeneous definitions mean the reported symptom differences may reflect reporting conventions rather than distinct phenomena.
individual_applicability: Illustrates the general clinical problem of distinguishing medication-induced activation from a mood episode, which applies to this case, but the population and drug class differ.
quality_reason: Registered review with duplicate screening, but the underlying literature lacks validated definitions, instruments and reliability data, and no quantitative outcomes are available.

citation: Meghan Fiske, Dominique L DiDomenico, Henry W Chase, Yvette Afriyie-Agyemang, Genna Bebko, Haris A Aslam, et al. Bipolar Disorder Psychosis Risk Predicts Cue Discrimination on the AX-Continuous Performance Task Paradigm. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(4):e70129. doi:10.1111/bdi.70129. PMID:42262032.
study_design: Cross-sectional study with dimensional linear regression aims and categorical group comparisons (ANCOVA)
population: Euthymic bipolar disorder (n=27) and bipolar-at-risk individuals (n=121), total analysed sample 148; ages NR
exposure_intervention: Lifetime mania/affective-lability risk (psychomotor activation, suicidality, mixed instability) and lifetime psychosis risk indexed by the Mood Spectrum Self Report
comparator: Lower-risk individuals within the same cohort; bipolar low-risk versus high-risk groups; no healthy control group described
outcome: AX-Continuous Performance Test measures d'context (target/context discrimination) and A-cue bias
main_result: Higher lifetime psychosis and mania/affective-lability risk were associated with reduced d'context but not with altered A-cue bias, and categorical group comparisons showed no significant differences; the associations survived adjustment for current depressive symptoms but disappeared after covarying current mania severity.
effect_estimate: Dimensional associations with d'context: absolute t values >2.015, p<0.047; after covarying current mania severity absolute t values <1.26, all p>0.203; no effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional design, small bipolar subgroup (n=27), reliance on retrospective self-report for lifetime risk, single laboratory task, no reported control of medication, sleep or substance exposure, and 'euthymic' status still permitted variable current mania severity.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the state-versus-trait question in this case, showing that residual current mood elevation can account for attention deficits that look trait-like; single-timepoint group data cannot classify one person.
quality_reason: Small cross-sectional sample with self-report exposure and a single task; the key finding is a covariate-attenuation result reported without effect sizes.

citation: Giulia Trotta, Isabelle Austin-Zimmerman, Edoardo Spinazzola, Senta Haussler, Lucia Sideli, Monica Aas, et al. Gene-Environment Correlation Across Trauma Subtypes and Developmental Timing: Evidence From the EU-GEI and ALSPAC. Biological psychiatry. 2026;S0006-3223(26)01130-3. doi:10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.03.1000. PMID:41933711.
study_design: Genetically informed observational analysis in two cohorts (case-control and prospective birth cohort)
population: EU-GEI case-control study (n=1,191) and ALSPAC birth cohort (n=8,141)
exposure_intervention: Polygenic risk scores for psychiatric and behavioural traits (PTSD, ADHD, schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, cannabis use disorder)
comparator: Lower polygenic risk within cohort; unexposed or later-exposed trauma groups
outcome: Timing (early 0-11 vs late 12-17 years) and type of trauma exposure: emotional, physical and sexual abuse, bullying, household discord
main_result: In EU-GEI, 20 PRS-trauma associations survived FDR correction: PTSD PRS with early emotional abuse (OR 3.37), sexual abuse (3.08), physical abuse (2.90) and bullying (2.19); ADHD PRS with early sexual abuse (1.49), emotional abuse (1.33), household discord (1.27) and bullying (1.24); schizophrenia PRS with early emotional abuse (1.90) and late bullying (1.46). Twenty associations were replicated in ALSPAC; variance explained was small in both cohorts and results held in control-only sensitivity analyses.
effect_estimate: Odds ratios 1.24-3.37 as listed; confidence intervals NR; variance explained described as small
major_limitations: European-ancestry samples; retrospective trauma reporting in EU-GEI; small variance explained; gene-environment correlation does not exclude genuine environmental effects; no daydreaming or functional outcome measured.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant as a confounding caution: genetic liability is associated with the likelihood of reporting bullying and abuse, so adversity-to-outcome sequences in this narrative may be partly non-causal.
quality_reason: Two-cohort design with replication and FDR control, but observational, ancestry-restricted, and dependent on retrospective exposure recall in one cohort.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. The risk of psychosis associated with cannabis use by people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of 3 heterogeneous studies; risk of bias rated fair (k=1) and good (k=2)
population: People with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder exposed to cannabis; sample sizes, ages and diagnostic methods NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use in individuals with ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD who use cannabis, and/or ADHD individuals without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis outcomes
main_result: Two of three studies indirectly suggested that cannabis use does not increase psychosis risk among people with ADHD, and the third indicated that cannabis had a similar impact on psychosis risk in people with and without ADHD; the authors conclude there is very little evidence for a heightened ADHD-specific risk.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates; synthesis without meta-analysis)
major_limitations: Only three studies, two of which addressed the question indirectly, almost certainly underpowered to detect an interaction, exposure and diagnostic ascertainment not described, and absence of evidence is reported rather than evidence of absence.
individual_applicability: Directly targets the proposed ADHD-by-cannabis interaction relevant to this case, but the evidence base is too thin to exclude a clinically meaningful individual effect.
quality_reason: Very small number of studies with indirect inference and no quantitative synthesis, despite generally fair-to-good individual study ratings.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies, with multiple regression on pooled correlation matrices to control symptom overlap
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples; total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Symptom dimensions of ADHD-inattention (ADHD-I), ADHD-hyperactivity/impulsivity (ADHD-HI) and cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS)
comparator: Each symptom dimension after controlling shared variance with the other dimensions
outcome: Cognitive correlates including social cognition, motor coordination, perceptual-motor functioning, attention, inhibition, working memory, processing speed
main_result: Profiles looked similar in bivariate correlations but diverged in regression: ADHD-HI was associated with weaker social cognition and focused/sustained attention yet better motor coordination; ADHD-I with weaker intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, perceptual-motor functioning and memory; CDS with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: ADHD-HI: social cognition and attention betas -.24 to -.11 (p<.001); motor coordination beta = .14 (p<.001). ADHD-I: betas -.21 to -.10 (p<.01). CDS: betas -.29 to -.13 (p<.001).
major_limitations: All constituent studies cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; dimensions defined by rating scales rather than diagnoses; pooling across child and adult samples; laboratory/rating cognitive proxies rather than real-world social or motor functioning.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult reporting both inattentive and hyperactive features, but findings are group-level, symptom-scale based, and cannot attribute this person's social or motor difficulties to a specific dimension.
quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

citation: Maria Giuseppina Petruzzelli, Emilia Matera, Lucia Margari, Lucia Marzulli, Alessandra Gabellone, Chiara Cotugno, et al. An update on the comorbidity of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and its clinical management. Expert review of neurotherapeutics. 2026;26(1):75-89. doi:10.1080/14737175.2025.2599856. PMID:41388592.
study_design: Targeted narrative expert review prioritising meta-analyses and umbrella reviews (PubMed search to 24 March 2025)
population: Individuals with ADHD, ASD, or both, across the lifespan
exposure_intervention: Co-occurring ADHD and ASD
comparator: Single-diagnosis presentations
outcome: Shared and distinct phenotypic, neuropsychological, genetic and neuroimaging correlates; assessment and management approaches
main_result: Reports both shared and distinct correlates of ADHD and ASD, states that the comorbidity should not be overlooked, and advises that comorbid diagnosis be made only after thorough differential assessment establishing that ADHD symptoms are not better explained by ASD; calls for research on personalised treatment and real-world outcomes.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Non-systematic targeted search with expert-opinion synthesis; no quantitative pooling, no risk-of-bias appraisal, no explicit eligibility criteria; recommendations are consensus rather than evidence-graded.
individual_applicability: Provides an explicit clinical sequencing principle for the case (differential before comorbid diagnosis) but is expert opinion, the lowest tier of the protocol's hierarchy.
quality_reason: Expert narrative review without systematic search, appraisal or effect estimates.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Barbara Franke, Catharina A Hartman, Pieter J Hoekstra, Nanda N J Rommelse, et al. Growing up with ADHD: findings from an 18-year longitudinal follow-up study of adults with childhood ADHD, their siblings, and controls. Psychiatry research. 2026;364:117308. doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2026.117308. PMID:42365682.
study_design: Prospective 18-year longitudinal follow-up cohort with sibling and control comparison groups
population: Adults with childhood ADHD (n=154, mean age 27.4, 68% male), siblings without childhood ADHD (n=138), controls (n=129)
exposure_intervention: Childhood ADHD diagnosis; secondary contrast of persistent versus remitted adult ADHD
comparator: Siblings without childhood ADHD and unrelated controls
outcome: Adult psychiatric status, behavioural/emotional problems, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognition, physical health, healthcare use
main_result: Childhood ADHD was associated with worse adult functioning on more than 60% of outcomes across all domains; siblings functioned comparably to controls; persistent ADHD showed worse functioning than remitted ADHD on psychiatric, behavioural/emotional, adaptive and physical health outcomes, while both ADHD groups were worse than controls.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as small to large; numeric estimates and confidence intervals NR in abstract
major_limitations: Attrition over 18 years not quantified in abstract; sex imbalance across groups (68% vs 35% vs 40% male); outcome instruments and covariate adjustment not specified; substantial within-group heterogeneity acknowledged.
individual_applicability: Closest available analogue to a lifelong developmental trajectory question, but group-level and cannot establish that this individual's adult difficulties originate in childhood ADHD.
quality_reason: Long prospective follow-up with two comparison groups is a strong design, downgraded for unreported effect sizes, unclear attrition, and abstract-only appraisal.

citation: Giulia Trotta, Isabelle Austin-Zimmerman, Edoardo Spinazzola, Senta Haussler, Lucia Sideli, Monica Aas, et al. Gene-Environment Correlation Across Trauma Subtypes and Developmental Timing: Evidence From the EU-GEI and ALSPAC. Biological psychiatry. 2026;S0006-3223(26)01130-3. doi:10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.03.1000. PMID:41933711.
study_design: Genetically informed observational analysis in two cohorts (case-control and prospective birth cohort)
population: EU-GEI case-control study (n=1,191) and ALSPAC birth cohort (n=8,141)
exposure_intervention: Polygenic risk scores for psychiatric and behavioural traits (PTSD, ADHD, schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, cannabis use disorder)
comparator: Lower polygenic risk within cohort; unexposed or later-exposed trauma groups
outcome: Timing (early 0-11 vs late 12-17 years) and type of trauma exposure: emotional, physical and sexual abuse, bullying, household discord
main_result: In EU-GEI, 20 PRS-trauma associations survived FDR correction: PTSD PRS with early emotional abuse (OR 3.37), sexual abuse (3.08), physical abuse (2.90) and bullying (2.19); ADHD PRS with early sexual abuse (1.49), emotional abuse (1.33), household discord (1.27) and bullying (1.24); schizophrenia PRS with early emotional abuse (1.90) and late bullying (1.46). Twenty associations were replicated in ALSPAC; variance explained was small in both cohorts and results held in control-only sensitivity analyses.
effect_estimate: Odds ratios 1.24-3.37 as listed; confidence intervals NR; variance explained described as small
major_limitations: European-ancestry samples; retrospective trauma reporting in EU-GEI; small variance explained; gene-environment correlation does not exclude genuine environmental effects; no daydreaming or functional outcome measured.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant as a confounding caution: genetic liability is associated with the likelihood of reporting bullying and abuse, so adversity-to-outcome sequences in this narrative may be partly non-causal.
quality_reason: Two-cohort design with replication and FDR control, but observational, ancestry-restricted, and dependent on retrospective exposure recall in one cohort.

citation: Yuan You, Tom McAdams, Yasmin I Ahmadzadeh, Tabea Schoeler, Filip Marzecki, Helena M S Zavos. The role of comorbid childhood mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions in the persistence of ADHD symptoms: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines. 2026;67(2):183-201. doi:10.1111/jcpp.70028. PMID:40801243.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel random-effects models; 26 studies
population: Children with ADHD followed to later developmental stages
exposure_intervention: Childhood comorbid internalizing, externalizing and neurodevelopmental conditions
comparator: ADHD without the specified comorbidity
outcome: Persistence of ADHD symptoms into later developmental stages
main_result: Childhood externalizing and, more weakly, internalizing comorbidity predicted ADHD persistence, but adjustment attenuated externalizing and eliminated the internalizing association; neurodevelopmental comorbidity did not predict persistence, and the externalizing effect appeared only with parent-reported data.
effect_estimate: Internalizing d=0.19 (adjusted d=0.06, non-significant); externalizing d=0.31 (adjusted d=0.24); neurodevelopmental comorbidity non-significant
major_limitations: Informant-dependent findings suggest common-method bias; residual confounding acknowledged; heterogeneous definitions of persistence and follow-up intervals.
individual_applicability: Shows persistence estimates are sensitive to comorbidity and informant, relevant given this individual's reported anxiety, mood and substance history.
quality_reason: Appropriate multilevel synthesis with adjusted analyses, limited by observational primary data and informant confounding.

citation: Francesco Maria Boccaccio, Renata Rizzo, Concetta Pirrone, Jan K Buitelaar. Mapping the association between cognitive disengagement syndrome and internalizing disorders: A systematic scoping review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122159. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122159. PMID:42341946.
study_design: Systematic scoping review with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression (82 studies, 2002-2025)
population: Children, adolescents and adults from healthy and clinical samples
exposure_intervention: Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome (CDS), previously Sluggish Cognitive Tempo
comparator: Lower CDS levels; analyses controlling for ADHD inattention
outcome: Depression, anxiety and broader internalizing symptoms; functional consequences
main_result: Elevated CDS was consistently associated with depression and anxiety, with more than one-third of individuals reaching clinical thresholds; associations remained significant after controlling for ADHD inattention and were seen across ages. Meta-analyses showed the strongest link for depression (r=0.56), then anxiety (r=0.46) and internalizing symptoms (r=0.44); meta-regression identified depression as a significant moderator and inflated effect sizes in same-informant studies.
effect_estimate: r=0.56 (depression), r=0.46 (anxiety), r=0.44 (internalizing); confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Abstract does not state that CDS items index daydreaming; scarce longitudinal and multi-informant studies; no analytic control for symptom overlap despite acknowledged phenomenological similarity; same-informant inflation.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an inattention-adjacent construct tracks depression strongly and independently of ADHD inattention, relevant to differentiating mood-driven from compensation-driven inner experience.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis with moderator testing, but construct-overlap confounding is explicitly unaddressed and longitudinal evidence is sparse.

citation: Simin Kang, Zhao Fu, Qiurong Li, Li Yang, Qingjiu Cao. Adult-diagnosed and childhood-diagnosed attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: cognitive and environmental contributions to symptom severity across different age of diagnosis. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1782999. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1782999. PMID:42147013.
study_design: Cross-sectional comparative study with hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analysis
population: 72 adults with ADHD: 37 childhood-diagnosed (26.32 +/- 4.69 years) and 35 adult-diagnosed (25.63 +/- 4.89 years), diagnosed by structured interview
exposure_intervention: Executive function (BRIEF-A) and environmental factors: childhood trauma (CTQ), resilience (CD-RISC), parental bonding (PBI)
comparator: Childhood-diagnosed versus adult-diagnosed ADHD groups; relative variance contribution of executive versus environmental predictors
outcome: ADHD core symptom severity (ASRS inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity); emotional symptoms (SAS, SDS)
main_result: Executive function was the strongest and most consistent predictor of both inattention (beta 0.64, p<0.001) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (beta 0.47, p<0.001), whereas environmental factors contributed minimal additional explanatory power, with only a modest association between parental overprotection and inattention (beta 0.28, p=0.016). No diagnosis-specific moderation effects were observed. Adult-diagnosed participants showed lower childhood symptoms but similar adult severity, with more psychiatric comorbidity and emotional distress.
effect_estimate: beta 0.64 (inattention) and 0.47 (hyperactivity-impulsivity) for executive function; beta 0.28 (p=0.016) for parental overprotection; confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Small single-site sample; cross-sectional; retrospective childhood trauma and parenting recall; outcome is symptom severity rather than real-world functional impairment; no formal mediation testing.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult with late-recognised ADHD, and supports executive rather than adversity-related variables as the dominant symptom correlate, but small-sample and symptom-level outcomes limit transfer.
quality_reason: Structured diagnostic ascertainment is a strength, but low power, cross-sectional design and retrospective exposure measures constrain interpretation.

citation: Lars Wichstrøm, Hanne Grønli, Jenny Sundbø Walstad, Andrea Raballo, Elfrida Hartveit Kvarstein, Silje Steinsbekk. Childhood predictors of cluster A personality disorder traits in adolescence: a seven-wave birth cohort study. European child & adolescent psychiatry. 2026;35(4):1309-1319. doi:10.1007/s00787-025-02936-x. PMID:41428080.
study_design: Seven-wave prospective birth-cohort study (ages 4-16, biennial assessment)
population: 1,077 children from two birth cohorts in Trondheim, Norway (50.9% female)
exposure_intervention: Childhood factors including having an imaginary friend, attachment insecurity/disorganisation, negative life events, autism spectrum symptoms, personality and emotional/behavioural difficulties
comparator: Within-cohort variation in intercept and growth of candidate predictors up to age 14
outcome: Cluster A personality disorder traits at age 16 (Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Personality Disorders)
main_result: Odd or eccentric behaviour, neuroticism, low conscientiousness, declining self-esteem and growing emotional and behavioural difficulties predicted paranoid and schizotypal traits, and insecure attachment predicted paranoid traits; having an imaginary friend, disorganised attachment, negative life events and autism spectrum symptoms were unpredictive. Any Cluster A prevalence at 16 was 2.41% (95% CI 1.12-3.69).
effect_estimate: Prevalence any Cluster A 2.41% (95% CI 1.12-3.69); paranoid 1.36% (0.42-2.31); schizoid 0.56% (-0.11-1.23); schizotypal 1.05% (0.23-1.87); predictor effect sizes NR
major_limitations: Imaginary friendship is not equivalent to maladaptive or immersive daydreaming; outcome is personality pathology rather than fantasy or impairment; single national cohort; low outcome base rates.
individual_applicability: Provides a developmental null for one form of childhood fantasy, but does not measure the immersive daydreaming described in this narrative.
quality_reason: Strong prospective seven-wave design with structured diagnostic outcome, but construct mismatch with the focal daydreaming claim and no reported predictor effect sizes.

citation: Rachael Sanders, Rachel Le Rossignol. Don't disable me: A scoping review of ADHD employees' experiences of working in open-plan offices. Work (Reading, Mass.). 2026;10519815261449927. doi:10.1177/10519815261449927. PMID:42132039.
study_design: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework; four databases plus reference-list searching; 22 items included
population: Adults with ADHD employed in open-plan office environments; total N and age range NR
exposure_intervention: Open-plan office work environment and related workplace conditions
comparator: Alternative or enclosed office environments and the general workforce; comparator largely implicit and NR
outcome: Creativity, productivity, wellbeing and workplace success for ADHD employees; nature and scope of existing research
main_result: The review identified 22 pieces of literature and a significant gap in empirical research on ADHD workers in open-plan offices. While empirical evidence was sparse, anecdotal evidence, professional opinion, the nature of ADHD and participants' lived experiences indicated that open-plan offices can impede the creativity and productivity of ADHD employees, with possible effects on the general workforce and organizational performance.
effect_estimate: NR; no pooled or comparative effect estimates reported
major_limitations: Predominantly non-empirical sources (anecdote, professional opinion, lived experience); no risk-of-bias appraisal reported; no controlled comparison of environments; publication and advocacy framing bias likely.
individual_applicability: Relevant to the hypothesis that standardized or high-stimulation work settings amplify impairment, but the near-absence of empirical data means it functions mainly to show the evidence gap.
quality_reason: Scoping design with explicitly sparse empirical evidence, no critical appraisal, and conclusions resting largely on opinion and lived-experience accounts.

citation: Michael El Boghdady, Hussayn Shinwari. Neurodiversity in surgery: Embracing cognitive difference in a demanding profession. The surgeon : journal of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons of Edinburgh and Ireland. 2026;24(3):160-164. doi:10.1016/j.surge.2026.01.001. PMID:41548993.
study_design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (PRISMA 2020); JBI and MMAT appraisal; 4 included studies (2 retrospective cohorts, 1 cross-sectional, 1 mixed-methods)
population: Neurodivergent surgeons and surgical trainees plus healthcare professionals; studies from Turkey, Canada and the UK; total participants NR
exposure_intervention: Neurodivergence (ADHD, autism, specific learning difficulties) within surgical training and workplace environments
comparator: Neurotypical trainees or general trainee population; comparator definition NR across included studies
outcome: Prevalence and disclosure, examination attainment, reported cognitive strengths, workplace supports, cultural implications
main_result: ADHD symptoms were identified in 31.6% of participating Turkish surgical trainees and 6-8% of UK trainees declared disabilities, most commonly specific learning difficulties. Neurodivergent trainees reported difficulties with assessments, sensory environments and professional expectations, with lower pass rates in early postgraduate examinations. Strengths including creativity, attention to detail and resilience were frequently cited, and supportive interventions and fair recruitment were reported to mitigate disadvantage.
effect_estimate: ADHD symptoms 31.6% of participating Turkish surgical trainees; 6-8% UK trainees declared disabilities; no comparative effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Only 4 studies from 13,268 records; heterogeneous designs and countries; strengths reported narratively and by self-report without objective measurement; no pooled estimates; disclosure-based prevalence subject to selection bias.
individual_applicability: Closely matched to a physician reporting occupational friction in hospital medicine and standardized assessment settings, but the strengths findings are testimonial and cannot support individual inference.
quality_reason: Very small included-study count, heterogeneous designs, self-reported strengths outcomes, and no comparative effect estimates despite appropriate PRISMA/JBI/MMAT methodology.

citation: Ellie Kiger Hodge, Katherine Kuhl Meltzoff. The relationship between autistic camouflaging and mental health: a scoping review. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1701615. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1701615. PMID:42311563.
study_design: Scoping review of 48 qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method studies with charting against an adapted Cochrane checklist
population: Autistic participants across studies; several studies also included non-autistic comparison samples; ages and total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Autistic camouflaging/masking, subdivided into assimilation, compensation and masking
comparator: Lower camouflaging and, in some studies, non-autistic samples
outcome: Depression, anxiety, stress, mental wellbeing, burnout
main_result: Camouflaging was positively associated with poorer mental health, most strongly for assimilation; qualitative findings suggested a bidirectional relationship; crucially, non-autistic participants showed similar camouflaging-mental health relationships.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as ranging from small to large; specific values NR
major_limitations: Scoping design without formal risk-of-bias grading; self-report camouflaging measures; predominance of cross-sectional data; construct heterogeneity; outcome is mental health rather than social-communication performance.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the case interpretation that masking hid impairment, but the presence of the same association in non-autistic samples means masking-related distress is not diagnostically specific.
quality_reason: Scoping methodology, heterogeneous self-report measures and largely cross-sectional evidence preclude causal or specificity claims.

citation: Andrea Jiménez-Mayoral, Dídac Florensa, Vicent Llorca-Bofí, María Irigoyen-Otiñano. Diagnostic Trends of Minors in Psychiatric Emergency Care: An Observational Study. Actas espanolas de psiquiatria. 2026;54(1):163-171. doi:10.62641/aep.v54i1.2061. PMID:41755570.
study_design: Retrospective observational cohort with 24-month follow-up and exploratory association-rule analysis
population: 583 patients aged 4-18 years attending a first psychiatric emergency visit in Spain (2017-2023); median age 14.9 years
exposure_intervention: Baseline emergency psychiatric diagnosis
comparator: Same patients at 24-month follow-up (within-person diagnostic transition)
outcome: Diagnostic stability and transition patterns
main_result: Diagnostic stability was heterogeneous, high for schizophrenia/psychosis (71%) and low for ADHD and eating disorders, with a notable transition pattern from autism plus ADHD to conduct disorders.
effect_estimate: Schizophrenia/psychosis stability 71%; intellectual disability with gender identity disorder 67%; mood disorders ~44%; eating disorders 26%; conduct disorders 17%; autism+ADHD to conduct disorder confidence 0.66, lift 2.55
major_limitations: Emergency-service sample with atypical case mix; diagnostic label stability is not the same as symptom or impairment persistence; retrospective electronic record extraction; no standardised reassessment protocol.
individual_applicability: Cautions that clinical diagnostic labels applied in crisis settings shift substantially over two years, relevant to interpreting any single diagnostic formulation.
quality_reason: Retrospective single-centre record review with a selected emergency population and outcome that only indirectly indexes trait persistence.

citation: Jae Kwang Shim, Soyoung Irene Lee, Shim-Gyeom Kim, Yujin Ko, HyunChul Youn, Jeewon Lee. Clinical Features of Adults With Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Focusing on Their Adherence to Medication. Psychiatry investigation. 2026;23(2):236-241. doi:10.30773/pi.2025.0283. PMID:41680598.
study_design: Retrospective chart review with 2-year follow-up of records
population: 174 adults diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood at a Korean tertiary university hospital (mean age 25.1; 73.6% male)
exposure_intervention: First ADHD diagnosis made in adulthood
comparator: None (single-cohort descriptive)
outcome: Presenting complaint, psychiatric comorbidity, medication adherence and persistence
main_result: Only 56.3% presented because of ADHD symptoms, with others presenting with interpersonal problems or depressed mood; 76.4% had at least one psychiatric comorbidity; adherence above 80% occurred in fewer than half, and persistence beyond one year was uncommon.
effect_estimate: 56.3% ADHD-related chief complaint; 76.4% comorbidity; 42.6% (methylphenidate) and 40.0% (atomoxetine) adherence >80%; 13.8% and 18.2% persistence >365 days
major_limitations: Single-site retrospective chart review without comparison group; referral and documentation bias; adult-onset recognition may reflect service access rather than masking.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that adult-first recognition of ADHD is common and frequently occurs via other presenting complaints, a pattern that resembles this narrative but does not explain its cause.
quality_reason: Uncontrolled retrospective case series at one centre; descriptive only and vulnerable to selection bias.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Barbara Franke, Catharina A Hartman, Pieter J Hoekstra, Nanda N J Rommelse, et al. Growing up with ADHD: findings from an 18-year longitudinal follow-up study of adults with childhood ADHD, their siblings, and controls. Psychiatry research. 2026;364:117308. doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2026.117308. PMID:42365682.
study_design: Prospective 18-year longitudinal follow-up cohort with sibling and control comparison groups
population: Adults with childhood ADHD (n=154, mean age 27.4, 68% male), siblings without childhood ADHD (n=138), controls (n=129)
exposure_intervention: Childhood ADHD diagnosis; secondary contrast of persistent versus remitted adult ADHD
comparator: Siblings without childhood ADHD and unrelated controls
outcome: Adult psychiatric status, behavioural/emotional problems, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognition, physical health, healthcare use
main_result: Childhood ADHD was associated with worse adult functioning on more than 60% of outcomes across all domains; siblings functioned comparably to controls; persistent ADHD showed worse functioning than remitted ADHD on psychiatric, behavioural/emotional, adaptive and physical health outcomes, while both ADHD groups were worse than controls.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as small to large; numeric estimates and confidence intervals NR in abstract
major_limitations: Attrition over 18 years not quantified in abstract; sex imbalance across groups (68% vs 35% vs 40% male); outcome instruments and covariate adjustment not specified; substantial within-group heterogeneity acknowledged.
individual_applicability: Closest available analogue to a lifelong developmental trajectory question, but group-level and cannot establish that this individual's adult difficulties originate in childhood ADHD.
quality_reason: Long prospective follow-up with two comparison groups is a strong design, downgraded for unreported effect sizes, unclear attrition, and abstract-only appraisal.

citation: Fredrik Serenius, Thomas Abrahamsson, Ulrika Ådén, Kerstin Hellgren, Karin Sävman, Andreas Ohlin, et al. Neurodevelopmental Outcomes 12 Years After Extremely Preterm Birth in Sweden. Pediatrics. 2026;157(3):e2025073742. doi:10.1542/peds.2025-073742. PMID:41638598.
study_design: National prospective population-based cohort (EXPRESS) with term-born comparison group, assessed at age 12 using standardised instruments and national register diagnoses
population: 462 of 492 surviving children born before 27 weeks' gestation in Sweden (April 2004-March 2007) and 373 term-born controls
exposure_intervention: Extremely preterm birth
comparator: Term-born controls
outcome: Moderate/severe neurodevelopmental disability, ASD, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, behaviour problems, and multimorbidity at age 12
main_result: Extremely preterm children had markedly higher rates of every outcome than controls, and co-occurrence was the norm among those with moderate/severe disability; a substantial minority nonetheless had no ASD, ADHD or DCD diagnosis.
effect_estimate: Moderate/severe NDD 37.4% vs 4.6%; ASD 14.9% vs 2.41%; ADHD 21.2% vs 8.9%; DCD 29.4% vs 5.7%; behaviour problems 35.3% vs 8.13% (all p<.001). 59% of EPT children with moderate/severe NDD had at least two co-occurring conditions; 24.9% with no/mild disability had comorbidity. Pairwise ADHD-DCD overlap NR.
major_limitations: High-risk perinatal population limits generalisability to idiopathic presentations; ADHD and ASD partly register-ascertained; outcomes at age 12 with no adult follow-up in this report; the specific ADHD-and-DCD co-occurrence proportion is not given.
individual_applicability: Demonstrates that neurodevelopmental multimorbidity including DCD is common and that perinatal history is a major competing explanation, so birth history should be established before attributing motor difficulty to idiopathic DCD.
quality_reason: Near-complete national cohort with a concurrent term-born control group and standardised cognitive, motor and behavioural instruments.

citation: Rebecca E Cooper, Amanda E Baker, Allysa D Quick, Lan Yu, Raul Gonzalez, Duncan B Clark, et al. Sleep Health Dimensions From Wearables and Transdiagnostic Mental Health in Young Adolescents. JAMA pediatrics. 2026;180(5):535-545. doi:10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.0335. PMID:41870441.
study_design: Multicentre longitudinal cohort (ABCD Study) with wearable actigraphy and factor analysis
population: 3393 early adolescents (median age 12 years; 49% female) in the United States
exposure_intervention: Fitbit-derived sleep dimensions over 7-21 days: irregularity, timing, social jetlag, duration, weekend oversleep, continuity
comparator: Within-cohort variation across sleep dimensions; cross-sectional and 1-year prospective contrasts
outcome: Transdiagnostic symptoms: internalizing, externalizing, attention, psychotic-like and mania symptoms
main_result: Greater sleep irregularity was associated with transdiagnostic symptoms cross-sectionally but not prospectively; shorter sleep duration was associated with total, internalizing, externalizing and attention symptoms cross-sectionally and with total, attention and psychotic symptoms one year later. Effect sizes were small.
major_limitations: Early-adolescent sample only, small effect sizes, symptom rather than diagnostic outcomes, irregularity effects did not persist prospectively; consumer-grade device.
individual_applicability: Provides objective, prospective adolescent evidence relevant to the developmental component of the model, but age and measurement differ from an adult clinical case.
quality_reason: Large multicentre cohort with objective sleep exposure, replicated factor structure and prospective outcomes, tempered by small effects and non-adult sample.

citation: Jade Desrosiers, David Gagnon, Alexia Ostrolenk, Alice Boutros, Boris C Bernhardt, Valérie Courchesne, et al. Calendar calculation: A systematic review of 100 years of research. Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews. 2025;178:106376. doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2025.106376. PMID:40972904.
study_design: Registered systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021254855) following PRISMA; 76 articles published 1920-2023
population: 105 documented calendar calculators (95 male), predominantly autistic savants; ages and settings varied
exposure_intervention: Calendar calculation ability as an exemplar of exceptional pattern-based skill
comparator: Within-person comparison of ability in the area of interest versus other cognitive domains; standardized IQ norms
outcome: Clinical characteristics, cognitive performance, developmental acquisition, behavioural correlates, empirical task effects and neuroimaging findings
main_result: Calendar calculation was associated with autism and typically acquired implicitly and autodidactically during school age. Participants generally demonstrated superior cognitive ability in their area of interest relative to other domains, while standardized full-scale IQ generally fell in the low range. 49.5% had a total calculation range under 100 years. Distance and priming effects were not consistently found, indicating performance variability. Neuroimaging implicated memory, visual and arithmetic networks.
effect_estimate: 105 calculators, 95 male; 49.5% with total calculation range under 100 years; no comparative effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Case-report and case-series literature spanning a century with severe selection bias toward extraordinary individuals; extreme sex imbalance; heterogeneous assessment methods; no representative autistic comparison sample; inconsistent experimental effects.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that exceptional pattern skill in autism is rare, domain-restricted and often accompanied by low measured IQ; it does not support generalizing pattern-recognition strength to autistic or ADHD adults broadly.
quality_reason: Registered and comprehensive review, but the underlying evidence is case-based, highly selected and methodologically heterogeneous, precluding population-level inference.

citation: Seong Ae Lee, Ah Rah Lee, Nan-He Yoon, Chae-Bin Kim, Geon Ho Bahn, Miae Oh. Effectiveness of Group Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and the Role of Cognitive Ability in Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Psychiatry investigation. 2025;22(11):1267-1276. doi:10.30773/pi.2025.0184. PMID:41089022.
study_design: Retrospective pre-post analysis of a 10-session group CBT programme, no control group
population: 24 adults with ADHD who completed group CBT in South Korea
exposure_intervention: Structured group CBT; subgroup stratification by full-scale IQ, attendance and comorbid depression
comparator: Pre-treatment baseline; IQ subgroups (below-average, average 90-109, high)
outcome: ADHD symptoms (ASRS, K-AARS) and functional impairment (K-AARS impairment subscale)
main_result: Clinically significant ADHD symptoms and functional impairment were present and improved across all IQ strata, including above-average IQ, with the most consistent improvement in the average-IQ subgroup and greater improvement with higher attendance.
effect_estimate: NR; significance reported without effect sizes or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Very small uncontrolled retrospective sample; multiple subgroup comparisons; regression to the mean and expectancy effects; no measure of effort or compensation.
individual_applicability: Weakly consistent with impairment coexisting with higher measured ability, but the sample is too small to support inference about high-achieving adults.
quality_reason: Uncontrolled retrospective design, n=24, no effect estimates, and post hoc IQ subgrouping.

citation: Fredrik Serenius, Thomas Abrahamsson, Ulrika Ådén, Kerstin Hellgren, Karin Sävman, Andreas Ohlin, et al. Neurodevelopmental Outcomes 12 Years After Extremely Preterm Birth in Sweden. Pediatrics. 2026;157(3):e2025073742. doi:10.1542/peds.2025-073742. PMID:41638598.
study_design: National prospective population-based cohort (EXPRESS) with term-born comparison group, assessed at age 12 using standardised instruments and national register diagnoses
population: 462 of 492 surviving children born before 27 weeks' gestation in Sweden (April 2004-March 2007) and 373 term-born controls
exposure_intervention: Extremely preterm birth
comparator: Term-born controls
outcome: Moderate/severe neurodevelopmental disability, ASD, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, behaviour problems, and multimorbidity at age 12
main_result: Extremely preterm children had markedly higher rates of every outcome than controls, and co-occurrence was the norm among those with moderate/severe disability; a substantial minority nonetheless had no ASD, ADHD or DCD diagnosis.
effect_estimate: Moderate/severe NDD 37.4% vs 4.6%; ASD 14.9% vs 2.41%; ADHD 21.2% vs 8.9%; DCD 29.4% vs 5.7%; behaviour problems 35.3% vs 8.13% (all p<.001). 59% of EPT children with moderate/severe NDD had at least two co-occurring conditions; 24.9% with no/mild disability had comorbidity. Pairwise ADHD-DCD overlap NR.
major_limitations: High-risk perinatal population limits generalisability to idiopathic presentations; ADHD and ASD partly register-ascertained; outcomes at age 12 with no adult follow-up in this report; the specific ADHD-and-DCD co-occurrence proportion is not given.
individual_applicability: Demonstrates that neurodevelopmental multimorbidity including DCD is common and that perinatal history is a major competing explanation, so birth history should be established before attributing motor difficulty to idiopathic DCD.
quality_reason: Near-complete national cohort with a concurrent term-born control group and standardised cognitive, motor and behavioural instruments.

citation: Armin Toghi, Azar Mohammadzadeh, Zahra Alemi, Anahita Khorrami Banaraki. Transdiagnostic eye-tracking biomarkers of inattention across psychiatric disorders: a systematic review. BMC psychiatry. 2025;25(1):1007. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-07415-w. PMID:41121040.
study_design: Systematic review of 75 eye-tracking studies mapped onto three attention domains (selective, sustained, executive control)
population: Participants across ADHD, ASD, Tourette syndrome, OCD, borderline personality disorder, developmental coordination disorder and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders; ages and sample sizes not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Psychiatric or neurodevelopmental diagnosis, assessed with oculomotor paradigms
comparator: Comparison across diagnostic conditions and against normative performance
outcome: Oculomotor metrics including antisaccade direction errors, fixation duration on relevant/irrelevant areas, latency to first fixation, anticipatory and intrusive saccades, and their relation to inattention
main_result: Impairments in several oculomotor metrics were shared across the psychiatric and neurodevelopmental conditions studied, including DCD, and correlated moderately with self-reported and behavioural inattention; the authors propose these as transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific markers.
effect_estimate: NR (correlations with inattention described as moderate; no pooled estimates)
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis with no pooling or risk-of-bias grading reported; heterogeneous paradigms and metrics; diagnostic groups not matched and not separately quantified; ages, sample sizes and DCD-specific findings not extractable from the abstract.
individual_applicability: Reinforces that candidate motor/oculomotor markers do not discriminate among ADHD, autism, DCD and other conditions, and that they track inattention, cautioning against reading such findings as diagnosis-specific.
quality_reason: Descriptive mapping review without pooling, matched comparisons, or reported sample characteristics.

citation: Yuxuan Han, Xinying Li, Ruolei Gu, Qingwen Ding, Xiaodi Qu, Yue He, et al. Genetic and environmental origins of the co-occurrence of autistic traits, anxiety and depression: Evidence from meta-analysis and twin study. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;122317. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122317. PMID:42508582.
study_design: Meta-analysis of six twin studies plus an empirical multivariate genetic twin study (common vs independent pathway models)
population: Study 1: predominantly Western child and adolescent twin samples. Study 2: 178 Chinese community twin pairs (109 monozygotic, 69 dizygotic) aged 24-35
exposure_intervention: Autistic traits
comparator: Co-twin design partitioning genetic, shared and non-shared environmental variance
outcome: Internalising symptoms, specifically anxiety and depressive symptoms
main_result: Genetic and non-shared environmental influences were shared between autistic traits and internalising symptoms; the adult sample tentatively favoured a common latent factor over independent pathways, aligning with a transdiagnostic account rather than one condition causing the other.
effect_estimate: Genetic correlation rA = 0.42; non-shared environmental correlation rE = 0.15; substantial heterogeneity across the six meta-analysed studies
major_limitations: Trait measures rather than diagnoses; small adult twin sample (178 pairs); common versus independent pathway models only tentatively distinguished; substantial between-study heterogeneity; aetiological covariance is not a social-functioning outcome.
individual_applicability: Argues against treating co-occurring anxiety/depression as simply secondary to autistic traits, but says nothing about which mechanism operates in one person.
quality_reason: Genetically informative design that can separate shared liability from causation, offset by trait-level measurement, small adult sample and heterogeneity.

citation: Gabriela Garcia de Carvalho Laguna, Baltazar Fernandes Andrade, Vanessa Souto Paulo, Marina Garcia Lorenzo Aguiar, Isadora Bagues Rodrigues, Jade Ponte da Cruz, et al. Differentiation between Autism Spectrum Disorder and Personality Disorders: a systematic review. Psychology, health & medicine. 2026;1-20. doi:10.1080/13548506.2026.2691413. PMID:42319023.
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA and registered on PROSPERO, covering original articles published 2020-2024
population: 684 individuals total: 550 clinical adult participants and 134 healthcare professionals
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic assessment of adult autism spectrum disorder
comparator: Personality disorders, particularly borderline personality disorder
outcome: Differential-diagnostic criteria and their impact on diagnostic accuracy
main_result: Feature overlap, especially between ASD and borderline personality disorder, compromises diagnostic accuracy; ASD was characterised by cognitive rigidity and difficulty interpreting social norms whereas personality disorders featured emotional instability, impulsivity and fear of abandonment, and self-harm had different antecedents in each; absent standardised criteria and reliance on subjective assessment increase diagnostic error and delay.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Small pooled sample; narrow 2020-2024 publication window; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias grading reported in abstract; heterogeneous designs including professional-survey data; distinguishing framework derived within the review rather than validated prospectively.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant: adult social difficulty with emotional dysregulation can be produced by personality-disorder processes as well as autism, and the two are frequently confused in adult assessment.
quality_reason: Systematic in method but based on few, heterogeneous studies with a small aggregate sample and no quantitative accuracy estimates.

citation: Ali Jami, Sajjad Abbaszade, Abdol-Hossein Vahabie. A review on exploration-exploitation trade-off in psychiatric disorders. BMC psychiatry. 2025;25(1):420. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-06837-w. PMID:40287643.
study_design: Systematic review of 46 studies using tasks probing exploration-exploitation balance across psychiatric disorders; PubMed search; narrative synthesis
population: Individuals with psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders including ADHD, schizophrenia, OCD, anxiety, mood disorders and addictive disorders; total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Diagnostic status assessed on decision-making tasks manipulating exploration versus exploitation, novelty and reward
comparator: Healthy controls and cross-disorder comparisons
outcome: Exploration-exploitation balance, decision stability, reward sensitivity, learning and adaptability
main_result: Disorders clustered into addictive patterns, emotional/cognitive disturbances and neurological conditions. Anxiety and mood disorders often showed enhanced exploratory behaviour, and depression affected decision stability and reward sensitivity. Schizophrenia, OCD and ADHD were characterized by excessive switching and difficulty balancing exploration and exploitation, leading to impaired learning and adaptability. Addiction-like presentations showed reduced exploration and impulsive or perseverative choices.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative synthesis of 46 studies without pooled effect estimates
major_limitations: Single-database (PubMed) search; narrative synthesis of highly heterogeneous computational tasks; no formal risk-of-bias appraisal; case-control designs cannot establish diagnostic specificity; ADHD findings not separated by age or medication status.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to whether novelty- and reward-linked performance patterns are ADHD-specific; indicates they are shared with anxiety, mood, OCD and substance-related conditions that are competing explanations in this case.
quality_reason: Systematic in intent but limited by single-database searching, absent bias appraisal, no quantitative synthesis, and marked task heterogeneity across the reviewed literature.

citation: Francesco Maria Boccaccio, Renata Rizzo, Concetta Pirrone, Jan K Buitelaar. Mapping the association between cognitive disengagement syndrome and internalizing disorders: A systematic scoping review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122159. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122159. PMID:42341946.
study_design: Systematic scoping review with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression (82 studies, 2002-2025)
population: Children, adolescents and adults from healthy and clinical samples
exposure_intervention: Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome (CDS), previously Sluggish Cognitive Tempo
comparator: Lower CDS levels; analyses controlling for ADHD inattention
outcome: Depression, anxiety and broader internalizing symptoms; functional consequences
main_result: Elevated CDS was consistently associated with depression and anxiety, with more than one-third of individuals reaching clinical thresholds; associations remained significant after controlling for ADHD inattention and were seen across ages. Meta-analyses showed the strongest link for depression (r=0.56), then anxiety (r=0.46) and internalizing symptoms (r=0.44); meta-regression identified depression as a significant moderator and inflated effect sizes in same-informant studies.
effect_estimate: r=0.56 (depression), r=0.46 (anxiety), r=0.44 (internalizing); confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Abstract does not state that CDS items index daydreaming; scarce longitudinal and multi-informant studies; no analytic control for symptom overlap despite acknowledged phenomenological similarity; same-informant inflation.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an inattention-adjacent construct tracks depression strongly and independently of ADHD inattention, relevant to differentiating mood-driven from compensation-driven inner experience.
quality_reason: Quantitative synthesis with moderator testing, but construct-overlap confounding is explicitly unaddressed and longitudinal evidence is sparse.

citation: Aja Louise Murray, Katie Dryburgh, Edmund J S Sonuga-Barke. Identifying Candidate Mediators Linking ADHD Symptoms and Internalising Problems in Adolescence: An Exploratory Longitudinal Mediation Analysis. Journal of attention disorders. 2026;30(8):986-998. doi:10.1177/10870547261419589. PMID:41789525.
study_design: Exploratory longitudinal mediation analysis using regularised structural equation modelling (lasso)
population: Millennium Cohort Study; 2,607 male and 2,791 female participants assessed at ages 11, 14 and 17
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms in adolescence
comparator: Lower ADHD symptom levels within the cohort
outcome: Internalising (anxiety and depressive) symptoms, with 14 candidate mediators including peer problems, conduct problems, self-esteem, injuries, parental relationships, academic performance, risky decision-making, parental mental health, educational motivation and general health
main_result: Regularisation did not de-select any of the 14 candidate mediators, but only two were statistically significant. The authors conclude there may be many mediators of small effect linking ADHD symptoms to later internalising problems, and identify self-esteem and parental mental health as priority mechanisms for future causal and interventional research.
effect_estimate: NR (individual path estimates and confidence intervals not reported in the abstract)
major_limitations: Explicitly exploratory with 14 simultaneous mediators and no confirmatory replication; observational, so mediation remains associational; abstract does not identify which two paths were significant with estimates.
individual_applicability: Tempers the expectation that any single anxiety- or rejection-related mediator carries the functional burden; suggests distributed small effects rather than one dominant pathway.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised national cohort with three waves and appropriate regularisation, but exploratory framing, absent effect estimates and untested causal assumptions limit inference.

citation: Yuan You, Tom McAdams, Yasmin I Ahmadzadeh, Tabea Schoeler, Filip Marzecki, Helena M S Zavos. The role of comorbid childhood mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions in the persistence of ADHD symptoms: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines. 2026;67(2):183-201. doi:10.1111/jcpp.70028. PMID:40801243.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel random-effects models; 26 studies
population: Children with ADHD followed to later developmental stages
exposure_intervention: Childhood comorbid internalizing, externalizing and neurodevelopmental conditions
comparator: ADHD without the specified comorbidity
outcome: Persistence of ADHD symptoms into later developmental stages
main_result: Childhood externalizing and, more weakly, internalizing comorbidity predicted ADHD persistence, but adjustment attenuated externalizing and eliminated the internalizing association; neurodevelopmental comorbidity did not predict persistence, and the externalizing effect appeared only with parent-reported data.
effect_estimate: Internalizing d=0.19 (adjusted d=0.06, non-significant); externalizing d=0.31 (adjusted d=0.24); neurodevelopmental comorbidity non-significant
major_limitations: Informant-dependent findings suggest common-method bias; residual confounding acknowledged; heterogeneous definitions of persistence and follow-up intervals.
individual_applicability: Shows persistence estimates are sensitive to comorbidity and informant, relevant given this individual's reported anxiety, mood and substance history.
quality_reason: Appropriate multilevel synthesis with adjusted analyses, limited by observational primary data and informant confounding.

citation: Shivahn Garvie, Maryam Sorkhou, Tony P George. Clinical Phenomenology of Bipolar Disorder With Substance Use Disorders: A Systematic Review. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(5):e70132. doi:10.1111/bdi.70132. PMID:42286971.
study_design: Systematic review of 48 clinical studies with narrative synthesis (PubMed, PsycINFO)
population: Adults with bipolar disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, stimulants, opioids); total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Specific substance use disorders, principally cannabis use disorder and alcohol use disorder
comparator: Bipolar disorder without the specific substance use disorder (comparator details NR)
outcome: Bipolar symptomatology, course of illness (manic episodes, rapid cycling, psychosis, age at onset, suicidality) and treatment outcomes
main_result: Cannabis use disorder was frequently associated with increased manic episodes, rapid cycling, psychosis and earlier bipolar onset, with mixed findings for depressive episodes, suicidality and treatment outcomes; alcohol use disorder was linked mainly to worse depression and suicidality, while tobacco, cocaine, opioid and methamphetamine comorbidity was underexplored and associated with increased suicidality, hospitalizations and medication nonadherence.
effect_estimate: NR (narrative synthesis; no pooled effect estimates or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Predominantly cross-sectional and observational studies synthesized narratively, no pooled effects, substantial risk of reverse causation and confounding by overall illness severity, and very sparse tobacco- and stimulant-specific evidence.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant to a person with reported bipolar history and cannabis and nicotine exposure, but the associations are group-level and cannot establish that substances caused this individual's episodes.
quality_reason: Large but methodologically weak observational evidence base without pooling, with authors explicitly noting the need for more rigorous designs.

citation: Ali Dadfar, Mia Ramklint, Sara von Wallenberg Pachaly. A systematic review of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)-induced activation and manic/hypomanic switch in children and adolescents. Scandinavian journal of child and adolescent psychiatry and psychology. 2025;13(1):117-134. doi:10.2478/sjcapp-2025-0011. PMID:41404486.
study_design: PROSPERO-registered PRISMA systematic review (CRD42023422133) of 30 articles with duplicate blinded screening; qualitative synthesis of definitions and assessments
population: 30 articles covering children and adolescents aged 6-18 years treated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; total N NR
exposure_intervention: SSRI treatment, with outcomes of drug-induced activation or manic/hypomanic switch
comparator: NR (comparison was between activation and manic/hypomanic switch constructs rather than between exposure groups)
outcome: Definitions, symptom profiles, assessment instruments and inter-rater reliability for activation versus manic/hypomanic switch
main_result: Only 8 of 30 articles clearly defined activation and 4 defined mania/hypomania, one instrument existed for activation and none for mania, and only 2 reported reliability; symptoms overlapped substantially, with aggression/hostility, anxiety/panic and suicidality more often reported under activation and cognitive/thought-process and mood changes more often under mania/hypomania.
effect_estimate: NR (no incidence rates, effect sizes or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Pediatric samples only, exposure is SSRIs rather than stimulants or cannabis, no incidence or effect estimates, and vague heterogeneous definitions mean the reported symptom differences may reflect reporting conventions rather than distinct phenomena.
individual_applicability: Illustrates the general clinical problem of distinguishing medication-induced activation from a mood episode, which applies to this case, but the population and drug class differ.
quality_reason: Registered review with duplicate screening, but the underlying literature lacks validated definitions, instruments and reliability data, and no quantitative outcomes are available.

citation: Marta Pozo-Rodríguez, Sara Cruz, Sabela Conde-Pumpido-Zubizarreta, Angel Carracedo, María Tubío-Fungueiriño, Montse Fernández-Prieto. A systematic review on the association between executive function and emotional regulation in autism, ADHD, and autism/ADHD. Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews. 2026;183:106570. doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.106570. PMID:41579913.
study_design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis of 22 empirical articles published January 2013 to October 2024
population: Children and adults with autism (4 studies), ADHD (16 studies), or co-occurring autism/ADHD (2 studies)
exposure_intervention: Executive function, measured by task-based and report-based instruments
comparator: Comparison across autism, ADHD and co-occurring autism/ADHD groups
outcome: Emotion regulation and emotional dysregulation
main_result: Evidence overall indicated an association between executive function difficulties and emotional dysregulation across all three conditions; age and measurement approach contributed to variability, and too few studies of the co-occurring group existed to draw conclusions about differential diagnosis.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Narrative synthesis without pooling; only two studies of the co-occurring group; heterogeneous EF and ER measures; mixed ages; publication window restricted to 2013 onward.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that an executive-function-to-emotional-dysregulation pathway is shared rather than diagnosis-specific, so this pattern in the case cannot discriminate ADHD from autism.
quality_reason: Small, heterogeneous evidence base with no quantitative synthesis and near-absent data on the co-occurring phenotype of interest.

citation: Simin Kang, Zhao Fu, Qiurong Li, Li Yang, Qingjiu Cao. Adult-diagnosed and childhood-diagnosed attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder: cognitive and environmental contributions to symptom severity across different age of diagnosis. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1782999. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1782999. PMID:42147013.
study_design: Cross-sectional comparative study with hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analysis
population: 72 adults with ADHD: 37 childhood-diagnosed (26.32 +/- 4.69 years) and 35 adult-diagnosed (25.63 +/- 4.89 years), diagnosed by structured interview
exposure_intervention: Executive function (BRIEF-A) and environmental factors: childhood trauma (CTQ), resilience (CD-RISC), parental bonding (PBI)
comparator: Childhood-diagnosed versus adult-diagnosed ADHD groups; relative variance contribution of executive versus environmental predictors
outcome: ADHD core symptom severity (ASRS inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity); emotional symptoms (SAS, SDS)
main_result: Executive function was the strongest and most consistent predictor of both inattention (beta 0.64, p<0.001) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (beta 0.47, p<0.001), whereas environmental factors contributed minimal additional explanatory power, with only a modest association between parental overprotection and inattention (beta 0.28, p=0.016). No diagnosis-specific moderation effects were observed. Adult-diagnosed participants showed lower childhood symptoms but similar adult severity, with more psychiatric comorbidity and emotional distress.
