effect_estimate: beta 0.64 (inattention) and 0.47 (hyperactivity-impulsivity) for executive function; beta 0.28 (p=0.016) for parental overprotection; confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: Small single-site sample; cross-sectional; retrospective childhood trauma and parenting recall; outcome is symptom severity rather than real-world functional impairment; no formal mediation testing.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult with late-recognised ADHD, and supports executive rather than adversity-related variables as the dominant symptom correlate, but small-sample and symptom-level outcomes limit transfer.
quality_reason: Structured diagnostic ascertainment is a strength, but low power, cross-sectional design and retrospective exposure measures constrain interpretation.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies, with multiple regression on pooled correlation matrices to control symptom overlap
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples; total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Symptom dimensions of ADHD-inattention (ADHD-I), ADHD-hyperactivity/impulsivity (ADHD-HI) and cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS)
comparator: Each symptom dimension after controlling shared variance with the other dimensions
outcome: Cognitive correlates including social cognition, motor coordination, perceptual-motor functioning, attention, inhibition, working memory, processing speed
main_result: Profiles looked similar in bivariate correlations but diverged in regression: ADHD-HI was associated with weaker social cognition and focused/sustained attention yet better motor coordination; ADHD-I with weaker intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, perceptual-motor functioning and memory; CDS with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: ADHD-HI: social cognition and attention betas -.24 to -.11 (p<.001); motor coordination beta = .14 (p<.001). ADHD-I: betas -.21 to -.10 (p<.01). CDS: betas -.29 to -.13 (p<.001).
major_limitations: All constituent studies cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; dimensions defined by rating scales rather than diagnoses; pooling across child and adult samples; laboratory/rating cognitive proxies rather than real-world social or motor functioning.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult reporting both inattentive and hyperactive features, but findings are group-level, symptom-scale based, and cannot attribute this person's social or motor difficulties to a specific dimension.
quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

citation: Noa E van der Plas, Siri D S Noordermeer, Barbara Franke, Catharina A Hartman, Pieter J Hoekstra, Nanda N J Rommelse, et al. Growing up with ADHD: findings from an 18-year longitudinal follow-up study of adults with childhood ADHD, their siblings, and controls. Psychiatry research. 2026;364:117308. doi:10.1016/j.psychres.2026.117308. PMID:42365682.
study_design: Prospective 18-year longitudinal follow-up cohort with sibling and control comparison groups
population: Adults with childhood ADHD (n=154, mean age 27.4, 68% male), siblings without childhood ADHD (n=138), controls (n=129)
exposure_intervention: Childhood ADHD diagnosis; secondary contrast of persistent versus remitted adult ADHD
comparator: Siblings without childhood ADHD and unrelated controls
outcome: Adult psychiatric status, behavioural/emotional problems, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognition, physical health, healthcare use
main_result: Childhood ADHD was associated with worse adult functioning on more than 60% of outcomes across all domains; siblings functioned comparably to controls; persistent ADHD showed worse functioning than remitted ADHD on psychiatric, behavioural/emotional, adaptive and physical health outcomes, while both ADHD groups were worse than controls.
effect_estimate: Effect sizes described as small to large; numeric estimates and confidence intervals NR in abstract
major_limitations: Attrition over 18 years not quantified in abstract; sex imbalance across groups (68% vs 35% vs 40% male); outcome instruments and covariate adjustment not specified; substantial within-group heterogeneity acknowledged.
individual_applicability: Closest available analogue to a lifelong developmental trajectory question, but group-level and cannot establish that this individual's adult difficulties originate in childhood ADHD.
quality_reason: Long prospective follow-up with two comparison groups is a strong design, downgraded for unreported effect sizes, unclear attrition, and abstract-only appraisal.

citation: Maria Giuseppina Petruzzelli, Emilia Matera, Lucia Margari, Lucia Marzulli, Alessandra Gabellone, Chiara Cotugno, et al. An update on the comorbidity of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and its clinical management. Expert review of neurotherapeutics. 2026;26(1):75-89. doi:10.1080/14737175.2025.2599856. PMID:41388592.
study_design: Targeted narrative expert review prioritising meta-analyses and umbrella reviews (PubMed search to 24 March 2025)
population: Individuals with ADHD, ASD, or both, across the lifespan
exposure_intervention: Co-occurring ADHD and ASD
comparator: Single-diagnosis presentations
outcome: Shared and distinct phenotypic, neuropsychological, genetic and neuroimaging correlates; assessment and management approaches
main_result: Reports both shared and distinct correlates of ADHD and ASD, states that the comorbidity should not be overlooked, and advises that comorbid diagnosis be made only after thorough differential assessment establishing that ADHD symptoms are not better explained by ASD; calls for research on personalised treatment and real-world outcomes.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Non-systematic targeted search with expert-opinion synthesis; no quantitative pooling, no risk-of-bias appraisal, no explicit eligibility criteria; recommendations are consensus rather than evidence-graded.
individual_applicability: Provides an explicit clinical sequencing principle for the case (differential before comorbid diagnosis) but is expert opinion, the lowest tier of the protocol's hierarchy.
quality_reason: Expert narrative review without systematic search, appraisal or effect estimates.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. The risk of psychosis associated with cannabis use by people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of 3 heterogeneous studies; risk of bias rated fair (k=1) and good (k=2)
population: People with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder exposed to cannabis; sample sizes, ages and diagnostic methods NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use in individuals with ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD who use cannabis, and/or ADHD individuals without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis outcomes
main_result: Two of three studies indirectly suggested that cannabis use does not increase psychosis risk among people with ADHD, and the third indicated that cannabis had a similar impact on psychosis risk in people with and without ADHD; the authors conclude there is very little evidence for a heightened ADHD-specific risk.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates; synthesis without meta-analysis)
major_limitations: Only three studies, two of which addressed the question indirectly, almost certainly underpowered to detect an interaction, exposure and diagnostic ascertainment not described, and absence of evidence is reported rather than evidence of absence.
individual_applicability: Directly targets the proposed ADHD-by-cannabis interaction relevant to this case, but the evidence base is too thin to exclude a clinically meaningful individual effect.
quality_reason: Very small number of studies with indirect inference and no quantitative synthesis, despite generally fair-to-good individual study ratings.

citation: Siyi Li, Huanqing Wang, Guoqiu Chen, Xi Cheng, Yuxi Wang, Wanyan Hu, et al. Social functioning in autism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nature human behaviour. 2026;10(7):1260-1273. doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02457-w. PMID:42120904.
study_design: Systematic review with two complementary quantitative meta-analyses of behavioural studies published 1990-2025
population: 94,114 clinically diagnosed autistic and 172,847 neurotypical individuals across 32 countries and 2,622 studies
exposure_intervention: Clinically diagnosed autism
comparator: Neurotypical controls
outcome: 22 social components clustered into five domains, plus developmental timing and cross-domain organisation
main_result: Substantial overall group differences in social functioning; earliest divergence in motivation-based processes (around six months), followed by motor, emotion and inference domains, with stronger cross-domain interdependency in autism and an organisation most consistent with serial relations among domains.
major_limitations: No ADHD or DCD comparator, so incremental variance beyond ADHD is not tested; methodological heterogeneity; many underpowered constituent samples; uneven cultural representation; pooling across a very wide age range and construct set.
individual_applicability: Establishes that autistic social differences are large and replicable at group level, but cannot indicate whether autistic features add explanatory value beyond ADHD in this person.
quality_reason: Exceptionally large, diagnosis-based synthesis with quantified effects, but heterogeneous constructs and absence of neurodevelopmental comparator groups limit inference for the claim as worded.

citation: Gonzalo Salazar de Pablo, Claudia Aymerich, Juan Pablo Chart-Pascual, Marco Solmi, Javier Torres-Cortes, Nessma Abdelhafez, et al. Occurrence of Psychosis and Bipolar Disorder in Individuals With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treated With Stimulants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA psychiatry. 2025;82(11):1103-1112. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2025.2311. PMID:40900605.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA/MOOSE) of 16 studies with Newcastle-Ottawa and RoB-2 appraisal
population: 391,043 individuals with DSM- or ICD-defined ADHD (mean age 12.6 years; 73.7% male)
exposure_intervention: Prescribed stimulant medication; amphetamines versus methylphenidate
comparator: Methylphenidate comparison group; unexposed comparisons largely unavailable
outcome: Psychotic symptoms, psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder
main_result: Non-negligible proportions of stimulant-treated individuals with ADHD developed psychotic symptoms, psychotic disorder or bipolar disorder, with higher occurrence for amphetamines than methylphenidate; the authors state causality cannot be established.
effect_estimate: Psychotic symptoms 2.76% (95% CI 0.73-9.88); psychotic disorder 2.29% (1.52-3.40); bipolar disorder 3.72% (0.77-16.05); amphetamine vs methylphenidate OR 1.57 (1.15-2.16); I²>95%
major_limitations: Extreme heterogeneity; no unexposed control arm in most studies; confounding by indication and by underlying illness severity; predominantly paediatric samples; causality explicitly disclaimed.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the safety-relevant question of medication- and state-related contributions in someone with reported bipolar-spectrum history and stimulant exposure, without attributing causation.
quality_reason: Large preregistered meta-analysis with formal appraisal, downgraded heavily for I²>95%, absent unexposed comparators and confounding by indication.

citation: Gonzalo Salazar de Pablo, Claudia Aymerich, Juan Pablo Chart-Pascual, Marco Solmi, Javier Torres-Cortes, Nessma Abdelhafez, et al. Occurrence of Psychosis and Bipolar Disorder in Individuals With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treated With Stimulants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA psychiatry. 2025;82(11):1103-1112. doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2025.2311. PMID:40900605.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of observational and other designs (PRISMA, MOOSE; Newcastle-Ottawa and Cochrane RoB2)
population: 16 studies, N=391,043 individuals with DSM/ICD-defined ADHD; mean age 12.6 years (range 8.5-31.1); 288,199 (73.7%) male
exposure_intervention: Prescribed stimulant medication (amphetamines or methylphenidate)
comparator: Mostly none (proportion estimates); head-to-head amphetamines versus methylphenidate for the psychosis comparison
outcome: Occurrence of psychotic symptoms, psychotic disorder, and bipolar disorder
main_result: Pooled occurrence was 2.76% for psychotic symptoms, 2.29% for psychotic disorder, and 3.72% for bipolar disorder; psychosis occurrence was higher with amphetamines than methylphenidate, and increased occurrence was associated with higher stimulant dose, higher proportion of female participants, smaller samples, North American setting, and longer follow-up.
effect_estimate: Psychotic symptoms 2.76% (95% CI 0.73-9.88, k=10, n=237,035); psychotic disorder 2.29% (1.52-3.40, k=4, n=91,437); bipolar disorder 3.72% (0.77-16.05, k=4, n=92,945); amphetamine vs methylphenidate psychosis OR 1.57 (1.15-2.16, k=3, n=231,325); I-squared >95%
major_limitations: Most estimates are uncontrolled proportions without unexposed comparators, heterogeneity exceeded 95%, samples were predominantly children and adolescents, and the authors state that included studies cannot establish causality.
individual_applicability: Quantifies the low but non-negligible occurrence relevant to stimulant decisions in an adult with bipolar vulnerability, though the pooled sample is much younger than this case.
quality_reason: Large registered meta-analysis with design-appropriate appraisal, downgraded for extreme heterogeneity, absent unexposed comparators, and confounding by indication.

citation: Andrea Jiménez-Mayoral, Dídac Florensa, Vicent Llorca-Bofí, María Irigoyen-Otiñano. Diagnostic Trends of Minors in Psychiatric Emergency Care: An Observational Study. Actas espanolas de psiquiatria. 2026;54(1):163-171. doi:10.62641/aep.v54i1.2061. PMID:41755570.
study_design: Retrospective observational cohort with 24-month follow-up and exploratory association-rule analysis
population: 583 patients aged 4-18 years attending a first psychiatric emergency visit in Spain (2017-2023); median age 14.9 years
exposure_intervention: Baseline emergency psychiatric diagnosis
comparator: Same patients at 24-month follow-up (within-person diagnostic transition)
outcome: Diagnostic stability and transition patterns
main_result: Diagnostic stability was heterogeneous, high for schizophrenia/psychosis (71%) and low for ADHD and eating disorders, with a notable transition pattern from autism plus ADHD to conduct disorders.
effect_estimate: Schizophrenia/psychosis stability 71%; intellectual disability with gender identity disorder 67%; mood disorders ~44%; eating disorders 26%; conduct disorders 17%; autism+ADHD to conduct disorder confidence 0.66, lift 2.55
major_limitations: Emergency-service sample with atypical case mix; diagnostic label stability is not the same as symptom or impairment persistence; retrospective electronic record extraction; no standardised reassessment protocol.
individual_applicability: Cautions that clinical diagnostic labels applied in crisis settings shift substantially over two years, relevant to interpreting any single diagnostic formulation.
quality_reason: Retrospective single-centre record review with a selected emergency population and outcome that only indirectly indexes trait persistence.

citation: Meghan Fiske, Dominique L DiDomenico, Henry W Chase, Yvette Afriyie-Agyemang, Genna Bebko, Haris A Aslam, et al. Bipolar Disorder Psychosis Risk Predicts Cue Discrimination on the AX-Continuous Performance Task Paradigm. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(4):e70129. doi:10.1111/bdi.70129. PMID:42262032.
study_design: Cross-sectional study with dimensional linear regression aims and categorical group comparisons (ANCOVA)
population: Euthymic bipolar disorder (n=27) and bipolar-at-risk individuals (n=121), total analysed sample 148; ages NR
exposure_intervention: Lifetime mania/affective-lability risk (psychomotor activation, suicidality, mixed instability) and lifetime psychosis risk indexed by the Mood Spectrum Self Report
comparator: Lower-risk individuals within the same cohort; bipolar low-risk versus high-risk groups; no healthy control group described
outcome: AX-Continuous Performance Test measures d'context (target/context discrimination) and A-cue bias
main_result: Higher lifetime psychosis and mania/affective-lability risk were associated with reduced d'context but not with altered A-cue bias, and categorical group comparisons showed no significant differences; the associations survived adjustment for current depressive symptoms but disappeared after covarying current mania severity.
effect_estimate: Dimensional associations with d'context: absolute t values >2.015, p<0.047; after covarying current mania severity absolute t values <1.26, all p>0.203; no effect sizes or confidence intervals reported (NR)
major_limitations: Cross-sectional design, small bipolar subgroup (n=27), reliance on retrospective self-report for lifetime risk, single laboratory task, no reported control of medication, sleep or substance exposure, and 'euthymic' status still permitted variable current mania severity.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to the state-versus-trait question in this case, showing that residual current mood elevation can account for attention deficits that look trait-like; single-timepoint group data cannot classify one person.
quality_reason: Small cross-sectional sample with self-report exposure and a single task; the key finding is a covariate-attenuation result reported without effect sizes.

citation: Giulia Trotta, Isabelle Austin-Zimmerman, Edoardo Spinazzola, Senta Haussler, Lucia Sideli, Monica Aas, et al. Gene-Environment Correlation Across Trauma Subtypes and Developmental Timing: Evidence From the EU-GEI and ALSPAC. Biological psychiatry. 2026;S0006-3223(26)01130-3. doi:10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.03.1000. PMID:41933711.
study_design: Genetically informed observational analysis in two cohorts (case-control and prospective birth cohort)
population: EU-GEI case-control study (n=1,191) and ALSPAC birth cohort (n=8,141)
exposure_intervention: Polygenic risk scores for psychiatric and behavioural traits (PTSD, ADHD, schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, cannabis use disorder)
comparator: Lower polygenic risk within cohort; unexposed or later-exposed trauma groups
outcome: Timing (early 0-11 vs late 12-17 years) and type of trauma exposure: emotional, physical and sexual abuse, bullying, household discord
main_result: In EU-GEI, 20 PRS-trauma associations survived FDR correction: PTSD PRS with early emotional abuse (OR 3.37), sexual abuse (3.08), physical abuse (2.90) and bullying (2.19); ADHD PRS with early sexual abuse (1.49), emotional abuse (1.33), household discord (1.27) and bullying (1.24); schizophrenia PRS with early emotional abuse (1.90) and late bullying (1.46). Twenty associations were replicated in ALSPAC; variance explained was small in both cohorts and results held in control-only sensitivity analyses.
effect_estimate: Odds ratios 1.24-3.37 as listed; confidence intervals NR; variance explained described as small
major_limitations: European-ancestry samples; retrospective trauma reporting in EU-GEI; small variance explained; gene-environment correlation does not exclude genuine environmental effects; no daydreaming or functional outcome measured.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant as a confounding caution: genetic liability is associated with the likelihood of reporting bullying and abuse, so adversity-to-outcome sequences in this narrative may be partly non-causal.
quality_reason: Two-cohort design with replication and FDR control, but observational, ancestry-restricted, and dependent on retrospective exposure recall in one cohort.

citation: Zoë E Laky, Daniel S Pine, Charles Y Zheng, Reut Naim. Data-Driven Profiles of Youth Executive Function and Their Longitudinal Associations With Externalizing Problems. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2026;S0890-8567(26)00279-0. doi:10.1016/j.jaac.2026.06.014. PMID:42336134.
study_design: Longitudinal cohort with unsupervised clustering (k-means) across baseline to 3-year follow-up (ABCD Study)
population: 5,501 youth assessed from approximately ages 9-10 to 12-13
exposure_intervention: Data-driven executive function profiles from Stop Signal and Emotional N-Back tasks
comparator: Higher executive function cluster versus lower executive function cluster
outcome: CBCL attention problems, aggressive and rule-breaking behaviour, ADHD diagnosis
main_result: Lower executive function cluster membership was associated with greater attention problems concurrently and longitudinally and with more ADHD diagnoses, with no association to aggressive or rule-breaking behaviour, but effects were small and cluster membership was only moderately stable over time.
effect_estimate: Attention problems rank-biserial r=0.06-0.11 (q<0.05); ADHD diagnosis OR 1.65-1.71 (q≤0.001); cluster stability Cohen's κ=0.41
major_limitations: Very small effect sizes; only moderate temporal stability of EF profiles; parent-reported behavioural outcomes; community sample limiting clinical extrapolation.
individual_applicability: Supports a specific but weak developmental link between objective executive performance and attention problems; the small effects argue against strong inference from lab tasks to individual life outcomes.
quality_reason: Large well-characterised longitudinal cohort with objective tasks, downgraded for small effects, modest profile stability and single-informant outcomes.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. The risk of psychosis associated with cannabis use by people with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of 3 heterogeneous studies; risk of bias rated fair (k=1) and good (k=2)
population: People with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder exposed to cannabis; sample sizes, ages and diagnostic methods NR
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use in individuals with ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD who use cannabis, and/or ADHD individuals without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis outcomes
main_result: Two of three studies indirectly suggested that cannabis use does not increase psychosis risk among people with ADHD, and the third indicated that cannabis had a similar impact on psychosis risk in people with and without ADHD; the authors conclude there is very little evidence for a heightened ADHD-specific risk.
effect_estimate: NR (no pooled estimates; synthesis without meta-analysis)
major_limitations: Only three studies, two of which addressed the question indirectly, almost certainly underpowered to detect an interaction, exposure and diagnostic ascertainment not described, and absence of evidence is reported rather than evidence of absence.
individual_applicability: Directly targets the proposed ADHD-by-cannabis interaction relevant to this case, but the evidence base is too thin to exclude a clinically meaningful individual effect.
quality_reason: Very small number of studies with indirect inference and no quantitative synthesis, despite generally fair-to-good individual study ratings.

citation: Blandine French, Victoria Newell, Gamze Nalbant, Hannah Wright, David Daley, Sarah Cassidy. Adverse outcomes for autistic people: an umbrella review of mental health, physical health, social and lifestyle domains. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2026;17:1702822. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1702822. PMID:42199907.
study_design: Umbrella review of 134 systematic, meta-analytic and narrative reviews identified from 13,841 records; five databases searched to June 2024; inductive narrative synthesis
population: Autistic people across the lifespan as represented in review-level evidence; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Autism diagnosis as exposure across mental health, physical health, and social and lifestyle domains
comparator: Non-autistic comparison populations as used within the included reviews; comparator definitions varied
outcome: Adverse outcomes including anxiety and mood disorders, suicidality, sleep problems, epilepsy, obesity, mortality risk, victimisation and bullying, quality of life, loneliness, relationship difficulties and unemployment
main_result: Across 134 reviews, elevated risk patterns were consistently reported for anxiety and mood disorders, suicidality and self-harm, eating and psychotic disorders, sleep problems, epilepsy, gastrointestinal difficulties, obesity, oral health problems, mortality, victimisation and bullying, reduced quality of life, loneliness, relationship difficulties and unemployment. Evidence strength varied across outcomes but elevated risk was reported across multiple independent reviews.
effect_estimate: NR; narrative umbrella synthesis of 134 reviews without pooled estimates or confidence intervals
major_limitations: Review-level rather than primary evidence with likely overlap between included reviews; narrative synthesis without pooled effects; heterogeneous review quality; does not test whether environmental modification alters these outcomes.
individual_applicability: Provides population-level context that substantial cross-domain burden persists in autism, cautioning against a formulation in which impairment is primarily attributable to environmental mismatch; not individually diagnostic.
quality_reason: Large, systematically conducted umbrella synthesis with dual screening, but narrative-only integration, unquantified review overlap and variable underlying evidence strength limit certainty.

citation: Shivahn Garvie, Maryam Sorkhou, Tony P George. Clinical Phenomenology of Bipolar Disorder With Substance Use Disorders: A Systematic Review. Bipolar disorders. 2026;28(5):e70132. doi:10.1111/bdi.70132. PMID:42286971.
study_design: Systematic review of 48 clinical studies with narrative synthesis (PubMed, PsycINFO)
population: Adults with bipolar disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, stimulants, opioids); total N and ages NR
exposure_intervention: Specific substance use disorders, principally cannabis use disorder and alcohol use disorder
comparator: Bipolar disorder without the specific substance use disorder (comparator details NR)
outcome: Bipolar symptomatology, course of illness (manic episodes, rapid cycling, psychosis, age at onset, suicidality) and treatment outcomes
main_result: Cannabis use disorder was frequently associated with increased manic episodes, rapid cycling, psychosis and earlier bipolar onset, with mixed findings for depressive episodes, suicidality and treatment outcomes; alcohol use disorder was linked mainly to worse depression and suicidality, while tobacco, cocaine, opioid and methamphetamine comorbidity was underexplored and associated with increased suicidality, hospitalizations and medication nonadherence.
effect_estimate: NR (narrative synthesis; no pooled effect estimates or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Predominantly cross-sectional and observational studies synthesized narratively, no pooled effects, substantial risk of reverse causation and confounding by overall illness severity, and very sparse tobacco- and stimulant-specific evidence.
individual_applicability: Highly relevant to a person with reported bipolar history and cannabis and nicotine exposure, but the associations are group-level and cannot establish that substances caused this individual's episodes.
quality_reason: Large but methodologically weak observational evidence base without pooling, with authors explicitly noting the need for more rigorous designs.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies with regression on pooled correlation matrices
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples
exposure_intervention: Dimensional inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity and cognitive disengagement symptoms
comparator: Shared variance between symptom dimensions statistically controlled
outcome: Intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, attention, processing speed, memory, motor coordination, social cognition
main_result: After controlling symptom overlap, inattention was associated with weaker measured intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory and memory, hyperactivity-impulsivity with weaker attention and social cognition but better motor coordination, and cognitive disengagement with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: Inattention βs -.21 to -.10 (p<.01); hyperactivity-impulsivity βs -.24 to -.11 (p<.001) and motor coordination β=.14 (p<.001); cognitive disengagement βs -.29 to -.13 (p<.001)
major_limitations: Entirely cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; pooled correlation-matrix regression assumes comparable measurement across studies; no within-person or achievement outcomes.
individual_applicability: At group level higher inattention accompanies lower, not preserved, measured ability, which complicates any assumption that strong ability implies masked impairment.
quality_reason: Large meta-analysis with overlap-controlled modelling, downgraded for exclusively cross-sectional data and imprecise sub-analyses.

citation: Nicole E Stuart, Andrew M C Sheridan, Carmela F Pestell, Gilles E Gignac, Charlotte Fox, Nicholas Badcock, et al. Hyperactivity-impulsivity, inattention, and cognitive disengagement syndrome: A meta-analytic investigation of overlapping and differential cognitive associations. Journal of psychopathology and clinical science. 2026;135(6):806-831. doi:10.1037/abn0001121. PMID:41989410.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 cross-sectional studies, with multiple regression on pooled correlation matrices to control symptom overlap
population: Children and adults from clinical and community samples; total N not reported in abstract
exposure_intervention: Symptom dimensions of ADHD-inattention (ADHD-I), ADHD-hyperactivity/impulsivity (ADHD-HI) and cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS)
comparator: Each symptom dimension after controlling shared variance with the other dimensions
outcome: Cognitive correlates including social cognition, motor coordination, perceptual-motor functioning, attention, inhibition, working memory, processing speed
main_result: Profiles looked similar in bivariate correlations but diverged in regression: ADHD-HI was associated with weaker social cognition and focused/sustained attention yet better motor coordination; ADHD-I with weaker intelligence, perceptual reasoning, inhibition, working memory, perceptual-motor functioning and memory; CDS with poorer interference control and processing speed.
effect_estimate: ADHD-HI: social cognition and attention betas -.24 to -.11 (p<.001); motor coordination beta = .14 (p<.001). ADHD-I: betas -.21 to -.10 (p<.01). CDS: betas -.29 to -.13 (p<.001).
major_limitations: All constituent studies cross-sectional; low precision for some pooled estimates; dimensions defined by rating scales rather than diagnoses; pooling across child and adult samples; laboratory/rating cognitive proxies rather than real-world social or motor functioning.
individual_applicability: Relevant to an adult reporting both inattentive and hyperactive features, but findings are group-level, symptom-scale based, and cannot attribute this person's social or motor difficulties to a specific dimension.
quality_reason: Large synthesis that explicitly controls construct overlap, but restricted to cross-sectional data with imprecision in several pooled estimates.

citation: Yujuan Zu, Tao Pang, Lingxue Luo, Chao Liufu, Zixuan Xu, Luxian Lv, et al. Dynamic relationship and pleiotropic loci of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with sleep traits. Translational psychiatry. 2026;10.1038/s41398-026-04166-4. doi:10.1038/s41398-026-04166-4. PMID:42297780.
study_design: Longitudinal cohort analysis (ABCD) with latent growth curve modelling, polygenic scores and pleiotropy analyses
population: 11,288 children/adolescents (52.1% male) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
exposure_intervention: ADHD symptoms, ADHD medication status, and genetic liability; sleep assessed with the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children
comparator: Within-cohort longitudinal contrasts and cross-cohort genetic comparison (UK Biobank insomnia)
outcome: Sleep disturbance traits over time and shared genetic loci
main_result: ADHD and sleep traits were positively correlated, ADHD medication weakened the association, and ADHD symptoms significantly predicted later sleep traits with a lag effect; polygenic associations were significant but explained very little variance and 14 pleiotropic loci were identified.
effect_estimate: Polygenic scores explained approximately 0.28-0.30% of variance; other estimates NR
major_limitations: Paediatric/adolescent sample, parent/self-reported sleep scale, lagged associations do not prove causation, very small genetic effect sizes; medication effects potentially confounded.
individual_applicability: Supports the counterclaim that ADHD symptom severity and treatment can drive apparent sleep problems rather than the reverse, an important alternative for the case's temporal interpretation.
quality_reason: Very large longitudinal cohort with genetic triangulation, but subjective sleep measure, non-adult sample and minimal explained variance.

citation: Simin Kang, Zhao Fu, Zili Fan, Xiao Sun, Li Yang, Qingjiu Cao. Predicting adult functional outcomes in childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder using multimodal MRI and machine learning: A prospective follow-up study. Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry. 2026;147:111702. doi:10.1016/j.pnpbp.2026.111702. PMID:41985649.
study_design: Prospective follow-up study with machine-learning prediction (random forest) using baseline clinical and multimodal MRI features
population: 104 children with ADHD followed into adulthood; mean follow-up 8.2 years
exposure_intervention: Childhood clinical characteristics, structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI
comparator: Within-cohort contrast of better versus worse adult functional outcome; no non-ADHD control group
outcome: Adult global functioning (Global Assessment of Functioning)
main_result: Adult functional outcomes in childhood-onset ADHD were heterogeneous and predictable above chance; multimodal models outperformed clinical-only models, indicating persisting but variable functional impairment into adulthood.
effect_estimate: AUC 0.816 (multimodal), 0.778 (rs-fMRI), 0.611 (sMRI), 0.589 (clinical only); confidence intervals NR
major_limitations: No healthy comparison group; modest sample for machine learning; outcome dichotomised; possible overfitting; external validation NR.
individual_applicability: Illustrates that adult functional outcome after childhood ADHD is variable, not uniform, which tempers deterministic persistence assumptions for any one person.
quality_reason: Prospective design but small N for predictive modelling, no control group, and prediction rather than persistence estimation as the primary aim.

citation: Fredrik Serenius, Thomas Abrahamsson, Ulrika Ådén, Kerstin Hellgren, Karin Sävman, Andreas Ohlin, et al. Neurodevelopmental Outcomes 12 Years After Extremely Preterm Birth in Sweden. Pediatrics. 2026;157(3):e2025073742. doi:10.1542/peds.2025-073742. PMID:41638598.
study_design: National prospective population-based cohort (EXPRESS) with term-born comparison group, assessed at age 12 using standardised instruments and national register diagnoses
population: 462 of 492 surviving children born before 27 weeks' gestation in Sweden (April 2004-March 2007) and 373 term-born controls
exposure_intervention: Extremely preterm birth
comparator: Term-born controls
outcome: Moderate/severe neurodevelopmental disability, ASD, ADHD, developmental coordination disorder, behaviour problems, and multimorbidity at age 12
main_result: Extremely preterm children had markedly higher rates of every outcome than controls, and co-occurrence was the norm among those with moderate/severe disability; a substantial minority nonetheless had no ASD, ADHD or DCD diagnosis.
effect_estimate: Moderate/severe NDD 37.4% vs 4.6%; ASD 14.9% vs 2.41%; ADHD 21.2% vs 8.9%; DCD 29.4% vs 5.7%; behaviour problems 35.3% vs 8.13% (all p<.001). 59% of EPT children with moderate/severe NDD had at least two co-occurring conditions; 24.9% with no/mild disability had comorbidity. Pairwise ADHD-DCD overlap NR.
major_limitations: High-risk perinatal population limits generalisability to idiopathic presentations; ADHD and ASD partly register-ascertained; outcomes at age 12 with no adult follow-up in this report; the specific ADHD-and-DCD co-occurrence proportion is not given.
individual_applicability: Demonstrates that neurodevelopmental multimorbidity including DCD is common and that perinatal history is a major competing explanation, so birth history should be established before attributing motor difficulty to idiopathic DCD.
quality_reason: Near-complete national cohort with a concurrent term-born control group and standardised cognitive, motor and behavioural instruments.

citation: Natalia G Docteur, Hayley G P Huston, Avery A Krupa, Brandy L Callahan. A systematic review of neuroimaging studies of adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic and genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2026;28(1):259-276. doi:10.1080/19585969.2026.2700984. PMID:42472451.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review of neuroimaging studies; 13 studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal
population: Adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD
exposure_intervention: ADHD diagnosis, symptom load or polygenic risk
comparator: Non-ADHD control participants
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations; cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD-associated fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic alterations persisted into middle and older adulthood, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation interpreted as compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR; 11 of 13 studies rated low risk of bias
major_limitations: Small number of heterogeneous studies; compensation is an interpretation of activation patterns, not a measured behavioural compensation outcome; cross-sectional designs predominate.
individual_applicability: Consistent with a neurodevelopmental substrate persisting in adulthood, but neuroimaging group differences cannot diagnose or characterise one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with formal risk-of-bias appraisal and mostly low-risk studies, downgraded for few studies and indirect outcomes.

citation: Natalia G Docteur, Hayley G P Huston, Avery A Krupa, Brandy L Callahan. A systematic review of neuroimaging studies of adults aged 35 and older with clinical, symptomatic and genetic risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2026;28(1):259-276. doi:10.1080/19585969.2026.2700984. PMID:42472451.
study_design: Preregistered systematic review of 13 neuroimaging studies; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale risk of bias (11 of 13 low risk)
population: Adults aged 35 years and older with clinical, symptomatic or genetic risk for ADHD, compared with controls; total N NR
exposure_intervention: Clinical ADHD diagnosis, elevated ADHD symptoms, or ADHD genetic risk in middle and later life
comparator: Controls without ADHD diagnosis or elevated ADHD risk
outcome: Structural and functional brain alterations, with summarised cognitive and clinical correlates
main_result: ADHD groups showed alterations in fronto-striatal, fronto-parietal and limbic systems implicated in executive control and attention; middle-aged adults with clinical ADHD showed more widespread cortical structural differences whereas older adults showed mainly frontal abnormalities, and two functional studies reported frontal hypoactivation with parietal hyperactivation consistent with compensatory recruitment.
effect_estimate: NR (narrative synthesis; no pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals reported)
major_limitations: Only 13 mostly cross-sectional studies, no control for current mood state, sleep or substance exposure, imaging-to-function inference is uncertain, and the authors state that longitudinal investigation is needed to clarify persistence.
individual_applicability: Consistent with ADHD-associated neurobiology persisting into mid-life, which is the age band of this case, but imaging group differences do not establish trait-level functional impairment in one person.
quality_reason: Preregistered review with mostly low-risk-of-bias studies, downgraded for small number of cross-sectional studies, absent state controls, and narrative synthesis.
